Turkey's annual [[greenhouse gas emissions]] are over 1% of the global total,<ref>{{cite web |title=Each Country's Share of CO2 Emissions |url=https://www.ucsusa.org/global-warming/science-and-impacts/science/each-countrys-share-of-co2.html |publisher=Union of Concerned Scientists |access-date=16 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181124214635/https://www.ucsusa.org/global-warming/science-and-impacts/science/each-countrys-share-of-co2.html |archive-date=24 November 2018 |url-status=live}}</ref> and [[energy policy of Turkey|energy policy]] includes [[energy subsidies#Turkey|subsidizing]] both [[fossil gas in Turkey|fossil gas]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ergur |first=Semih |date=2023-05-12 |title=Turkey Spent Over $200,000,000 in Fossil Fuel Subsidies in 2022 |url=https://www.climatescorecard.org/2023/05/turkey-spent-over-200000000-in-fossil-fuel-subsidies-in-2022/ |access-date=2023-11-30 |website=Climate Scorecard |language=en-US |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231212202730/https://www.climatescorecard.org/2023/05/turkey-spent-over-200000000-in-fossil-fuel-subsidies-in-2022/ |archive-date=12 December 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref> and [[coal in Turkey|coal]].<ref name="OECD">{{Cite web |title=Fossil Fuel Support - TUR |url=https://stats.oecd.org/Index.aspx?DataSetCode=FFS_TUR |access-date=2023-11-30 |website=stats.oecd.org |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112004527/https://stats.oecd.org/Index.aspx?DataSetCode=FFS_TUR |archive-date=12 November 2020 |url-status=live}}</ref> Per person emissions since the late-2010s have varied around six and a half&nbsp;[[tonne]]s a year,<ref name=":46">{{Cite web |title=Greenhouse Gas Emissions Statistics, 1990-2024 |url=https://veriportali.tuik.gov.tr/en/press/58000 |access-date=2026-04-22 |website=[[Turkish Statistical Institute]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260425234106/https://veriportali.tuik.gov.tr/en/press/58000 |archive-date=25 April 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> which is about [[List of countries by greenhouse gas emissions per person|the global average]].<ref name="Website-3">{{Cite web |title=Are per capita CO₂ emissions above or below the global average? |url=https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/per-capita-co2-vs-average |access-date=2024-06-05 |website=Our World in Data |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260220201646/https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/per-capita-co2-vs-average |archive-date=20 February 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> However historical emissions are less than 1% of the global total.<ref>{{Cite web |website=Türkiye Cumhuriyeti Cumhurbaşkanlıği |title=2053 yılı itibarıyla net sıfır emisyon hedefini gerçekleştirmeyi öngörüyoruz |url=https://www.tccb.gov.tr/haberler/410/150389/-2053-yili-itibariyla-net-sifir-emisyon-hedefini-gerceklestirmeyi-ongoruyoruz- |access-date=2023-12-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231202050714/https://www.tccb.gov.tr/haberler/410/150389/-2053-yili-itibariyla-net-sifir-emisyon-hedefini-gerceklestirmeyi-ongoruyoruz- |archive-date=2 December 2023 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The [[Ministry of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change#Directorate of Climate Change|Directorate of Climate Change]] co-ordinates [[Climate change adaptation|adaptation to climate change]], which has been planned for water resources by [[river basin]], and for [[Agriculture in Turkey|agriculture]]. Certificate caps in [[Turkish Emissions Trading System|the emission trading system]] are unclear as of 2026. Housing is not energy efficient, the pathway to the 2053 [[Net-zero emissions|net zero]] target is unclear, and there is no plan for [[coal phase-out]].<ref name="Bosse1">{{Cite web |last=Bosse |first=Jolana |date=2025-11-18 |title=Türkiye – Climate Performance Ranking 2026 {{!}} Climate Change Performance Index |url=https://ccpi.org/country/tur/ |access-date=2026-07-26 |language=en-US |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251228025452/https://ccpi.org/country/tur/ |archive-date=28 December 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>__TOC__

== Greenhouse gas emissions ==
[[File:Control room of Zetes-3 power station.jpg|thumb|Coal-fired power stations, such as the [[ZETES power stations]], are the largest source of greenhouse gas.<ref name="2021report">{{cite tech report 
 |work=[[Turkish Statistical Institute]]
 |title=Turkish Greenhouse Gas Inventory 1990 - 2021 [TurkStat report]
 |date=14 April 2023
 |url=https://unfccc.int/documents/627786
 }}</ref>{{Rp|459}}]]

[[Coal in Turkey|Coal]], cars and lorries vent more than a third of [[Turkey]]'s annual [[greenhouse gas emissions]], which total about six hundred million tonnes.<ref name=":46" /><ref name=":53">{{Cite web |title=Country/Territory Inventory - Turkey |url=https://climatetrace.org/inventory?region=T%C3%BCrkiye+%28TUR%29%3A247%3ATUR%3Acountry&timeframe=100 |access-date=2026-02-27 |website=[[Climate TRACE]] |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251008170024/https://climatetrace.org/inventory?region=T%C3%BCrkiye+(TUR):247:TUR:country&timeframe=100 |archive-date=8 October 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>  They are mostly [[carbon dioxide]] and part of the cause of climate change in Turkey. A quarter of the emissions are from [[Electricity sector in Turkey|electricity generation]].<ref name=":55" />{{Rp|location=section 4.2.1}}

The government estimated 2024 emissions at 517.4 Mt with and 584.5 Mt without LULUCF,<ref name="2026report">{{cite tech report 
 |work=[[Turkish Statistical Institute]]
 |title=Greenhouse Gas Inventory of Türkiye 1990 - 2024
 |date=April 2026
 |url=https://unfccc.int/documents/656425
 }}
 </ref>{{Reference page|page=v}} and uncertainty at 7.9%, or 5.1% without LULUCF.<ref name="2026report" />{{Reference page|page=23}} [[Climate Trace]] estimate 646 million tonnes (Mt) of GHG was emitted in 2025 excluding [[land use, land-use change, and forestry]],<ref name=":53" /> and 43 Mt from LULUCF.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Country/Territory Inventory - Turkey |url=https://climatetrace.org/ |access-date=2026-09-25 |website=[[Climate TRACE]] |language=en}}</ref> Their estimate of 72 Mt of GHG from waste in 2023 and 2024 and 2025<ref name="Climate TRACE">{{Cite web |title=Climate TRACE |url=https://climatetrace.org/ |access-date=2026-02-27 |website=Climate TRACE |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260122113914/https://climatetrace.org/ |archive-date=22 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> is much higher than the official figure of 15 Mt in 2023 and 2024.<ref name=":46" /> Official figures do not detail individual sources, but the largest in 2025 according to Climate Trace were [[ZETES power stations]], [[Istanbul Airport]], [[Cenal power station]], [[İÇDAŞ Biga power station]] and [[Isdemir Payas steel plant]].<ref name="Climate TRACE" /> The [[Transnational Institute]] estimated 2023 military emissions at 4.7 million tonnes,<ref>{{Cite web| title=Climate in the crosshairs - The planetary impact of NATO's spending increases | url=https://www.tni.org/files/2024-07/Climate%20in%20the%20Crosshairs.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240709130109/https://www.tni.org/files/2024-07/Climate%20in%20the%20Crosshairs.pdf | archive-date=2024-07-09}}</ref> but this estimate may not have used official [[NATO]] methodology.<ref>{{Cite web| title=The NATO Greenhouse Gases Emission Mapping and Analytical Methodology | url=https://www.nato.int/nato_static_fl2014/assets/pdf/2023/7/pdf/230710-NATO-GHG-Methodology.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230712125955/https://www.nato.int/nato_static_fl2014/assets/pdf/2023/7/pdf/230710-NATO-GHG-Methodology.pdf | archive-date=2023-07-12}}</ref> 

The energy sector, including [[Transport in Turkey|transport]], emitted 420 million tonnes in 2024.<ref name=":46" /> [[List of active coal-fired power stations in Turkey|The nation's coal-fired power stations]] emit the most carbon dioxide, and road vehicles running on [[gasoline|petrol]] or [[diesel fuel|diesel]] are also significant. After coal<ref name=":49">{{Cite news |date=15 November 2022 |title=Turkey's Climate Plan Points to 32% Rise in Emissions by 2030 |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-11-15/turkey-s-climate-plan-points-to-32-rise-in-emissions-by-2030?leadSource=uverify%20wall |access-date=2022-11-15 |newspaper=Bloomberg |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221115142245/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-11-15/turkey-s-climate-plan-points-to-32-rise-in-emissions-by-2030?leadSource=uverify%20wall |archive-date=15 November 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref> and [[oil in Turkey|oil]] the third most polluting [[fossil fuel|fuel]] is [[gas in Turkey|fossil gas]]; which is burnt in [[List of power stations in Turkey#Natural Gas|Turkey's gas-fired power stations]], homes and workplaces. Much [[methane emissions from livestock|methane is belched by livestock]]; cows alone produce half of the greenhouse gas from [[agriculture in Turkey]].<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table 3 Cells I12 and I20}}

Economists say that major reasons for Turkey's greenhouse gas emissions are [[Coal subsidies in Turkey|subsidies for coal-fired power stations]],<ref name=":43">{{Cite web|title=Still Not Getting Energy Prices Right: A Global and Country Update of Fossil Fuel Subsidies|url=https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/WP/Issues/2021/09/23/Still-Not-Getting-Energy-Prices-Right-A-Global-and-Country-Update-of-Fossil-Fuel-Subsidies-466004|access-date=2021-10-06|website=IMF|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230111182236/https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/WP/Issues/2021/09/23/Still-Not-Getting-Energy-Prices-Right-A-Global-and-Country-Update-of-Fossil-Fuel-Subsidies-466004|archive-date=11 January 2023|url-status=live}}</ref>{{Rp|18}}<ref>{{Cite web |author=Prashant Vaze |author2=Archie Gilmour |author3=Bengisu Ozenc |author4=Evrim Ozyorulmaz-Akcura |date=2024-12-25 |title=Low-Carbon Transition Risks Facing Coal in Türkiye |url=https://sefia.org/en/publications/low-carbon-transition-risks-facing-coal-in-turkiye/ |access-date=2025-04-06 |website=SEFiA |language=en-US |quote=These capacity payments have grown markedly over time and now provide an important revenue line for local coal (1.16 billion Turkish lira (TL) in 2023) and gas power (TL2.5 billion). |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251210205842/https://sefia.org/en/publications/low-carbon-transition-risks-facing-coal-in-turkiye/ |archive-date=10 December 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> and the lack of a [[Turkish Emissions Trading System|price on carbon pollution]].<ref name=":44">{{Cite journal|last1=Steckel|first1=Jan C.|last2=Dorband|first2=Ira I.|last3=Montrone|first3=Lorenzo|last4=Ward|first4=Hauke|last5=Missbach|first5=Leonard|last6=Hafner|first6=Fabian|last7=Jakob|first7=Michael|last8=Renner|first8=Sebastian|date=23 September |hdl=1887/3238835|hdl-access=free}}</ref>{{Rp|1}}

Turkey's [[List of countries by greenhouse gas emissions|share of current global greenhouse gas emissions]] is slightly over 1%.<ref>{{Cite web |title=EDGAR - The Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research |url=https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/report_2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260103095711/https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/report_2025 |archive-date=2026-01-03 |access-date=2026-01-19 |website=edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu |language=en}}</ref> Annual per person emissions are six and a half&nbsp;[[tonne]]s,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-09-28 |title=Total greenhouse gas emissions (without LULUCF) |url=https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/europe-environment-2025/countries/turkiye/total-greenhouse-gas-emissions |access-date=2026-01-19 |website=www.eea.europa.eu |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260214224505/https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/europe-environment-2025/countries/turkiye/total-greenhouse-gas-emissions |archive-date=14 February 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> which is around [[List of countries by greenhouse gas emissions per person|the global average]].<ref name="Website-3" /> Although greenhouse gas totals are reported some details, such as the split between cars and lorries, are not published.<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|page=Table1.A(a)s3 Col G}}

The government supports [[Reforestation#Turkey|reforestation]], [[Automotive industry in Turkey|electric vehicle manufacturing]] and [[Low-carbon power|low-carbon]] [[Electricity sector in Turkey|electricity generation]]; and is aiming for [[Carbon neutrality|net zero carbon emissions]] by 2053. But its long-term plan omits [[coal phase-out]],<ref name=":55">{{Cite report |date=November 2024 |title=2053 long term climate strategy |url=https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/Turkiye_Long_Term_Climate_Strategy.pdf |publisher=[[Ministry of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251113110826/https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/Turkiye_Long_Term_Climate_Strategy.pdf |archive-date=13 November 2025 |access-date=22 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":39">{{Cite web |date=2024-11-11 |title=Türkiye iklim yol haritasını paylaştı, 2053'e kadar 'net sıfır' gerçekçi mi? |url=https://www.bbc.com/turkce/articles/cjw092p8356o |access-date=2024-11-11 |website=BBC News Türkçe |language=tr |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251218234853/https://www.bbc.com/turkce/articles/cjw092p8356o |archive-date=18 December 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> and there is no clear pathway to net zero.<ref name="Bosse1" /> Turkey's [[Nationally Determined Contributions|nationally determined contribution]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=NDC 3.0 {{!}} UNFCCC |url=https://unfccc.int/ndc-3.0 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250204033728/https://unfccc.int/ndc-3.0 |archive-date=2025-02-04 |access-date=2025-02-11 |website=unfccc.int |language=en}}</ref> to the [[Paris Agreement]] on [[Climate change mitigation|limiting climate change]] is 643 million tonnes in 2035,<ref>{{Cite news |title=Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan BM İklim Zirvesi'nde konuştu |url=https://www.iletisim.gov.tr/turkce/haberler/detay/cumhurbaskani-erdogan-bm-iklim-zirvesinde-konustu |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260729153917/https://www.iletisim.gov.tr/turkce/haberler/detay/cumhurbaskani-erdogan-bm-iklim-zirvesinde-konustu |archive-date=2026-07-29 |access-date=2026-07-29 |language=tr-TR}}</ref> which has been criticised as an increase on current emissions. In 2024 environment minister [[Murat Kurum]] said that by Turkey's [[Net-zero emissions|net zero]] year of 2053 half of primary energy would be from renewables and 30% from [[Nuclear power in Turkey|nuclear]], but did not explain how the remaining 20% could be decarbonised.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Türkiye plans to increase renewable energy to reach 50% of primary energy by 2053 |url=https://www.aa.com.tr/en/environment/turkiye-plans-to-increase-renewable-energy-to-reach-50-of-primary-energy-by-2053/3392926 |access-date=2024-12-16 |website=www.aa.com.tr |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251211102206/https://www.aa.com.tr/en/environment/turkiye-plans-to-increase-renewable-energy-to-reach-50-of-primary-energy-by-2053/3392926 |archive-date=11 December 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Paris in dreams, Baku in reality {{!}} Heinrich Böll Stiftung {{!}} Derneği Türkiye Temsilciliği |url=https://tr.boell.org/en/2024/12/17/paris-in-dreams-baku-in-reality |access-date=2025-03-06 |website=tr.boell.org |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260208203325/https://tr.boell.org/en/2024/12/17/paris-in-dreams-baku-in-reality |archive-date=8 February 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> Although [[Turkish Emissions Trading System|carbon emission trading]] is due to start its pilot phase,<ref>{{Cite report |title=Why a weak Turkish ETS fails both the climate and Turkish exporters |url=https://carbonmarketwatch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Turkish-ETS_final-version.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260513174711/https://carbonmarketwatch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Turkish-ETS_final-version.pdf |archive-date=13 May 2026 |access-date=26 July 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> unless Turkey's climate and energy policies are changed the 2053 net zero target may be missed.<ref>{{cite web |title=Global climate policy forecast predicts 'well below 2°C' Paris Agreement climate goals will be met |work=PRI |url=https://www.unpri.org/news-and-press/global-climate-policy-forecast-predicts-well-below-2c-paris-agreement-climate-goals-will-be-met/11790.article |access-date=22 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250727053329/https://www.unpri.org/news-and-press/global-climate-policy-forecast-predicts-well-below-2c-paris-agreement-climate-goals-will-be-met/11790.article |archive-date=27 July 2025 |url-status=dead}}</ref>
[[File:Ghg pie chart Turkey.svg|thumb|alt=Chart showing the top sources of greenhouse gases are, in order: coal-fired electricity, road transport, home fuel, cement, cattle and gas-fired electricity|Coal-fired power stations emit the most, followed by diesel fuel burned in lorries and other road vehicles.]]

Turkey emitted 585&nbsp;Mt of GHG in 2024.<ref name=":46" /> Istanbul Policy Center has suggested a total national [[carbon budget]] of about 13 Gt after 2023, as a part of the global carbon budget to keep below 2 degrees.<ref name=":30">{{Cite report |title=Turkey's Decarbonization Roadmap: Towards Net Zero by 2053 |url=https://ipc.sabanciuniv.edu/Content/Images/CKeditorImages/20251001-15101101.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260426222314/https://ipc.sabanciuniv.edu/Content/Images/CKeditorImages/20251001-15101101.pdf |archive-date=26 April 2026 |access-date=22 April 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=5}} Per-person emissions are around the world average,<ref name="Website-3" /> at around 7 t in 2024.<ref name=":46" /> Turkey's cumulative CO<sub>2</sub> emissions are estimated at around 13&nbsp;Gt, which is less than 1% of the world's cumulative total (Turkey's population is about 1% of world population).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/cumulative-co-emissions?country=~TUR|title=Cumulative CO₂ emissions &#124; Our World in Data}}</ref> Turkey's emissions can be looked at differently to the standard IPCC classification: for example a 2021 study by [[İzmir University of Economics|Izmir University of Economics]] estimated that food, "from farm to fork", accounts for about a third of national emissions,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Üçtuğ|first1=Fehmi Görkem|last2=Günaydin|first2=Dorukhan|last3=Hünkar|first3=Beliz|last4=Öngelen|first4=Cansu|date=1 April 2021|title=Carbon footprints of omnivorous, vegetarian, and vegan diets based on traditional Turkish cuisine|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2352550920314263|journal=Sustainable Production and Consumption|volume=26|pages=597–609|doi=10.1016/j.spc.2020.12.027|bibcode=2021SusPC..26..597G |s2cid=230577702|issn=2352-5509|access-date=16 February 2021|archive-date=17 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210417022658/https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2352550920314263|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref> which is similar to the global emissions share of food.<ref>{{cite web|last=Lynch|first=John|title=Global food system emissions alone threaten warming beyond 1.5°C – but we can act now to stop it|url=http://theconversation.com/global-food-system-emissions-alone-threaten-warming-beyond-1-5-c-but-we-can-act-now-to-stop-it-149312|access-date=17 March 2021|website=[[The Conversation (website)|The Conversation]]|date=5 November 2020 |archive-date=1 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210301234607/https://theconversation.com/global-food-system-emissions-alone-threaten-warming-beyond-1-5-c-but-we-can-act-now-to-stop-it-149312|url-status=live}}</ref>
=== Monitoring, reporting and verification ===

[[File:Ghg gases by year Turkey.svg|thumb|alt=Graph showing the types of greenhouse gases emitted by Turkey |As in most countries carbon dioxide, mostly from burning fossil fuels, is the main GHG]]

[[Greenhouse gas monitoring|Monitoring]], reporting and verification (MRV) includes tracking national GHG emissions and action to limit them,<ref>{{Cite web |title=What is MRV? {{!}} MRV |url=http://carbon-turkey.org/en/what-is-mrv |access-date=2026-10-06 |website=carbon-turkey.org |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260829171647/http://carbon-turkey.org/en/what-is-mrv |archive-date=29 August 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> and sharing information and lessons learned.<ref>{{Cite web|title=What is MRV?|url=https://www.carbon-turkey.org/en/what-is-mrv|access-date=6 September 2021|website=www.carbon-turkey.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210729215239/https://carbon-turkey.org/en/what-is-mrv|archive-date=29 July 2021|url-status=dead}}</ref> The [[Directorate of Climate Change]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=iklim.gov.tr |title=About Us - İklim Değişikliği Başkanlığı |url=https://iklim.gov.tr/en/about-us-i-75#:~:text=Directorate%20of%20Climate%20Change&text=It%20is%20responsible%20for%20determining,change%20mitigation%20and%20adaptation%20efforts. |access-date=2024-12-16 |website=iklim.gov.tr |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260217074919/https://iklim.gov.tr/en/about-us-i-75#:~:text=Directorate%20of%20Climate%20Change&text=It%20is%20responsible%20for%20determining,change%20mitigation%20and%20adaptation%20efforts. |archive-date=17 February 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> and [[Turkish Statistical Institute|Turkish government's Statistical Institute]] (Turkstat) follow the [[United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change]] (UNFCCC) reporting guidelines, so use [[Greenhouse gas emissions accounting#Production-based accounting|production-based GHG accounting]] to compile the country's [[greenhouse gas inventory]]. Using [[Greenhouse gas emissions accounting#Consumption-based accounting|consumption-based accounting]] would give a similar total.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Territorial and consumption-based CO₂ emissions, Turkey |url=https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/production-vs-consumption-co2-emissions?country=~TUR |access-date=22 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241218195010/https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/production-vs-consumption-co2-emissions?country=~TUR |archive-date=18 December 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> Turkstat sends the data to the UNFCCC annually during the second year following the reported year, for example 2023 emissions were reported in 2025 in the annual National Inventory Document (NID) and Common Reporting Tables (CRT).<ref>{{cite web|title=Reporting requirements|url=https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/transparency-and-reporting/reporting-and-review-under-the-convention/greenhouse-gas-inventories-annex-i-parties/reporting-requirements|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200810200216/https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/transparency-and-reporting/reporting-and-review-under-the-convention/greenhouse-gas-inventories-annex-i-parties/reporting-requirements|archive-date=10 August 2020|access-date=8 October 2019|website=[[UNFCCC]]}}</ref> In years when a [[Biennial transparency report]] (BTR) is submitted to the UNFCCC the data may be included with the report, as was done in 2024 with Turkey's first BTR.<ref name=":48">{{Cite report |date=November 2024 |title=First Biennial Transparency Report of Türkiye |url=https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/T%C3%BCrkiye_1BTR.pdf |publisher=[[Ministry of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241111090312/https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/T%C3%BCrkiye_1BTR.pdf |archive-date=11 November 2024 |access-date=22 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> Emissions from fuels sold in the country for international aviation and shipping are accounted separately in reports to the UNFCCC, and are not included in a country's total.<ref name="2021report" />{{Rp|46}} In 2024 [[jet kerosene]], supplied at Turkish airports and burnt by international flights, emitted 15&nbsp;Mt [[Global warming potential|{{CO2}}e (carbon dioxide equivalent)]];<ref name="2026report" />{{Reference page|page=54}} (there are also indirect effects from [[Contrail|contrails]] and [[ozone]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Carbon Footprint and Environmental Health Impacts of Airline Fleets: The Case of Turkish Airlines |url=https://jast.msu.edu.tr/index.php/JAST/article/view/685/464}}</ref>) and [[diesel oil]] and [[residual fuel oil]] from Turkish ports powering international shipping 2 Mt&nbsp;{{CO2}}e.<ref name="2026report" />{{Reference page|page=55}}

The [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]] (IPCC) defines three methodological tiers to measure emissions. Tier 1 uses global defaults and simplified assumptions, so is the easiest but least accurate. Tier 2 uses country specific values and more detailed data. Tier 3 uses the most detailed data and modelling, so is the most difficult to compile but the most accurate. To make best use of human resources each nation may decide to only use higher tiers to estimate its particular "key categories". Turkstat selects these categories depending on either the absolute level of emissions from that category, or whether it is trending, or uncertain.<ref name="2021report" />{{Rp|439}} For example, CO2 from [[Lime (material)|lime]] production was a key category for 2024 solely because of its quickly rising emissions: most of the key categories selected in 2024 are both trending up and the largest emitting sectors, [[Cement kiln|cement production]] for example.<ref name="2026report" />{{Reference page|page=22}} Turkey uses Tier 2 and Tier 3 methodology for some key categories, for example a power plant might [[Coal assay|analyse the lignite]] it burns, which differs from mine to mine.<ref name="2021report" />{{Rp|72}} Turkey has a high rate of car ownership even in urban areas,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=OECD |date=2025-09-25 |title=Decarbonising Health Systems Across OECD Countries |url=https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/decarbonising-health-systems-across-oecd-countries_5ac2b24b-en.html |journal=OECD Health Policy Studies |language=en |doi=10.1787/5ac2b24b-en |isbn=978-92-64-89270-5 |url-access=subscription |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260114133316/https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/decarbonising-health-systems-across-oecd-countries_5ac2b24b-en.html |archive-date=14 January 2026 |access-date=22 January 2026 |url-status=live }}</ref>{{Reference page|page=31}}and although road transport is a key category, it is not split between cars and lorries as is done in some countries. In 2021 the UNFCCC asked Turkey why it reported negligible indirect GHGs ([[carbon monoxide]], [[nitrogen oxides]], non-methane [[volatile organic compounds]] and [[sulfur oxides]]) in 2018.<ref name=":24">{{cite tech report |url=https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/trr4_TUR.pdf |title=Report on the technical review of the fourth biennial report of Turkey |date=2 June 2021 |work=[[UNFCCC]] |id=FCCC/TRR.4/TUR}}</ref>{{Rp|12}} Legislation for the [[Turkish Emissions Trading System]] to monitor some private sector emissions was passed in 2026, but does not include methane from [[biomass]] such as [[Waste management in Turkey|waste]].<ref name=":31">{{Cite news |last1=Carrington |first1=Damian |last2=Michaelson |first2=Ruth |last3=Aldatmaz |first3=Ayça |date=2026-10-05 |title=Revealed: the methane mega-leaks from UN climate summit host Turkey |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/05/methane-mega-leaks-from-un-climate-summit-host-turkey |access-date=2026-10-05 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

=== Greenhouse gas sources ===
==== Fossil fuels ====
{{See also|Energy in Turkey}}
[[File:CO₂ emissions by fuel or industry, Turkey, OWID chart.png|thumb|alt=Graph shows carbon dioxide emitted by coal, oil, and natural gas over the years from 1990|Emissions from gas increased, but remain far below coal. Emissions from oil products, such as petrol and diesel, increased more slowly than gas and coal.]]

Burning [[coal in Turkey]] was the largest emitter in 2024, followed by [[Oil in Turkey|oil]] then [[Gas in Turkey|gas]].<ref name="2026report" />{{Reference page|page=52}} That year, Turkey's energy sector emitted over 70% of the country's GHG,<ref name=":46" /> mostly through electricity generation,<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table1.A(a)s1 Cell G31}} followed by road transport.{{efn|1=Under IPCC guidelines, the energy sector includes fuel for transport.}}<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table1.A(a)s3 Cell G20}} In contrast agriculture contributed 13% of emissions and industrial processes and product use (IPPU) also 13%.<ref name=":46" /> [[Carbon capture and storage]] is not economically viable.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Esmaeili |first1=Danial |date=June 2018 |title=Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage in the Context of Turkish Energy Market |publisher=[[Sabancı University]] |url=http://research.sabanciuniv.edu/36807/1/1806_IICECE%26CPaperCCUSinTurkey_0.pdf |page=15 |quote=Having an emissions trading market is critical for a successful implementation of the carbon capturing technology in Turkey. |access-date=14 May 2019 |archive-date=14 May 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190514155754/http://research.sabanciuniv.edu/36807/1/1806_IICECE%26CPaperCCUSinTurkey_0.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> The GHG [[emission intensity]] of energy consumption is higher than in the EU.<ref>{{Cite web |title=European Innovation Scoreboard 2022 |url=https://ec.europa.eu/assets/rtd/eis/2022/ec_rtd_eis-country-profile-tr.pdf |access-date=22 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251112164850/https://ec.europa.eu/assets/rtd/eis/2022/ec_rtd_eis-country-profile-tr.pdf |archive-date=12 November 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Turkey expects to greatly increase gas production.<ref>{{cite web|last=O'Byrne|first=David|date=21 April 2021|title=Turkey to begin field tests at Sakarya gas find next month: minister|url=https://www.spglobal.com/platts/en/market-insights/latest-news/natural-gas/042121-turkey-to-begin-field-tests-at-sakarya-gas-find-next-month-minister|access-date=15 May 2021|website=[[S&P Global Platts]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210515110955/https://www.spglobal.com/platts/en/market-insights/latest-news/natural-gas/042121-turkey-to-begin-field-tests-at-sakarya-gas-find-next-month-minister|archive-date=15 May 2021|url-status=live}}</ref> In 2021, IEA head [[Fatih Birol]] called for fossil-fuel producing countries to include limits on [[methane leaks]] in their climate pledges,<ref>{{cite web|title=IEA calls on companies, governments and regulators to take urgent action to cut methane emissions from oil and gas sector|url=https://www.iea.org/news/iea-calls-on-companies-governments-and-regulators-to-take-urgent-action-to-cut-methane-emissions-from-oil-and-gas-sector|access-date=15 May 2021|website=[[International Energy Agency|IEA]]|date=18 January 2021 }}</ref> but {{As of|2026|lc=y}} Turkey has not signed the [[Global Methane Pledge|global methane pledge]].<ref name=":31" />

Production of public heat and electricity emitted 150 [[Tonne#Symbol and abbreviations|megatonnes]] of {{CO2}}e in 2024,<ref name="2026table" />{{Rp|table 1 cell B10}} mainly through coal burning.{{efn|The carbon content ([[tonne|t]]/[[Terajoule|TJ]]), oxidation factor and CO<sub>2</sub> [[emission intensity]] (t/TJ [[Heat of combustion#Lower heating value|NCV]]), respectively, of lignite burnt in Turkish power stations in 2021 was as follows:<ref name=2021report/>{{Rp|50 & 51, table 3.5, 3.6, 3.7}}
* [[lignite]]: 30, 0.97, 104

The extremely low-quality lignite is explained in detail in [[Coal in Turkey]]. The {{CO2}} emission intensity (or emission factor) shown above is the mass of {{CO2}} emitted for each unit of heat produced by burning a fuel. In contrast, the grid emission intensity is the mass of {{CO2}}e produced per unit of electricity supplied to the [[electrical grid]]. Because [[thermal power station]]s generally convert less than half of the heat energy into electrical energy,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Zhang|first=Tongjun|date=2020|title=Methods of Improving the Efficiency of Thermal Power Plants|journal=J. Phys.: Conf. Ser.|language=en|volume=1449|issue=1|article-number=012001|doi=10.1088/1742-6596/1449/1/012001|bibcode=2020JPhCS1449a2001Z|doi-access=free}}</ref> their numbers for grid emission intensity are much greater than the emission intensity figures shown above.}} Investment in wind and [[Solar power in Turkey|solar]] is hampered by subsidies for coal.<ref>{{Cite report

{{anchor|Fuel to heat buildings and cook}}

Subsidised coal burnt by poor families contributes a bit to climate change, and more importantly its [[soot]] [[air pollution in Turkey|pollutes local air]]. Residential fuel, such as natural gas and coal, contributed 51&nbsp;Mt {{CO2}}e in 2024.<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table1.A(a)s4 G37}} Burning [[fossil fuels]] such as coal and natural gas for commercial and institutional buildings, such as for heating, emitted 13&nbsp;Mt {{CO2}}e in 2024.<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table1.A(a)s4 Cell G17}} According to the [[Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources (Turkey)|Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources]], "The energy sector, which is an emission-intensive and resource-intensive sector, will be one of the sectors that will be most affected by the regulations brought or to be brought by [the Paris and UNFCCC] agreements. In this context, our country is determined to use its energy resources effectively, efficiently and with the least impact on the environment, within the framework of sustainable development goals.".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Climate Change and International Negotiation |url=https://enerji.gov.tr/infobank-climate-change-and-international |access-date=2026-08-28 |website=[[Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200714212811/https://enerji.gov.tr/infobank-climate-change-and-international |archive-date=14 July 2020 |url-status=live}}</ref>{{efn|The goals they are referring to may be [[Sustainable Development Goal 7]] and [[Sustainable Development Goal 13]]}}

===== <span class="anchor" id="Coal fired power stations"></span>Coal-fired power stations =====
[[File:Yatağan Termik Santrali.jpg|thumb|Some old power stations like [[Yatağan power station|Yatağan]] pollute but are subsidised.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Turkey's electricity supply security and Akbelen |url=https://www.birgun.net/haber/turkeys-electricity-supply-security-and-akbelen-734155 |access-date=2026-10-07 |website=birgun.net |language=Turkish |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260911195835/http://www.birgun.net/haber/turkeys-electricity-supply-security-and-akbelen-734155 |archive-date=11 September 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>|alt=white smoke rises into a blue sky from 3 large chimneys]]
[[List of coal fired power stations in Turkey|Turkey's coal-fired power stations]] are the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions by Turkey, at 123 Mt (over 20% of national emissions) in 2024.<ref name="2026table">{{cite tech report 
 |work=[[Turkish Statistical Institute]]
 |title=Türkiye. 2026 Common Reporting Table (CRT)
 |date=14 April 2026
 |url=https://unfccc.int/documents/656426
 |format=TUR-CRT-2026-V1.0-2024
 }}</ref>{{Rp|table 1.A(a)s1 cell G26 "solid fuels"}} Over a kilogram of {{CO2}} is emitted for every [[Kilowatt-hour|KWh]] of electricity generated in Turkey by coal-fired power stations.<ref name="AtAz">{{cite journal |last1=Atilgan |first1=Burcin |last2=Azapagic |first2=Adisa |date=2016 |title=An integrated life cycle sustainability assessment of electricity generation in Turkey |journal=Energy Policy |volume=93 |pages=168–186 |bibcode=2016EnPol..93..168A |doi=10.1016/j.enpol.2016.02.055 |doi-access=free}}</ref>{{Rp|177}} 

Almost all coal burnt in power stations is local [[lignite]] or imported [[Bituminous coal|bituminous (hard) coal]]. [[Coal analysis]] of Turkish lignite shows that it is high in ash and moisture, low in [[energy value of coal|energy value]] and high in [[emission intensity]];<ref name=":38" /> that is Turkish lignite emits more {{CO2}} than other countries' lignites.<ref name=":38">{{Cite web|url=https://www.powerengineeringint.com/coal-fired/cfb-in-turkey-the-right-timing-for-the-right-technology/|title=CFB in Turkey: The right timing for the right technology|website=www.powerengineeringint.com|date=December 2017|access-date=8 September 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200801065509/https://www.powerengineeringint.com/coal-fired/cfb-in-turkey-the-right-timing-for-the-right-technology/|archive-date=1 August 2020|url-status=live}}</ref> When carbon dioxide ({{CO2}}) from coal used by industry and for heating buildings, and [[methane emissions]] from [[coal mining]], are added to those from coal-fired electricity generation, over 30% of Turkey's annual emissions come from coal. In 2024, burning coal emitted 159&nbsp;Mt {{CO2}} in total.<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table1.A(a)s1 Cell G12}} Methane leaks from coal mines in 2024 were equivalent to 7&nbsp;Mt {{CO2}}.<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table 1 Cell I39}} [[Eren Holding]] (via Eren Enerji's coal-fired [[ZETES power stations]]) emits over 2% of Turkey's GHG, and [[İÇDAŞ]] emits over 1% from its Bekirli coal-fired power stations.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Pearce|first1=Rosamund|last2=Evans|first2=Simon|title=Global coal power map|url=https://www.carbonbrief.org/mapped-worlds-coal-power-plants|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190205154748/https://www.carbonbrief.org/mapped-worlds-coal-power-plants|archive-date=5 February 2019|access-date=14 May 2020|website=[[Carbon Brief]]}}</ref> Emissions of [[black carbon]] are not published for individual power stations,<ref name=":21">{{Cite report|title=Cobenefits Policy Report: Unlocking the co-benefits of decarbonising Turkey's power sector|url=https://www.cobenefits.info/country-studies-infographics/studies/turkey/|date=December 2020|publisher=International Climate Initiative: IASS IPC/UfU|editor1-last=Akyazı|editor1-first=Pınar Ertör|editor2-last=Sperfeld|editor2-first=Franziska|editor3-last=Helgenberger|editor3-first=Sebastian|editor4-last=Şahin|editor4-first=Ümit|editor5-last=Nagel|editor5-first=Laura|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251201064032/https://www.cobenefits.info/country-studies-infographics/studies/turkey/|archive-date=1 December 2025|access-date=22 January 2026|url-status=live}}</ref>{{Rp|2}} as Turkey has not ratified the [[Gothenburg Protocol]] on air pollution.<ref>{{cite web|title=United Nations Treaty Collection|url=https://treaties.un.org/Pages/ViewDetails.aspx?src=IND&mtdsg_no=XXVII-1-h&chapter=27&clang=_en|access-date=31 March 2021|website=treaties.un.org|archive-date=17 April ===== <span class="anchor" id="Gas fired power stations"></span>Gas-fired power stations =====

[[List of power stations in Turkey#Natural Gas|Gas-fired power stations]] emitted 27&nbsp;Mt {{CO2}}e in 2024.<ref name="2026table" />{{Rp|table 1.A(a)s1 cell G27}} Electricity generation from gas tends to increase when hydropower is limited by droughts.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Turkey's power output from gas up 21 pct due to drought – Latest News|url=https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkeys-power-output-from-gas-up-21-pct-due-to-drought-162258|access-date=6 September 2021|website=Hürriyet Daily News|date=8 February 2021|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211204012327/https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkeys-power-output-from-gas-up-21-pct-due-to-drought-162258|archive-date=4 December 2021|url-status=live}}</ref> The cost of natural gas is expected to fall in the late 2020s with the expiry of expensive import agreements with Russia and Iran, and increasing production from the [[Sakarya Gas Field]] in the [[Black Sea]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sellars |first=William |date=2025-01-03 |title=Turkey hopes to offer Russia a gas route into Europe |url=https://www.agbi.com/oil-and-gas/2025/01/turkey-hopes-to-offer-russia-gas-route-into-europe/ |access-date=2025-01-05 |website=AGBI |language=en-US |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251119074152/https://www.agbi.com/oil-and-gas/2025/01/turkey-hopes-to-offer-russia-gas-route-into-europe/ |archive-date=19 November 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-10-01 |title=Strength in LNG? The gas market in Turkey |url=https://www.osw.waw.pl/en/publikacje/analyses/2024-10-01/strength-lng-gas-market-turkey |access-date=2025-01-05 |website=OSW Centre for Eastern Studies |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260417053510/https://www.osw.waw.pl/en/publikacje/analyses/2024-10-01/strength-lng-gas-market-turkey |archive-date=17 April 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

===== Transport =====
[[File:Traffic jam in Istanbul's road.JPG|thumb|alt=Photograph of two lanes of cars, buses and taxis at a standstill in a traffic jame|A traffic jam in [[Istanbul]], one of the few major European cities without a [[low-emission zone]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Urban Access Regulations in Europe|url=https://urbanaccessregulations.eu/|url-status=live|access-date=14 March 2021|website=Urban Vehicle Access Regulations & Low Emission Zones|archive-date=10 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210310071240/https://urbanaccessregulations.eu/}}</ref>]]

Transport emitted 101&nbsp;Mt of {{CO2}}e in 2024, a bit over one tonne per person, over 90% from [[Road transport in Turkey|road transport in the country]] (and agricultural vehicles).<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table1.A(a)s3 Cells G10/21}} Over half of Turkey's transport emissions come from [[diesel fuel]] burnt in road vehicles, but the proportion from cars compared to other vehicles such as lorries is not known.<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|page=Table1.A(a)s3 Col G}} The train network is underused and, unlike some other countries, {{As of|2026|lc=y}} Turkey has no binding transport specific targets.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2 March 2026 |title=Türkiye's Net Zero Emission Target: Road Map for Transport |url=https://emisyonsuzulasim.uab.gov.tr/api/reports/Best-Practices-and-Benchmarking-Report.pdf}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=21}} Fuel quality and emissions standards for new cars are less strict than those in the EU.<ref name="EC2020">{{Cite report |url=https://ec.europa.eu/neighbourhood-enlargement/sites/near/files/turkey_report_2020.pdf |title=Turkey 2020 Report (see chapters: 15 Energy, 27 Environment and Climate change) |publisher=[[European Commission]] |year=2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201103090805/https://ec.europa.eu/neighbourhood-enlargement/sites/near/files/turkey_report_2020.pdf |archive-date=3 November 2020 |access-date=28 February 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref>{{Rp|102}} Domestic flights{{efn|1=Emissions from international trips are not included in a country's emissions total, but fuel sales for international aviation can be found in Common Reporting Format category 1.A.3.a.1A. Turkey has joined the [[Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation]].}} emitted 4&nbsp;Mt of {{CO2}}e in 2024.<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|page=|location=Table1.A(a)s3 Cell G18}}

===== Cement =====
Turkey is the sixth-largest [[cement]] producer in the world and the largest in Europe,<ref name=":42">{{cite web |date=21 December 2020 |title=Turkey cement exports reach US$1bn in 2020 |url=https://www.cemnet.com/News/story/170047/turkey-cement-exports-reach-us-1bn-in-2020.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201222000537/https://www.cemnet.com/News/story/170047/turkey-cement-exports-reach-us-1bn-in-2020.html |archive-date=22 December 2020 |access-date=16 March 2021 |website=International Cement Review}}</ref> and by far the largest exporter to the EU.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024 |title=EU Cement Industry Trade Statistics |url=https://cembureau.eu/media/5irpnycs/cembureau-trade-report-first-6-months-2024.pdf |access-date=2025-01-13 |publisher=Cembureau, The European Cement Association |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251116161308/https://www.cembureau.eu/media/5irpnycs/cembureau-trade-report-first-6-months-2024.pdf |archive-date=16 November 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> Cement (clinker) production in 2024 emitted 45&nbsp;Mt {{CO2}},<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table 2(I) Cell N12}} 8% of the country's total GHG. [[Climate TRACE|Climate Trace]] has estimated the contributions of individual factories, sometimes from kiln heat visible from satellites,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cement |website=[[GitHub]] |archive-date=15 April 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref> and says that Nuh, Göltaş, and  [[Eren Holding|Medcem cement plants]] emitted more than 1 Mt each in 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Explore map - Climate TRACE |url=https://climatetrace.org/explore/#admin=Turkey%20(TUR):247:TUR:country&gas=co2e&year=2023&timeframe=100&sector=manufacturing,cement&asset=3165683 |access-date=2024-11-25 figures<ref>{{Cite web |title=2023 Sustainability Report |url=https://medcem.com.tr/uploads/Medcem-SR-EN.pdf |page=39}}</ref> whereas Göltaş has less GHG info.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Göltaş Çimento ===== Iron, steel and aluminium =====
Turkish steel, primarily from [[minimill]]s, averages about one tonne of {{CO2}} per tonne of steel produced.<ref name=":40">{{cite web|title=How an EU Carbon Border Tax Could Jolt World average is less polluting than China,<ref name=":40" /> three steelworks—[[Erdemir]], [[İsdemir]] and [[Kardemir]]—use [[blast furnaces]] and thus emit more than those using [[electric arc furnace]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=ricardo |date=2026-02-11 |title=Hasan Akbulut: Türkiye's steel industry has a competitive advantage with its low emission production structure - EUROMETAL |url=https://eurometal.net/hasan-akbulut-turkiyes-steel-industry-has-a-competitive-advantage-with-its-low-emission-production-structure/ |access-date=2026-09-25 |language=en-GB |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260925082132/https://eurometal.net/hasan-akbulut-turkiyes-steel-industry-has-a-competitive-advantage-with-its-low-emission-production-structure/ |archive-date=25 September 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> The EU [[Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism]] (CBAM) includes a carbon tariff on Turkish steel produced in blast furnaces,<ref>{{Cite products such as Chinese steel.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.shura.org.tr/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/SHURA_Agora_Border_Carbon_Adjustment_Turkey_EU.pdf|title=The European Green Deal's Border Carbon investing in [[solar power in Turkey]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=INFOGRAPHIC: Turkish steel sector lowers energy costs, carbon footprint with massive solar investments ==== Agriculture and fishing ====

[[File:Jersey cattle in Sisdağı 04.jpg|thumb|alt=brown Jersey cow wearing a fancy halter in a green field|Around half of agricultural emissions are from cows.]]

Agriculture accounted for 74&nbsp;Mt which was 13% of Turkey's total 2024 GHG, including 62% of its methane emissions and 78% of its [[nitrous oxide]] emissions.<ref name=":46" /> These are due primarily to [[enteric fermentation]], [[Agricultural soil science|agricultural soils]], and [[fertilizer|synthetic fertilizer]] application.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Climate TRACE |url=https://climatetrace.org/ |access-date=2026-09-25 |website=Climate TRACE |language=en}}</ref> Cattle emit about half of the GHG from agriculture, made up in 2024 of 30 Mt from enteric fermentation<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table 3 Cell I12}} and 7 Mt from manure management.<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table 3 Cell I20}}

About three quarters of red meat production in Turkey is beef.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Red Meat sector|url=http://www.turkishanimalpro.org/en-US/uyeler-sektorler/et-urunleri/23|access-date=1 October 2021|website=Turkish Animal Pro|language=}}</ref> Turks eat an average of {{convert|15|kg}} of [[beef]] per person each year (which is more than the world average<ref>{{Cite web |title=World Beef Consumption Per Capita (Ranking of Countries) |url=https://beef2live.com/story-world-beef-consumption-per-capita-ranking-countries-0-111634 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160114181559/http://beef2live.com/story-world-beef-consumption-per-capita-ranking-countries-0-111634 |url-status=usurped |archive-date=14 January 2016 |access-date=2022-05-01 |website=beef2live.com |language=en}}</ref>), and the country produced 1 million tonnes of beef in 2021.<ref name=":3">{{Cite report|date=7 April 2022|title=Turkey Livestock and Products Semiannual|url=https://www.fas.usda.gov/data/turkey-livestock-and-products-semi-annual|website=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250228060335/https://www.fas.usda.gov/data/turkey-livestock-and-products-semi-annual|archive-date=28 February 2025|access-date=22 January 2026|url-status=live}}</ref> Cattle are subsidized by the "Rural Prosperity, Livestock Support Project" until 2028.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Livestock and Products Annual Türkiye |url=https://apps.fas.usda.gov/newgainapi/api/Report/DownloadReportByFileName?fileName=Livestock+and+Products+Annual_Ankara_Turkiye_TU2025-0044.pdf |access-date=28 August 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260205015228/https://apps.fas.usda.gov/newgainapi/api/Report/DownloadReportByFileName?fileName=Livestock+and+Products+Annual_Ankara_Turkiye_TU2025-0044.pdf |archive-date=5 February 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> VAT on meat and dairy is 1% like other "staple foods". Being [[ruminant]]s sheep, goats and cattle belch methane. Fertilizers can emit the GHG nitrous oxide, but estimates of the effects of government policy on the agricultural and waste sectors' emissions are lacking.<ref name=":25">{{cite tech report |url=https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/idr7_TUR.pdf |title=Report on the technical review of the seventh national communication of Turkey |date=17 June 2019 |work=[[UNFCCC]] |id=FCCC/IDR.7/TUR}}</ref>{{Rp|28}} Turkey is one of the top ten nitrous oxide emitters.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.leeds.ac.uk/news-environment/news/article/5592/study-warns-of-alarming-rise-in-long-lived-greenhouse-gas | title=Study warns of 'alarming rise' in long-lived greenhouse gas | date=13 June 2024 | access-date=22 January 2026 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250915040424/https://www.leeds.ac.uk/news-environment/news/article/5592/study-warns-of-alarming-rise-in-long-lived-greenhouse-gas | archive-date=15 September 2025 | url-status=live }}</ref> [[Plastic pollution#Plastic pollution as a cause of climate change|Production of plastic]], such as for agriculture, may release significant GHG in future.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Diaz |first=Clarisa |title=Plastic use in agriculture is contributing to climate change |url=https://qz.com/2150031/plastic-use-in-agriculture-is-contributing-to-climate-change/ |access-date=2022-05-01 |website=Quartz |date=11 April 2022 |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250708221341/https://qz.com/2150031/plastic-use-in-agriculture-is-contributing-to-climate-change |archive-date=8 July 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> National GHG inventories do not yet include [[bottom trawling]], such as in parts of the [[Black Sea]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yildiz |first1=Taner |last2=Cömert |first2=Nurdan |last3=Ferrà |first3=Carmen |last4=Şaşmaz |first4=Uygar |last5=Galdelli |first5=Alessandro |last6=Tassetti |first6=Anna Nora |date=2025-09-25 |title=Environmental and behavioral drivers of Automatic Identification System gaps of Turkish trawlers in the Black Sea |journal=Frontiers in Marine Science |language=English |publisher=Frontiers |volume=12 |article-number=1647930 |doi=10.3389/fmars.2025.1647930  |doi-access=free|bibcode=2025FrMaS..1247930Y |issn=2296-7745}}</ref> as the IPCC has yet to issue accounting guidelines.<ref>{{cite web|last=Lo|first=Joe|date=17 March 2021|title=Scientists push to add "huge" fish trawling emissions to national inventories|url=https://www.climatechangenews.com/2021/03/17/scientists-push-add-huge-fish-trawling-emissions-national-inventories/|access-date=27 May 2021|website=Climate Home News|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210420115725/https://www.climatechangenews.com/2021/03/17/scientists-push-add-huge-fish-trawling-emissions-national-inventories/|archive-date=20 April 2021|url-status=live}}</ref> Bottom trawling is forbidden in some parts of [[Marine protected area|Marine Protected Areas]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-04-28 |title='Economic failure': Bottom trawling costs EU taxpayers €16bn a year |url=https://www.euronews.com/2026/04/28/taxpayer-funded-bottom-trawling-costs-europe-billions-has-turkiye-found-the-solution |access-date=2026-08-28 |website=euronews |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260829000523/https://www.euronews.com/2026/04/28/taxpayer-funded-bottom-trawling-costs-europe-billions-has-turkiye-found-the-solution |archive-date=29 August 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> In 2024 the government said that farming subsidies would be "reviewed through the lens of climate change".<ref name=":55" />{{Rp|location=section 4.2.6.1}}

==== Waste ====
Municipalities collect about 1&nbsp;kg of waste per person per day.<ref name=":55" />{{Rp|location=section 4.2.5}} The government says the waste sector contributed 15&nbsp;Mt (3%) of Turkey's 2024 GHG,<ref name=":46" /> with almost half of that from the tenth of waste sent to unmanaged [[landfill]]s.<ref name=":55" />{{Rp|location=section 4.2.5}} However Climate Trace estimates CO2e from solid waste disposal at 68 Mt in 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Country/Territory Inventory |url=https://climatetrace.org/inventory?sector=waste&region=Türkiye+%28TUR%29%3A247%3ATUR%3Acountry&timeframe=100 |access-date= |website=[[Climate TRACE]] |language=en}}</ref> Senem Abak at [[Boğaziçi University]] has suggested possible reasons for this large discrepancy; perhaps the differences in methodology, or official figures could be missing some open burning.<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Abak |first=Senem |title=Comparison of the national-contributed emissions with the climate trace's global emissions inventory |date=2025-01-01 |degree=Thesis |publisher=Boğaziçi University |url=https://thesis.rawdatalibrary.net/thesis/comparison-national-contributed-emissions-climate-trace-s-global-emissions |language=en}}</ref>{{Reference page|location=Section 4.5}}

Satellite methane measurements in 2025 and 2026 highlight [[landfill]] sites serving Istanbul (such as one in [[Seymen, Silivri]]) and [[İzmir|Izmir]] as large emitters.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Spotlight on the Top 25 Methane Plumes in 2025: Landfills {{!}} UCLA Law |url=https://law.ucla.edu/news/spotlight-top-25-methane-plumes-2025-landfills |access-date=2026-09-30 |website=law.ucla.edu |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260930200022/https://law.ucla.edu/news/spotlight-top-25-methane-plumes-2025-landfills |archive-date=30 September 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> Completely phasing out the little remaining open dumping is important, and in 2026 an academic claimed that MSW could become a carbon sink by 2035 by recovering materials and energy.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Maçin |first1=Kadriye Elif |title=Decarbonizing municipal solid waste management in Türkiye: A scenario-based life cycle assessment from historical baseline to 2035 recovery targets |journal=Environmental Pollution and Management |date=2026 |volume=3 |page=328 |doi=10.1016/j.epm.2026.06.003 |bibcode=2026EnvPM...3..328M |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2950305126000239|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Landfilling is the most common waste-disposal method.<ref name=":1">{{cite journal |last1=Yaman |first1=Cevat |title=Investigation of greenhouse gas emissions and energy recovery potential from municipal solid waste management practices |journal=[[Environmental Development]] |date=March 2020 |volume=33 |article-number=100484 |doi=10.1016/j.envdev.2019.100484 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2020EnvDe..3300484Y }}</ref> Climate Trace estimate [[Istanbul Waste Power Plant|Odayeri]] (even though it has a [[biogas]] facility<ref>{{Cite web |title=Odayeri Çöp Gazı Santrali - Biyogaz |url=https://www.enerjiatlasi.com/biyogaz/odayeri-cop-gazi-santrali.html |access-date=2022-11-12 |website=Enerji Atlası |language=tr-TR |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260121134424/https://www.enerjiatlasi.com/biyogaz/odayeri-cop-gazi-santrali.html |archive-date=21 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>) on the European side of Istanbul to have been by far the biggest single emitter of methane from waste in 2025 with 3.6 Mt CO2e.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Odayeri |url=https://climatetrace.org/ |access-date=2026-09-25 |website=[[Climate TRACE]] |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260122113914/https://climatetrace.org/ |archive-date=22 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> Organic waste sent to landfills emits methane, but the country is working to improve [[Waste management in Turkey|its waste and resource management]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lo |first=Joe |date=2026-02-13 |title=Turkiye prioritises cleaning up garbage emissions for COP31 |url=https://www.climatechangenews.com/2026/02/13/turkiye-prioritises-cleaning-up-garbage-emissions-in-cop31-action-agenda/ |access-date=2026-09-30 |website=Climate Home News |language=en-GB}}</ref> One third of organic waste is [[compost]]ed,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=İkizoğlu|first1=Bahar|last2=Koçak|first2=Emel|date=15 December 2020|title=Types of waste in the context of waste management and general overview of waste disposal in Turkey|journal=International Journal of Agriculture Environment and Food Sciences|language=en|volume=4|issue=4|pages=520–527|doi=10.31015/jaefs.2020.4.17|doi-access=free}}</ref> but others argue for [[incineration]].<ref name=":1" /> Some refrigerants are sent to Turkey from other countries for destruction.<ref>{{Cite web |year=2023 |title=Workshop on Kigali Implementation Plans |url=https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2023-07/KIP2023-Session%208.pdf |access-date=22 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260117164902/https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2023-07/KIP2023-Session%208.pdf |archive-date=17 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Climate ==

==Impacts on the natural environment==
According to [[Boğaziçi University]]'s Center for Climate Change and Policy Studies, human-caused climate change in Turkey started in the 1970s.<ref>{{Cite news|date=9 October 2020|title=Turkey in the midst of climate change, says climate expert|newspaper=[[Hürriyet Daily News]]|url=https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkey-in-the-midst-of-climate-change-says-climate-expert-158990|access-date=2020-11-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210124023116/https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkey-in-the-midst-of-climate-change-says-climate-expert-158990|archive-date=24 January 2021|url-status=live}}</ref> Turkey is forecast to be more severely affected than many other countries,<ref name="TPQ">{{cite web|title=Warming a Frozen Policy: Challenges to Turkey's Climate Politics After Paris|work=Turkish Policy Quarterly|url=http://turkishpolicy.com/article/818/warming-a-frozen-policy-challenges-to-turkeys-climate-politics-after-paris|access-date=25 February 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190903060552/http://turkishpolicy.com/article/818/warming-a-frozen-policy-challenges-to-turkeys-climate-politics-after-paris|archive-date=3 September 2019|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="3rd BR">{{cite report
 |work=[[Ministry of Environment and Urban Planning (Turkey)|Ministry of Environment and Urban Planning]]
 |title=Seventh National Communication of Turkey under the UNFCCC
 |version=V. 2
 |date=August 2019
 |url=https://www.tr.undp.org/content/turkey/en/home/library/environment_energy/NC7-2019.html
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210501221745/https://www.tr.undp.org/content/turkey/en/home/library/environment_energy/NC7-2019.html
 |archive-date=1 May 2021
 |access-date=28 November 2020
 |url-status=dead 
 }}</ref> but effects vary considerably across its regions.<ref name="TemaWWF" /> [[Coupled Model Intercomparison Project#CMIP Phase 6]] (CMIP6) models it well,<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2021-07-01 |title=Intercomparison of the expected change in the temperature and the precipitation retrieved from CMIP6 and CMIP5 climate projections: A Mediterranean hot spot case, Turkey |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0169809521001289 |journal=Atmospheric Research |language=en |volume=256 |article-number=105576 |doi=10.1016/j.atmosres.2021.105576 |issn=0169-8095 |last1=Bağçaci |first1=S. Çağatay |last2=Yucel |first2=Ismail |last3=Duzenli |first3=Eren |last4=Yilmaz |first4=M. Tuğrul |bibcode=2021AtmRe.25605576B |s2cid=233546613 |url-access=subscription |hdl=11492/5003 |hdl-access=free |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211005170841/https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0169809521001289 |archive-date=5 October 2021 |access-date=26 August 2021 |url-status=live }}</ref> however the CMIP6 Multi-Model Ensemble Mean is too coarse a resolution  (2° × 1.5°) for the higher parts of Turkey.<ref>{{Cite journal |title= Recent and projected changes in climate patterns in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region|journal=Scientific Reports|date=2024 |pmc=11069548 |last1=Francis |first1=D. |last2=Fonseca |first2=R. |volume=14 |issue=1 |page=10279 |doi=10.1038/s41598-024-60976-w  |doi-access=free|pmid=38704514 |bibcode=2024NatSR..1410279F }}</ref> 

One example of climate change's impact will be on the distribution of rainfall: the expansion of the [[Hadley cell]] (an area of circulation near the equator) may move the descending edge northwards towards Turkey, whose southern border is around 36 degrees north, and this may reduce rainfall.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Daher |first1=Houraa |last2=Kirtman |first2=Ben P. |date=2025-11-07 |title=Future climate assessment in the Mediterranean region using downscaled CMIP6 data |journal=Frontiers in Climate |language=English |publisher=Frontiers |volume=7 |article-number=1691944 |doi=10.3389/fclim.2025.1691944 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2025FrCli...791944D |issn=2624-9553}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Boza |first1=Burcu |last2=Ezber |first2=Yasemin |last3=Sen |first3=Omer Lutfi |title=A Seesaw of Anatolian Winter Precipitation from the Last Glacial Maximum to the Future |url=https://essopenarchive.org/doi/full/10.22541/essoar.15001810/v1 |journal=ESS Open Archive |volume=2026 |issue=409 |doi=10.22541/essoar.15001810/v1|hdl=11527/81071 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

The temperature has been increasing since at least the 1980s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Asikoglu |first=Omer Levend |last2=Alp |first2=Harun |last3=Temel |first3=Ibrahim |last4=Kamali |first4=Pegah |date=2025-10-22 |title=Examination of Long-Term Temperature Change in Türkiye: Comparative Evaluation of an Advanced Quartile-Based Approach and Traditional Trend Detection Methods |url=https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4433/16/11/1225 |journal=Atmosphere |language=en |volume=16 |issue=11 |pages=1225 |doi=10.3390/atmos16111225  |doi-access=free|issn=2073-4433}}</ref> {{As of|2026}}, the hottest year (since international standard measurements began in 1971) was 2024, followed by 2010, 2018, 2023 and 2025.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |date=2025-01-15 |title=Türkiye records hottest year in 2024 |url=https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkiye-records-hottest-year-in-2024-204697 |access-date=2025-01-23 |website=[[Hürriyet Daily News]] |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250119041203/https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkiye-records-hottest-year-in-2024-204697 |archive-date=19 January 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":29" />{{Reference page|page=5}} {{As of|2026}} the [[OECD]] thinks that with a low-carbon scenario the rise can be kept below 1.7 degrees.<ref name=":10a">{{Cite web |date=2021-10-19 |title=Turkey |url=https://www.g20climaterisks.org/turkey/ |access-date=2026-01-18 |website=G20 Climate Risk Atlas |language=en-US ===Water===
[[File:Lake Marmara.webp|thumb|[[Lake Marmara]] has completely dried out; perhaps there is not enough rainfall for upstream irrigation dams.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=3b0aee4a-20c6-4400-b356-bd0b4e75cbe5 | title=Green Claim and Green Litigation in Türkiye | date=2 April 2024 | access-date=18 April 2024 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240418170529/https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=3b0aee4a-20c6-4400-b356-bd0b4e75cbe5 | archive-date=18 April 2024 | url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":4a">{{Cite news |last=Tridimas |first=Beatrice |date=2023-09-25 |title=Turkey's fishermen fight to save wetlands as water scarcity bites |language=en |work=[[Reuters]] |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/idUSL8N3AR3MX/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231209203022/https://www.reuters.com/article/idUSL8N3AR3MX/ |archive-date=9 December 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gunacti |first1=Mert Can |last2=Gul |first2=Gulay Onusluel |last3=Cetinkaya |first3=Cem P. |last4=Gul |first4=Ali |last5=Barbaros |first5=Filiz |date=2023-05-01 |title=Evaluating Impact of Land Use and Land Cover Change Under Climate Change on the Lake Marmara System |journal=Water Resources Management |language=en |volume=37 |issue=6 |pages=2643–2656 |doi=10.1007/s11269-022-03317-8 |bibcode=2023WatRM..37.2643G |s2cid=252081287 |issn=1573-1650}}</ref>|alt=dried cracked mud with sparse metre-high green plants]]
[[File:Mount Ararat from Armash (3).jpg|thumb|[[Mount Ararat#Summit ice cap|Mount Ararat's glacier]] is [[Retreat of glaciers since 1850|retreating]] due to climate change,<ref name="Baldasso1" /> and will be gone before the end of the century.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal|last1=Azzoni|first1=Roberto Sergio|last2=Sarıkaya|first2=Mehmet Akif|last3=Fugazza|first3=Davide|date=2020-04-01|title=Turkish glacier inventory and classification from high-resolution satellite data|journal=Mediterranean Geoscience Reviews|volume=2|issue=1|pages=153–162|doi=10.1007/s42990-020-00029-2|bibcode=2020MGRv....2..153A |issn=2661-8648|hdl=2434/745029|s2cid=216608789|hdl-access=free}}</ref>|alt=not very sharp snow-capped mountain peak in the distance, under a blue sky with a few small clouds]]

Climate change has reduced rainfall in some regions and has made it less regular,  which has put stress on [[Hydroelectricity in Turkey|hydroelectric power plants]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Bulut |first1=U |last2=Sakalli |first2=A |date=2021 |title=Impacts of climate change and distribution of precipitation on hydroelectric power generation in Turkey |doi=10.1088/1757-899X/1032/1/012043|journal=IOP Conference Series: Materials Science and Engineering|volume=1032|issue=1 |bibcode=2021MS&E.1032a2043B |s2cid=234299802 |at=Article 012043|doi-access=free }}</ref> Between 1979 and 2019 annual precipitation fluctuated from over 60&nbsp;cm to under 45&nbsp;cm,<ref name=":6" /> and average annual temperatures varied by 4 degrees.<ref name=":6" /> Dams are collecting less drinking water due to reduced pricipitation due to climate change.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Demirbaş |first1=Furkan |last2=Özbaş |first2=Emine Elmaslar |last3=Can Sarıkap |first3=Mehmet |last4=Nur Ciner |first4=Mirac |last5=Yurtseven |first5=Hüseyin |last6=Özcan |first6=Hüseyin Kurtuluş |date=2026-03-12 |title=Modelling the Impact of Climate Change on the Reservoir Filling Rates of Dams Used for Drinking Water Supply Through Artificial Neural Networks |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s11269-026-04527-0 |journal=Water Resources Management |volume=40 |issue=5 |pages=187 |doi=10.1007/s11269-026-04527-0 |bibcode=2026WatRM..40..187D |issn=1573-1650|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Turkey is already a [[water stress]]ed country, because the amount of water per person is only about {{convert|1,500|m3}} a year: and due to [[Turkey#Demographics|population increase]] and climate change it is highly likely the country will suffer [[water scarcity]] (less than 1,000 m³) by the 2070s.<ref name=":13" /> Higher temperatures can increase evaporation from lakes, making them more saline.<ref>{{Cite web |last=ClimateChangePost |title=Fresh water resources |url=https://www.climatechangepost.com/countries/turkey/fresh-water-resources/ |access-date=2026-08-28 |website=www.climatechangepost.com |language=en-us |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250905214459/https://www.climatechangepost.com/countries/turkey/fresh-water-resources/ |archive-date=5 September 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> Little change has been forecast for water resources in the northern [[Drainage basin|river basins]], but a substantial reduction has been forecast for the southern river basins.<ref name=":13" /> [[Konya]] in central Turkey is also vulnerable.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gedik |first=Furkan |date=2021 |title=Meteorological Drought Analysis in Konya Closed Over 200 thousand people live in areas at risk if [[sea level rise]]s by 1 meter.<ref name=":6b">{{Cite web|title=Potential Impacts of Sea Level Rise on the Coasts of Turkey|url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/327151922.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210501150532/https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/327151922.pdf |archive-date=2021-05-01 }}</ref> The [[Aegean Sea|Aegean]] rose by an estimated 4&nbsp;mm a year in the early 21st century.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Calafat |first1=F.
