==D==
{{glossary}}
{{term|[[dale (landform)|dale]]}}
{{defn|Another name for a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|valley}}.}}

{{term|[[dam]]}}{{anchor|dams}}
{{ghat|Also '''impoundment'''.}}
{{defn|Any barrier, either natural or artificial, that stops or restricts the flow of water, either on the surface or underground. Man-made dams are most commonly built to impound rivers or streams, generally to retain water for purposes such as human consumption, irrigation, aquaculture, or power generation (whereas related structures such as [[floodgate]]s and {{gli|levee|levees}} are more specifically designed to manage or prevent water flow into particular areas).}}

{{term|[[dasymetric map]]}}
{{defn|A type of thematic {{gli|map}} that uses areal symbols to visualize a {{gli|field|spatially dependent variable}} (e.g. population density) by refining a {{gli|choropleth map}} with ancillary information about the distribution of the variable. The dasymetric method attempts to improve the resolution of maps based on average or per-capita figures calculated for discrete administrative units, which tend to show sharp contrasts between adjacent areas, by supplementing these figures with additional geographic data that allow more precise categories to be constructed. Dasymetric maps are a hybrid of choropleth and {{gli|isarithmic map|isarithmic maps}}, combining their strengths and weaknesses in order to more accurately depict quantities that vary continuously across space.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|datum plane}}
{{ghat|Also '''datum level''' or '''datum line'''.}}
{{defn|The zero-elevation baseline or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|vertical datum}} to which a measurement of {{gli|elevation}} or {{gli|altitude}} is relative, e.g. the {{gli|mean sea level}} calculated for a given location over a given period of time.<ref name="Clark"/> See also ''{{gli|geodetic datum}}''.}}

{{term|[[de facto segregation|''de facto'' segregation]]}}
{{defn|The spatial and social separation of populations that occurs without legal sanction.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[de jure segregation|''de jure'' segregation]]}}
{{defn|The spatial and social separation of populations that occurs because of legal measures.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[debouch]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''debouche'''.}}
{{defn|A place where water runoff from a relatively small, confined space emerges into a much larger, broader space, or where a {{gli|body of water}} pours forth from a narrow opening, such as where a stream or river enters a lake or ocean.}}

{{term|[[deciduous forest]]}}
{{defn|A forest composed of trees which lose their leaves each year.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|decolonization}}
{{defn|The process of ending the colonization of a region or a state.}}

{{term|deep}}
{{defn|A trough-like {{gli|depression}} or trench in the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ocean floor}}, of limited extent but great depth, generally more than {{convert|5500|m|ft}} below sea level.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|deferred junction}}
{{defn|A {{gli|confluence}} of two {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|watercourses}} in which a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|tributary}} stream is prevented by {{gli|levees}}, natural or artificial, from immediately joining another stream or river and consequently is forced to flow parallel beside it, usually within a large {{gli|floodplain}}, for a considerable distance before the channels eventually merge, often at the convex bend of a large {{gli|meander}}.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[defile (geography)|defile]]}}
{{defn|A narrow {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|pass}} or {{gli|gorge}} between {{gli|mountains}} or {{gli|hills}}.}}

{{term|[[deforestation]]}}
{{defn|The destruction of {{gli|forests}} by any means, whether naturally or by human activity.}}

{{term|[[degree (angle)|degree]]}}{{anchor|degrees}}
{{defn|A unit of angular measure, represented by the º symbol. A circle is divided into 360 degrees; subdivisions of the degree include the {{gli|minute}} ({{frac|60}} of one degree) and the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|second}} ({{frac|3600}} of one degree). Degrees are commonly used to divide the roughly spherical shape of the Earth for geographic and cartographic purposes, e.g. when reporting {{gli|latitudes}} and {{gli|longitudes}}.<ref name="OERI 1996"/>}}

{{term|[[degree day]]}}
{{defn|Deviation of one-degree temperature for one day from an arbitrary standard, usually the long-term average temperature for a place.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[dell (landform)|dell]]}}
{{defn|A small, secluded hollow, usually within a grassy, park-like, partially wooded {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|valley}}.}}

{{term|[[river delta|delta]]}}{{anchor|deltas}}
{{defn|A landform at the {{gli|mouth}} of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|river}} where the {{gli|main stem}} splits up into several {{gli|distributary|distributaries}}. It is formed from the deposition of the sediment carried by the river as the flow leaves the mouth of the river. It is often affected by incoming tides. Compare ''{{gli|estuary}}''.<ref name="NRCS 2018"/>}}
[[File:Skokomish River Delta 07773.JPG|thumb|500px|The [[Skokomish River]] '''{{gli|delta}}''' in the northwestern United States, where the river flows into [[Puget Sound]]]]

{{term|[[demilitarized zone]] (DMZ)}}{{anchor|demilitarized zone}}
{{defn|A politically neutral area or [[buffer zone]] in which treaties or agreements between polities or other competing factions forbid military installations, activities, or personnel. These zones are usually situated along an established {{gli|boundary}} or {{gli|frontier}} separating territories controlled by adjacent military powers or alliances.}}

{{term|[[demography]]}}{{anchor|demographic}}
{{defn|The study and systematic analysis of {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|population}}, particularly human population.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|demoiselle}}
{{defn|A pillar of rock weathered from volcanic [[breccia]] or similar material and capped by a large boulder which has protected the material underneath.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[demonym]]}}{{anchor|demonyms}}
{{ghat|Also '''gentilic'''.}}
{{defn|A word identifying a person or a group of people in relation to a particular place, usually derived from the name of the place (which may be any kind of place, formal or informal, of any size or scale, from a town or city to a region, province, country, or continent) and used to describe all residents or natives of that place, regardless of any ethnic, linguistic, religious, or cultural differences which may exist within the local population. Examples include "Vietnamese", describing a person from Vietnam; "Detroiter" for a person from the city of Detroit, Michigan; and "Macedonian" for a person from North Macedonia or the wider historical region of Macedonia.}}

{{term|[[denudation]]}}
{{defn|The uncovering of deeper layers of rock by any natural process, e.g. {{gli|erosion}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|weathering}}, or {{gli|mass movement}}.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[dependent territory|dependency]]}}{{anchor|dependencies|dependent territory|dependent territories}}
{{ghat|Also '''dependent territory'''.}}
{{defn|A {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|territory}} relying on or subject to the control of another {{gli|country}}, neither possessing full political independence nor forming an integral part of the controlling country's political or economic interests.}}

{{term|[[deposition (geology)|deposition]]}}{{anchor|depositional|deposit|deposits|deposited|depositing}}
{{defn|Any natural process by which material such as soil and rocks is added to a {{gli|landform}} or {{gli|landmass}}, e.g. by the action of wind, water, ice, or gravity in transporting previously {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|weathering|weathered}} surface material, which comes to rest when sufficient kinetic energy is lost and accumulates in layers of sediment. See also ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|sedimentation}}''.}}

{{term|[[depression (geology)|depression]]}}{{anchor|depressions}}
{{defn|Any {{gli|landform}} that is sunken or depressed below the surrounding area. Depressions include an enormous variety of landforms and can form by a number of different mechanisms, including {{gli|erosion}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|subsidence|ground collapse}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|plate tectonics|tectonic activity}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|volcano|volcanism}}, and {{gli|impact crater|meteorite impacts}}.}}

{{term|derelict land}}
{{defn|An area of land which has been damaged or devalued by some process, either natural or man-made (e.g. extractive industry), and/or simply neglected, causing it to be abandoned by human interests (and often other organisms) and leaving it incapable of being used productively in its present condition.<ref name="Clark"/> See also ''{{gli|brownfield land}}''.}}

{{term|[[desert]]}}{{anchor|deserts}}
{{defn|An arid, barren area of land where little [[precipitation]] occurs and living conditions are consequently unfavorable for most plant and animal life. Deserts are characterized by exposure of the unprotected ground surface to processes of {{gli|denudation}} as well as large variations in temperature between night and day. They are often classified by the amount of precipitation they receive, by their average temperature, by the causes of their {{gli|desertification}}, or by their geographical location.}}

{{term|[[desert pavement]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''reg''', '''serir''', '''gibber''', '''saï''', and '''desert mosaic'''.}}
{{defn|A ground surface often found in arid environments, consisting of interlocking rock fragments of pebble and cobble size, closely packed after the removal of finer rock material and smoothed or polished by blown sand so that eventually their upper surfaces are more or less uniformly flat.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[desert varnish]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''desert patina''', '''rock varnish''', and '''rock rust'''.}}
{{defn|A conspicuous orange-yellow to black coating often present on exposed rock surfaces in arid environments, consisting of thin, hard, polished layers of metal oxides, especially iron and manganese, which form when minute quantities of matter migrate to the surface of the rock by [[capillary action]] and are then precipitated by evaporation.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[desertification]]}}
{{defn|The process by which a previously fertile area becomes increasingly arid, infertile, or {{gli|desert}}-like; a type of land degradation in which biological productivity is lost due either to natural or man-made processes, e.g. [[climate change]] or [[overexploitation]] of soils for agriculture.}}

{{term|desire line}}
{{defn|A straight line drawn on a {{gli|map}} between the point of origin and the destination of a trip, i.e. the shortest distance between these two points, indicating the route a person would like or desire to follow if it were possible.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[desire path]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''social trail'''.}}
{{defn|Any path or trail, often a footpath, created as a consequence of erosion caused by repeated human or animal traffic, usually because it is the shortest or easiest {{gli|route}} to navigate between an origin and a destination. Desire paths often emerge as shortcuts where constructed paths or roads are circuitous, have gaps, or are non-existent.}}

{{term|[[dew pond]]}}
{{defn|A shallow artificial {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|pond}} built to capture and hold rainwater or sea mist in order to provide water for livestock, made especially in areas where natural supplies of surface water are not readily available, such as on the chalk downlands of southern England.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[diapir]]}}
{{defn|A type of {{gli|igneous intrusion}} in which a more mobile, ductile, or deformable rock or other material is forced to intrude into relatively brittle overlying rocks.}}

{{term|[[diaspora]]}}
{{defn|The scattered dispersion of a human population from its original homeland; or the members of a dispersed population, now residing in various locations to which they are not indigenous.}}

{{term|[[digital elevation model]] (DEM)}}{{anchor|digital elevation model}}
{{defn|A three-dimensional computer graphics representation of a geographic {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|terrain}} surface created from {{gli|elevation}} data. DEMs are the most common basis for digitally produced relief maps.}}

{{term|[[levee|dike]]}}{{anchor|dikes}}
{{defn|no=1|A ditch, wall, embankment, or ridge, natural or man-made, that is an obstacle to something else; another name for a {{gli|levee}}.}}
{{defn|no=2|In {{gli|geology}}, an [[intrusion]] in which molten rock has ascended through an approximately vertical {{gli|fissure}} and solidified into a wall of rock that is often harder or less permeable than the rocks of the surrounding strata.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[diocese]]}}
{{defn|A type of administrative division used by certain Christian churches for religious purposes.}}

{{term|[[Cardinal direction|direction]]}}{{anchor|directions|directional|directionally}}
{{defn|The {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|position}} of one point relative to another without reference to the distance between them, usually expressed as the angular distance in {{gli|degrees}} between a line connecting the two points and a reference direction. In {{gli|cartography}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|navigation}}, and {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|orienteering}}, direction is often considered only with respect to a two-dimensional plane (see {{gli|compass rose}}), but it is also commonly interpreted in three dimensions.<ref name="USDMATC"/>}}

{{term|[[discharge (hydrology)|discharge]]}}
{{defn|In {{gli|hydrology}}, the volumetric flow rate of water through a cross-sectional area, i.e. the volume of water that passes a particular point along a waterway (e.g. a cross-section of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|stream}} {{gli|channel}}) per unit time. The measure includes the volumes of any suspended solids, dissolved chemicals, or organic matter in addition to the water itself. Discharge is commonly measured for both natural and man-made hydrological systems, where it may be referred to by various names including ''streamflow'' and ''outflow''.}}

{{term|[[discordant coastline]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''Atlantic-type coastline'''.}}
{{defn|A {{gli|coastline}} which cuts transversely across the predominant orientation of the local geological strata, i.e. not parallel to them, as with a {{gli|concordant coastline}}.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[dissected plateau]]}}
{{defn|A landscape produced by significant {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|stream}} erosion and incision of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|plateau}} such that only a small part of the plateau surface is at or near the original elevation of the summit; much of the area instead occurs as eroded {{gli|hills}} or {{gli|badlands}}.<ref name="NRCS 2018"/>}}

{{term|[[distance decay]]}}
{{defn|The decrease in cultural or spatial interactions between two places as the distance between them increases. This effect may be noticeable in {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|towns}} and {{gli|cities}}, where certain characteristics such as pedestrian traffic, building height, and land value tend to decline with greater distance from the {{gli|city center}}.}}

{{term|[[distributary]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|stream}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|river}} that [[river bifurcation|branches off]] and flows away from a {{gli|main stem|main channel}} and does not return to it. Distributaries are common near {{gli|delta|river deltas}}. Contrast ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|tributary}}''.}}

{{term|[[district]]}}{{anchor|districts}}
{{defn|A type of {{gli|administrative subdivision}} used by governments and institutions worldwide, typically at regional or local levels. Districts are commonly drawn to define the jurisdictions of special local government services, such as law enforcement and education, and often function more or less independently of the {{gli|municipality|municipal}} or {{gli|county}} governments that designate them. The term can refer to a wide variety of official and colloquial subdivisions, including [[electoral district]]s, [[school district]]s, and [[shopping district]]s.}}

{{term|divide}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|drainage divide}}''.}}

{{term|[[doab]]}}
{{defn|In parts of South Asia, the low {{gli|alluvial plain}} lying between and reaching to the {{gli|confluence}} of two rivers or streams.<ref name="Goudie"/> See also ''{{gli|interfluve}}''.}}

{{term|[[doline]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''vrtače''' and '''shakehole'''.}}
{{defn|A shallow enclosed {{gli|basin}} or funnel-shaped {{gli|depression}} typical of {{gli|karst}} landscapes, usually with a flat floor and linked to the underlying drainage system by a vertical shaft.<ref name="Clark"/> See also ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|sinkhole}}''.}}

{{term|[[dome (geology)|dome]]}}
{{defn|no=1|A steep-sided {{gli|mound}} that forms when very viscous lava is extruded from a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|volcanic vent}}.<ref name="USGS 2010"/>}}
{{defn|no=2|An uplifted area of [[sedimentary rock]] with a downward dip in all directions, often caused by molten rock material pushing upward from below. The sediments have often eroded away, exposing the rocks that resulted when the molten material cooled.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|donga}}
{{defn|In southern Africa, another name for a {{gli|gully}} or {{gli|badland}} carved by extreme erosion.<ref name="Goudie"/>}}

{{term|[[dormant volcano]]}}
{{defn|An active {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|volcano}} that is in repose (quiescence) but is expected to erupt in the future.<ref name="USGS 2010"/>}}

{{term|dormitory town}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|commuter town}}''.}}

{{term|[[downland]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''down''' and '''downs'''.}}
{{defn|An open, treeless expanse of gently undulating, elevated {{gli|grassland}}, usually of chalk and supporting grazing for livestock. The term is used primarily in southern England, Australia, and New Zealand.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[downtown]]}}
{{defn|In English-speaking North America, the commercial, cultural, and often historical and/or geographical {{gli|city center|center}} of a {{gli|city}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|town}}, especially a large city within a major {{gli|metropolitan area}}, often synonymous with its {{gli|central business district}}.}}

{{term|[[drainage]]}}
{{defn|The natural or artificial removal of surface and/or sub-surface water from an area with excess water, e.g. via {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|surface runoff|runoff}} facilitated by {{gli|channels}} such as {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|streams}} and {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|rivers}}, into which water collects and is transported to {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|sea level}} by gravity. The patterns, hierarchies, and evolution of drainage networks are widely studied in {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|physical geography}} disciplines.}}

{{term|[[drainage basin]]}}{{anchor|drainage basins}}
{{ghat|Also '''catchment''', '''drainage area''', '''river basin''', '''water basin''', or '''watershed'''.}}
{{defn|Any area of land where precipitation collects and drains into a common outlet, such as into a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|river}}, {{gli|lake}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ocean}}, or any other {{gli|body of water}}. The drainage system includes all of the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|surface water}} from precipitation {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|surface runoff|runoff}} and [[snowmelt]], as well as all of the {{gli|groundwater}} beneath the Earth's surface. Each drainage basin is separated topographically from adjacent basins by a {{gli|drainage divide}}.}}

{{term|[[drainage divide]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''ridgeline''', '''watershed''', '''water parting''', '''water divide''', or simply '''divide'''.}}
{{defn|The topographical barrier that separates neighboring {{gli|drainage basins}}. Divides are often, though not always, located along conspicuous elevated {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ridges}} or {{gli|mountain ranges}}.}}

{{term|[[draw (terrain)|draw]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''re-entrant'''.}}
{{defn|no=1|A terrain feature formed by two parallel {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ridges}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|spurs}} with low ground in between them.}}
{{defn|no=2|Another name for an {{gli|arroyo}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ravine}}, or {{gli|gulch}}, especially one with a broad floor and gently sloping sides.<ref name="NRCS 2018"/>}}

{{term|draw down}}
{{defn|The maximum extent to which the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|water table}} is reduced in {{gli|elevation}} as a result of pumping water from a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|well}} that penetrates an {{gli|aquifer}}. The amount of draw down diminishes logarithmically with distance from the site of the well, a fact which determines the shape of the subsurface {{gli|cone of depression}} in the area surrounding the well.<ref name="Goudie"/>}}

{{term|[[drift (geology)|drift]]}}
{{defn|All sediment transported by a {{gli|glacier}}, sorted or {{gli|glacial till|unsorted}}, whether deposited directly by the ice or by glacial {{gli|meltwater}}.}}

{{term|[[drift ice]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''brash ice'''.}}
{{defn|A type of {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|sea ice}} consisting of multiple {{gli|ice floe|ice floes}} that are not attached to the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|shoreline}} or any other fixed object such as a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|shoal}}, and which are therefore free to "drift" under the influence of winds and {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ocean current|ocean currents}}. Contrast ''{{gli|fast ice}}''.}}

{{term|[[drowned valley]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|valley}} which was originally formed on land but later partially or entirely submerged beneath the sea due to a rise in sea level. See also ''{{gli|fjord}}'', ''{{gli|calanque}}'', and ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ria}}''.}}

{{term|[[drumlin]]}}{{anchor|drumlins}}
{{defn|An elongated {{gli|hill}} in the shape of an inverted spoon or half-buried egg which is formed by {{gli|glacial}} ice acting on underlying unconsolidated {{gli|glacial till|till}} or ground {{gli|moraine}}.}}

{{term|[[dry farming]]}}
{{defn|A type of farming practiced in semi-arid or dry grassland areas without irrigation, instead using such approaches as [[fallowing]], maintaining a finely broken surface, and growing drought-tolerant crops.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|dry gap}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|wind gap}}''.}}

{{term|[[dry point]]}}
{{defn|An area of firm or dry ground in a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|wetland}}, {{gli|marsh}}, or {{gli|floodplain}}, often capable of supporting a human {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|settlement}}.}}

{{term|[[dryland]]}}{{anchor|drylands}}
{{defn|An {{gli|ecoregion}} or more generally any land area defined by a relative scarcity of water, where precipitation is evenly balanced or exceeded by evaporation from surfaces and evapotranspiration by plants. Drylands encompass all sub-humid and arid environments, from tropical {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|savannas}} to hyper-arid extremes such as {{gli|deserts}}.}}

{{term|[[dune]]}}{{anchor|dunes|sand dune|sand dunes}}
{{defn|A hill of loose [[sand]] built by the movements and erosional and {{gli|depositional}} processes of [[wind]] or water, often occurring in {{gli|deserts}} and {{gli|coastal}} areas.}}

{{glossary end}}

==E==
{{glossary}}
{{term|[[Earth science]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''Earth sciences''' or '''geoscience'''.}}
{{defn|no=1|A collective term for the various fields of natural science related to the planet [[Earth]].}}
{{defn|no=2|The branch of science that studies the physical constitution and characteristics of the Earth and its atmosphere, using methods and tools from {{gli|geography}}, geology, physics, chemistry, biology, and mathematics to build a quantitative understanding of how the Earth works and changes over time.}}

{{term|[[earthquake]]}}
{{defn|A sudden and intense shaking of the ground due to {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|plate tectonics|tectonic}} activity.}}

{{term|[[Eastern Hemisphere]]}}
{{defn|The {{gli|hemisphere|half sphere}} of the Earth that is east of the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|Prime Meridian}} and west of the {{gli|antimeridian}}. It is opposite the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|Western Hemisphere}}.}}

{{term|[[easting]]}}
{{defn|}}

{{term|economic distance}}
{{defn|The physical distance a commodity may travel before its value is exceeded by the costs of transporting it.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[economic geography]]}}
{{defn|A sub-discipline of geography which studies the location, distribution, and spatial organization of [[economics|economic]] activities across the world.}}

{{term|economic tiger}}
{{defn|A country with rapid economic growth due to cheap labor, quickly advancing technology, and/or policies favoring aggressive exports.}}

{{term|[[economies of agglomeration]]}}
{{defn|The economic advantages that accrue to an activity by locating close to other activities; benefits that follow from complementarity or shared public services.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|econym}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|oeconym}}''.}}

{{term|[[ecoregion]]}}
{{ghat|Also called an '''ecological region'''.}}
{{defn|A type of {{gli|biogeography|biogeographic}} province that is smaller than a {{gli|bioregion}} and which contains characteristic, ecologically and geographically distinct, and relatively uniform assemblages of biological [[community (biology)|communities]] and species. Ecoregion boundaries often overlap within {{gli|ecotones}} and mosaic habitats, and most ecoregions contain habitats that differ from those described for their assigned [[biome]].}}

{{term|[[ecotone]]}}{{anchor|ecotones}}
{{defn|A transition area between two biological [[community (ecology)|communities]], where different communities meet and integrate. It may manifest as a gradual blending of the communities across a broad area, or as an abrupt boundary line.}}

{{term|[[ecumene]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''oecumene'''.}}
{{defn|no=1|The habitable world according to the ancient Greeks; the part of the Earth's surface that is suitable for permanent human settlement, e.g. because it is climatically tolerable and physically occupiable.<ref name="Clark"/>}}
{{defn|no=2|All of human civilization considered collectively.}}

{{term|[[edge city]]}}
{{defn|A concentration of businesses, commercial buildings, or retail and entertainment venues situated outside of a traditional {{gli|downtown}} or [[central business district]] in what was previously a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|suburban}} residential or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|rural}} area.}}

{{term|[[edgelands]]}}
{{defn|The transitional areas of "fringe" space at the boundaries of a {{gli|country}}, {{gli|city}}, or other artificial geographical entity, often distinguished by a partly man-made, partly natural landscape that is in the earliest stages of human management and organization. Compare ''{{gli|hinterland}}''.}}

{{term|effective accessibility}}
{{defn|The extent to which a place or service is actually accessible, governed not only by the distance to be traveled but also by whether or not the means of transport, the time available, and social circumstances make access possible.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[ekistics]]}}
{{defn|The scientific study of human {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|settlements}} of all types, incorporating concepts such as regional, metropolitan, and community [[urban planning|planning]] and dwelling design with the goal of achieving harmony between the inhabitants of a settlement and their physical, social, and cultural environments.}}

{{term|[[electoral geography]]}}
{{defn|A branch of {{gli|human geography}} concerned with analysis of the organization, methods, results, and consequences of political [[election]]s in the context of geographic space and using geographical techniques.}}

{{term|[[elevation]]}}{{anchor|elevations|elevational}}
{{defn|no=1|The height of a geographic location above or below a fixed reference point; in particular, the height of a point on the Earth's surface with respect to {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|sea level}} (or at least to a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|reference ellipsoid|reference}} {{gli|geoid}} used as an approximation of the Earth's mean sea level). Compare ''{{gli|altitude}}'', ''{{gli|geopotential height}}'', and ''{{gli|depth}}''.<ref name="OERI 1996"/>}}
{{defn|no=2|The vertical angle between the horizontal and a high point, e.g. between the {{gli|horizon}} and a star in the night sky, or between the base of a mountain and its {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|summit}}.<ref name="Clark"/>}}
{{defn|no=3|In architecture, a view of one of the sides of a building, or a drawing of this view.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[ellipsoid]]}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|reference ellipsoid}}''.}}

{{term|emergence}}
{{defn|no=1|The rise of the level of a land surface with respect to the sea, so that land formerly under the sea becomes dry.<ref name="Clark"/>}}
{{defn|no=2|The location at which an {{gli|groundwater|underground stream}} or {{gli|aquifer}} comes to the surface.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[emergent coastline]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|coast}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|shore|shoreline}} resulting from a rise in land surface elevation relative to sea level.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[polder|empolder]]}}
{{defn|To {{gli|land reclamation|reclaim}} by the creation of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|polder}}.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[enclave]]}}{{anchor|enclaves}}
{{defn|A tract or territory completely surrounded by and enclosed within the territory of exactly one other state, country, or other political entity. Unlike enclaves, {{gli|exclaves}} can be surrounded by more than one other state.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}
[[File:Base Map of South Africa.png|thumb|400px|right|The independent country of [[Lesotho]] is completely '''{{gli|enclave|enclaved}}''' by the country of [[South Africa]]. The country of [[Eswatini]], to the east, is not an enclave because it borders two countries: South Africa and [[Mozambique]].]]

{{term|[[endemic]]}}
{{defn|Restricted or exclusive to a certain place, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|region}}, or people, having originated there, and existing nowhere else.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[endorheic basin]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''endoreic basin''', '''closed basin''', or '''terminal basin'''.}}
{{defn|A closed {{gli|drainage basin}} that allows little or no outflow to external bodies of water but converges instead into internal {{gli|lakes}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|swamps}} which equilibrate through evaporation.}}

{{term|englacial}}
{{defn|Embedded within a {{gli|glacier}}. Contrast ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|subglacial}}'' and ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|superglacial}}''.}}

{{term|[[entrepôt]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''entrepot''' or '''transshipment port'''.}}
{{defn|A place (e.g. a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|port}}, city, or trading post) to which physical goods or merchandise are brought to be stored temporarily while awaiting export to another country, and where they are not liable to [[customs]] duties.<ref name="Clark"/> Though the term once described important commercial centers situated along long-distance trade routes, modern customs areas have largely made such entrepôts obsolete, and the term is now more commonly used to refer to [[duty-free]] ports with a high volume of re-export trade.}}

{{term|[[Natural environment|environment]]}}
{{defn|Everything on and around the Earth's surface and atmosphere; the complex of physical, chemical, and biological elements which comprise the natural world, especially as contrasted with {{gli|built environment|man-made objects or spaces}}.}}

{{term|[[wikt:environs|environs]]}}
{{defn|The area surrounding a particular geographical place, i.e. its surroundings or {{gli|environment}}.}}

{{term|[[epeiric sea]]}}
{{defn|A large, shallow body of {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|salt water}} on a {{gli|continental shelf}} which is connected to the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ocean}};<ref name="Goudie"/> an {{gli|inland sea}}. See also ''{{gli|marginal sea}}''.}}

{{term|[[epicenter]]}}
{{defn|The point on the Earth's surface directly above the {{gli|focus}} of an {{gli|earthquake}}, near which the seismic waves produced by the earthquake are usually most noticeable.}}

{{term|[[equal-area projection]]}}
{{defn|}}

{{term|[[equator]]}}
{{defn|no=1|An imaginary line dividing a spheroid such as a planet into northern and southern {{gli|hemispheres}}, defined by the intersection of the spheroid's surface and the plane perpendicular to its [[axis of rotation]], which results in a {{gli|great circle}} exactly midway between and hence equidistant from the planet's {{gli|geographic poles}} and is therefore defined as zero degrees {{gli|latitude}}.}}
{{defn|no=2|The Earth's equator in particular (often capitalized as the '''Equator'''): the imaginary circle of latitude halfway between the geographic poles which is assigned a latitude of zero degrees (0°) and therefore used as a reference point from which all other {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|parallel|lines of latitude}} are measured. At {{convert|40074|km|mi}} in circumference, is the largest great circle of the Earth.<ref name="OERI 1996"/> Places located on or near the Equator experience approximately the same amount of daylight year-round, which causes local daytime temperatures and climate patterns to be relatively stable throughout the year.}}
[[File:Robinson projection with major circles of latitude and prime meridian labeled.png|thumb|600px|{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|Robinson projection}} of the globe showing the five major circles of latitude – the '''{{gli|Arctic Circle}}''' and '''{{gli|Antarctic Circle}}''' (purple), the '''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|Tropic of Cancer}}''' and '''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|Tropic of Capricorn}}''' (orange), and the '''{{gli|Equator}}''' (green) – plus the '''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|Prime Meridian}}''' (pink).]]

{{term|equatorial cylindrical orthomorphic map projection}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|Mercator projection}}''.}}

{{term|[[equidistant]]}}
{{defn|Equally distant from a point, object, or location; e.g. a given location ''{{math|A}}'' is said to be equidistant from two other locations ''{{math|B}}'' and ''{{math|C}}'' if ''{{math|B}}'' and ''{{math|C}}'' each have the same distance from ''{{math|A}}''.}}

{{term|[[equinox]]}}
{{defn|A solar equinox is a moment in time when the Sun appears directly above the equator, rather than to its north or south.}}

{{term|[[equirectangular projection]]}}
{{defn|}}

{{term|[[erg (landform)|erg]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''reg''' and '''hamada'''.}}
{{defn|A broad, flat {{gli|desert}} area covered by wind-swept sand and having little or no vegetative cover.}}

{{term|[[erosion]]}}
{{defn|The wearing away of the Earth's surface caused by the movement of water, ice, or wind.}}

{{term|[[glacial erratic|erratic]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''glacial erratic'''.}}
{{defn|A boulder that has been carried from its source by a {{gli|glacier}} and deposited as the glacier melted. Such boulders are often conspicuous because they differ geologically from the surrounding rock.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[escarpment]]}}{{anchor|escarpments}}
{{defn|A long {{gli|cliff}} or steep slope separating two comparatively level or more gently sloping surfaces and resulting from erosion or faulting.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[esker]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''os''', '''eskar''', or '''eschar'''.}}
{{defn|A long, winding ridge of [[stratum|stratified]] sand and gravel, usually occurring in {{gli|glaciated}} or formerly glaciated areas.}}

{{term|[[estavelle]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''inversac'''.}}
{{defn|A {{gli|karstic}} {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|sinkhole}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ponor}} which, depending on the season and weather conditions, can serve as either a sink or a source of {{gli|freshwater}}.}}

{{term|[[estuary]]}}{{anchor|estuaries}}
{{defn|The broad lower course of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|river}} where it enters the ocean and is affected by the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|tides}}. Compare ''{{gli|delta}}''.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|étang}}
{{defn|A shallow pool or {{gli|lake}} caused by the ponding of {{gli|backwash}} draining from a {{gli|beach}} by material brought ashore by the sea.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[etchplain]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|plain}} beneath which the {{gli|bedrock}} has been subjected to considerable subsurface [[weathering]], known as "etching". Erosion of the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|regolith}} overlying an etchplain often exposes topographical irregularities such as {{gli|inselbergs}}.}}

{{term|ethnic group}}
{{defn|A group of people in a country who share a unique culture and identity.}}

{{term|[[pothole (landform)|evorsion]]}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|pothole}}''.}}

{{term|exaration}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|plucking}}''.}}

{{term|[[exclave]]}}{{anchor|exclaves}}
{{defn|A portion of a state or territory that is geographically separated from the main part by surrounding foreign territory of one or more other states or political entities. Many exclaves are also {{gli|enclaves}}.}}

{{term|exotic stream}}
{{defn|A {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|stream}} found in an area that is too dry to have spawned such a flow. The flow originates in some moister section.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[extinct volcano]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|volcano}} that is not expected to erupt again.<ref name="USGS 2010"/>}}

{{term|[[exurb]]}}
{{defn|A region or district that lies outside a {{gli|city}} and usually beyond its {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|suburbs}}; a place of this type is called an ''exurb''. Compare ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|rural}}''.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{glossary end}}

==F==
{{glossary}}
{{term|[[fairway (navigation)|fairway]]}}
{{defn|The part of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|navigable waterway}} containing the navigable {{gli|channel}}, in particular the central, deepest, widest, or most commonly used channel.<ref name="ASCE/ACSM/ASPRS"/>}}

{{term|[[fall line]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|geomorphologic}} [[unconformity]] between an {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|upland}} region of relatively hard [[basement (geology)|crystalline basement rock]] and a {{gli|coastal plain}} of softer [[sedimentary rock]].}}

{{term|[[fallow]]}}
{{defn|Agricultural land that is plowed or tilled but left unseeded during a {{gli|growing season}}. Fallowing is usually done to conserve moisture and soil nutrients.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[false origin]]}}
{{defn|A selected point in a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|projected coordinate system}} from which the position of any place can be expressed in terms of its coordinates with respect to the selected point. The false origin differs from the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|true origin}} in order to exclude negative values.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[fast ice]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''land-fast ice''' and '''shore-fast ice'''.}}
{{defn|{{gli|sea ice|Sea ice}} that is more or less securely "fastened" to a {{gli|coastline}}, {{gli|anchor ice|to the sea floor}}, or to grounded {{gli|icebergs}}, and which therefore does not move with currents and winds (unlike {{gli|drift ice}}). The formation of fast ice is usually seasonal and its properties vary with water depth, {{gli|topography}} of the sea floor, {{gli|tides}}, and pressure from adjacent drift ice.}}

{{term|[[fault (geology)|fault]]}}{{anchor|faults}}
{{defn|A fracture in the Earth's {{gli|crust}} accompanied by a displacement of one side of the fracture.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[fault-block mountain]]}}
{{defn|A mountain mass created by either the uplift of land between {{gli|faults}} or the subsidence of land outside the faults.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[fault zone]]}}
{{defn|An area of numerous {{gli|fault|fractures}} in the Earth's crust along which movement has occurred. The movement may be in any direction and involve material on either or both sides of the fractures.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[federation]]}}
{{defn|A form of government in which powers and functions are divided between a central government and a number of political subdivisions that have a significant degree of political autonomy.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[fell]]}}
{{defn|A wild, barren, high-altitude {{gli|moor}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|upland}}, or a treeless {{gli|alpine}} {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|tundra}}, often studded with boulders or rock {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|outcrops}}; or a broad, isolated mountain {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|summit}}. The term is used primarily in northern England, Scotland, and Fennoscandia.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|felsenmeer}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|blockfield}}''.}}

{{term|[[fen]]}}{{anchor|fens}}
{{defn|An area of spongy, waterlogged ground containing decaying vegetation that accumulates over time into [[peat]], and which is supplied with an input of mineral-rich {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|surface water|surface}} or {{gli|groundwater}} by a direct connection to a larger hydrological system. This external input typically results in higher mineral concentrations and a more alkaline [[pH]] than other peat-forming ecosystems such as {{gli|bogs}}. Fens are one of four main types of {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|wetland}}, along with bogs, {{gli|marshes}}, and {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|swamps}}.}}

{{term|field}}
{{defn|no=1|Any large, open, outdoor space, natural or man-made, especially one with a natural surface covering such as grass or soil and having few trees and structures, permitting long {{gli|line of sight|sightlines}}.}}
{{defn|no=2|([[field (geography)|variable]]) A property, quantity, or observation (e.g. temperature, soil moisture, population density, etc.) that can be theoretically assigned to any point of space and which varies across space. Both scalar and vector fields are found in {{gli|GIS}} applications, although the former is more common. Also '''spatially dependent variable'''.}}

{{term|[[figure of the Earth]]}}
{{defn|The size and shape of the Earth as studied in {{gli|geodesy}}. Applications requiring varying levels of precision have led to the development of many different models of the Earth, ranging from simple spheres to much more accurate approximations such as {{gli|geoids}}.}}

{{term|[[firn]]}}
{{defn|A type of ice that is at an intermediate stage between [[snow]] and {{gli|glacial}} ice. More specifically, firn is partially compacted {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|névé}} left over from past seasons which has subsequently recrystallized into a form that is harder and denser than névé.}}

{{term|first bottom}}
{{defn|A colloquial term loosely applied to the topographically lowest step of a {{gli|floodplain}} that experiences regular flooding (though the frequency considered "regular" is inconsistently specified), i.e. the first part to be inundated when a flood occurs. The term is used primarily in the Midwestern United States.}}

{{term|[[first law of geography|First Law of Geography]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''Tobler's First Law of Geography'''.}}
{{defn|A fundamental assumption of {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|spatial analysis}} articulated by the Swiss-American geographer [[Waldo Tobler]] as "Everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things." This principle is considered foundational to the concepts of {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|spatially dependent variable|spatial dependence}} and {{gli|autocorrelation}},<ref name="Wade and Sommer 2006"/> and is expressed mathematically in the [[inverse distance weighting]] method of spatial {{gli|interpolation}} and in {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|regionalized variable theory}} as the basis for {{gli|kriging}}.}}

{{term|[[firth]]}}
{{defn|Another name for a coastal {{gli|inlet}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|strait}}, or {{gli|bay}} associated with the {{gli|mouth}} of a large {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|river}}, where the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|tidal}} effects of {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|salt water|seawater}} passing upriver have widened the riverbed into an {{gli|estuary}}. The term is used primarily in Scotland.}}

{{term|[[fish ladder]]}}
{{defn|A series of shallow steps down which water is allowed to flow, designed to permit [[salmon]] or other anadromous fish to circumvent artificial barriers such as {{gli|dams}} as they swim upstream to spawn.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[fissure]]}}{{anchor|fissures}}
{{defn|A long, narrow opening or line of breakage made by cracking or splitting, especially in rock or earth.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[fjard]]}}{{anchor|fjards}}
{{defn|A large, open, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|navigable}} {{gli|body of water}} between the {{gli|islands}} of an {{gli|archipelago}} or between an island and the {{gli|mainland}}, either on the sea coast or in freshwater lakes or rivers.}}

{{term|[[fjord]]}}{{anchor|fjords|fiord|fiords}}
{{ghat|Also '''fiord'''.}}
{{defn|A long, narrow, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|navigable}} marine {{gli|inlet}} with steep sides or {{gli|cliffs}} created by {{gli|glacial}} erosion.}}
[[File:View to Tafjorden, Fjord, Norway, 2019 July.jpg|thumb|350px|A '''{{gli|fjord}}''' in Norway]]

{{term|[[flark]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|hollow}} or {{gli|depression}} within a {{gli|bog}}, often water-filled and usually occurring as part of a repeated series of such depressions which are elongated and parallel to each other and separated by intervening ridges known as ''strings''.}}

{{term|[[flood bypass]]}}
{{defn|}}

{{term|[[flood wall]]}}
{{defn|A primarily vertical artificial barrier designed to temporarily contain the waters of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|river}} or other {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|waterway}} which may rise to high levels during flooding events. Flood walls are narrower and typically easier to build than {{gli|dikes}} or {{gli|levees}}, so they are mainly used in locations where space is limited or where building more traditional flood-control structures would interfere with other interests.}}

{{term|floodbank}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|levee}}''.}}

{{term|[[floodplain]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''bottomland'''.}}
{{defn|A broad, flat area of land adjacent to a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|river}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|stream}} which is leveled by annual flooding and by the lateral and downstream movement of {{gli|meanders}}.}}

{{term|[[flood control channel|floodway]]}}
{{defn|no=1|Another name for a {{gli|flood bypass}}.}}
{{defn|no=2|A large-capacity {{gli|channel}} or {{gli|culvert}} designed to capture and divert floodwaters or excess streamflow from populous or flood-prone areas and eventually drain it into a river or other body of water, e.g. an artificial drainage canal bounded by {{gli|levee|levees}}. They often run below street level in larger cities.}}
{{defn|no=3|A road crossing of a flood-prone channel, built at or close to the natural ground level. It is similar to a {{gli|causeway}} but crosses a shallow and often dry {{gli|depression}} that is subject to flooding, rather than a continuously flooded waterway.}}
{{defn|no=4|A part of a {{gli|floodplain}} kept clear of encumbrances and reserved for emergency diversion of floodwaters.}}

{{term|floor}}
{{defn|The level or nearly level lower part of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|valley}} or {{gli|basin}}, or the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|streambed|bed}} of any {{gli|body of water}}, such as a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|stream}}, {{gli|lake}}, or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ocean}}.}}

{{term|flow regime}}
{{defn|The general behavior of a river or other {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|watercourse}} as defined by its average flow conditions throughout the year, including seasonal variations in {{gli|discharge}}, size and frequency of floods, and frequency and duration of droughts.<ref name="Mayhew"/>}}

{{term|[[flute (glacial)|flute]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|glacial}} landform created by the movement of a glacier around a boulder, consisting of a lineation or streamlined furrow or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ridge}} parallel to the direction of ice movement. They generally form in newly deposited {{gli|glacial till|till}} or older {{gli|drift}} and can reach heights of {{convert|25|m|ft}} and lengths of {{convert|20|km|mi}}.}}

{{term|[[fluvial]]}}
{{defn|Of or pertaining to {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|rivers}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|streams}}; produced by the action of a river or stream.<ref name="NRCS 2018"/>}}

{{term|[[fluvial terrace]]}}
{{defn|}}

{{term|focality}}
{{defn|The characteristic of a place that follows from its interconnections with more than one other place. When interaction within a region comes together at a single place (i.e. when the movement focuses on that location), the place is said to possess focality.}}

{{term|[[focus (earthquake)|focus]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''hypocenter'''.}}
{{defn|The point inside the [[Earth's crust]] from which an {{gli|earthquake}} originates.}}

{{term|[[foothills]]}}
{{defn|A geographic transition zone defined by gradual increases in elevation between {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|plains}} or low-relief {{gli|hills}} and adjacent topographically higher hills, {{gli|mountains}}, or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|uplands}}.}}

{{term|footslope}}
{{defn|The part of the profile of a {{gli|grade|hillslope}} that forms the concave surface at the base of the slope. It is a transition area between sites of erosion and transport higher up the slope (e.g. the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|shoulder}} and {{gli|backslope}}) and sites of deposition further down the slope (the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|toeslope}}).<ref name="NRCS 2018"/>}}

{{term|[[ford (crossing)|ford]]}}
{{defn|A place, natural or man-made, where a river or stream is shallow enough to be crossed by wading, or by getting a vehicle's wheels wet (as opposed to crossing a permanently dry {{gli|bridge}}). Fords may be seasonal or temporary, becoming impassable during high water.}}

{{term|foredeep}}
{{defn|A relatively narrow, deep, elongated, and steep-sided trough in the {{gli|floor|ocean floor}}, usually near or parallel to a mountainous land area or associated with an {{gli|archipelago}}, or such a trough when infilled with sediment.<ref name="Clark"/> See also ''{{gli|foreland basin}}''.}}

{{term|foreland}}
{{defn|no=1|Any land area or territory located in front of something else.}}
{{defn|no=2|A landform projecting into the sea, e.g. a {{gli|cape}} or {{gli|headland}}.}}
{{defn|no=3|The seaward trading area associated with a particular {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|port}} or {{gli|harbor}}.<ref name="Clark"/>}}
{{defn|no=4|([[glacier foreland|glaciology]]) The area between the current leading edge of a {{gli|glacier}} and the {{gli|moraines}} of the most recent maximum.}}

{{term|[[foreland basin]]}}
{{defn|A type of structural {{gli|endmember basin}} that develops adjacent and parallel to a {{gli|mountain range}} as a result of [[lithospheric flexure]] during its orogeny. Topographic loading and downflexure creates space in the basin that is filled by sediment eroded from the range. Compare ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|rift basin}}''.}}

{{term|[[foreshore]]}}
{{defn|The part of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|shore|seashore}} located between the lowest {{gli|mean low water|low water line}} and the {{gli|mean high water|mean high water line}}.<ref name="Clark"/> See also ''{{gli|intertidal zone}}''; contrast ''{{gli|backshore}}''.}}

{{term|[[forest]]}}{{anchor|forests}}
{{defn|Any extensive area dominated by [[community (biology)|communities]] of trees.}}

{{term|formal region}}
{{defn|An area of the Earth that is unified by some measurable physical or human characteristic.}}

{{term|form line}}
{{defn|A {{gli|contour line}} whose precise position on a map has not been accurately surveyed but rather {{gli|interpolated}} from surrounding contours.<ref name="Goudie"/>}}

{{term|[[fresh water]]}}
{{defn|Any naturally occurring water characterized by low concentrations (typically less than 0.05% by volume) of dissolved salts and other solids relative to either {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|salt water}} or [[brackish water]]. Sources of fresh water on Earth include {{gli|glaciers}}, {{gli|ice caps}}, {{gli|icebergs}}, {{gli|bogs}}, {{gli|lakes}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|rivers}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|streams}}, and most {{gli|groundwater}}.}}

{{term|[[friction of distance]]}}
{{defn|The influence and restraining effect of distance on all forms of movement, based on the fundamental geographical principle that movement necessarily incurs one or more costs, in the form of physical effort, energy, time, and/or other resources, and that these costs are directly proportional to the distance traveled. Such costs effectively resist the propensity for movement, akin to the friction of classical mechanics, and hence the concept of physical distance is a critical factor in determining whether or not a given movement, event, or process occurs.}}

{{term|[[wikt:frontalier|frontalier]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''cross-border worker''' and '''frontier worker'''.}}
{{defn|Someone who lives in one country and works in a neighboring country, commuting across the international {{gli|border}} each workday and returning to their country of residence on a nightly or weekly basis;<ref>{{cite web |title=Working Across Borders |url=https://www.remaininfrance.fr/workingacrossbordersnew |website=Remain in France Together (RIFT)}}</ref> someone who lives and works across political or geographical {{gli|frontiers}}.}}

{{term|frontcountry}}
{{defn|}}

{{term|[[frontier]]}}{{anchor|frontiers}}
{{defn|no=1|The area near or beyond a political or geographical {{gli|border|boundary}}; a {{gli|march}} or borderland.}}
{{defn|no=2|The area near or beyond the edge of a settled or civilized area, consisting of sparsely populated or uninhabited {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|wilderness}}. See also ''{{gli|hinterland}}'' and ''{{gli|edgeland}}''.}}

{{term|frost hollow}}
{{ghat|Also '''frost pocket'''.}}
{{defn|A hollow or {{gli|depression}} surrounded on all sides by higher terrain, such as the {{gli|floor}} of a deep {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|valley}}, where very cold, dense air tends to concentrate as strong terrestrial radiation on the slopes above forces the cold air downslope, often at nighttime. Temperatures in these hollows can be tens of degrees colder than the immediate surroundings.}}

{{term|functional diversity}}
{{defn|The characteristic of a place where a variety of different activities (economic, political, or social) occur, most often associated with {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|urban}} places.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|functional region}}
{{defn|An area of the Earth's surface that is defined by its interaction with or connectivity to other regions.}}

==G==
{{glossary}}
{{term|[[gallery forest]]}}
{{defn|A narrow strip of trees or shrubs lining both {{gli|banks}} of a river or stream in otherwise treeless, open country. Above very narrow streams, the foliage on each side may meet in the canopy.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[gazetteer]]}}
{{defn|A geographical dictionary or directory used in conjunction with a {{gli|map}} or {{gli|atlas}} and containing information concerning the geographical make-up, social statistics, and physical features of a {{gli|country}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|region}}, or {{gli|continent}}.}}

{{term|gentilic}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|demonym}}''.}}

{{term|[[geo (landform)|geo]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''gio'''.}}
{{defn|A narrow {{gli|inlet}} within a deep cleft in a rocky {{gli|coastline}}, sheltered by tall, near-vertical cliffs created by wave-driven erosion along faults and bedding planes in the rock. The term is primarily used in the islands of northern Scotland.}}

{{term|[[geoblocking]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''geolocking'''.}}
{{defn|A technology that restricts access to online content according to an Internet user's geographical location, which may be determined by any of various geolocation techniques, including checking the user's [[IP address]] against a blacklist, triangulating {{gli|GPS}} queries, and measuring the [[network delay|latency]] of a signal traveling between the user's computer and another endpoint in the network.}}

{{term|[[geocode]]}}
{{defn|A concise, human-readable series of letters, numbers, and/or other symbols which represents and uniquely identifies a particular geographic entity so as to distinguish it from other geographic entities in a finite set or database.}}

{{term|[[geocoding]]}}
{{defn|The conversion of a text-based description of a physical location, such as the name of a place or a street address, into {{gli|geographic coordinates}}, e.g. {{gli|latitude}} and {{gli|longitude}}, which can then be plotted in a spatial {{gli|coordinate system}} and represented on a {{gli|map}} to locate and uniquely identify its position on the Earth's surface. The reverse process, where geographic coordinates are converted into a text-based description, is known as '''reverse geocoding'''.}}

{{term|[[geocell (cartography)|geocell]]}}
{{defn|In many {{gli|geographic information systems}}, an imaginary polygon on the surface of the Earth with dimensions 1 {{gli|degree}} of {{gli|latitude}} by 1 degree of {{gli|longitude}}, or approximately {{convert|111|x|111|km|mi|abbr=off}} at the {{gli|Equator}}, representing an area equal to about {{convert|12321|sqkm|sqmi|abbr=off}}. The east-west distance equal to 1 degree of longitude gradually decreases as one approaches the poles, such that the shape of a geocell becomes increasingly trapezoidal at higher latitudes.}}

{{term|[[geodata]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''geospatial data''', '''georeferenced information''', and '''geoinformation'''.}}
{{defn|Any data or information having an implicit or explicit association with one or more locations on the Earth, especially that used for {{gli|georeferencing}} in {{gli|geographic information system|GIS}} databases.}}

{{term|[[geodesics on an ellipsoid|geodesic]]}}{{anchor|geodesics}}
{{ghat|Also '''orthodrome''', '''geodesic line''', and '''geodetic line'''.}}
{{defn|In {{gli|geodesy}}, the shortest line on a specific surface between two particular points on that surface. The geodesic between a given two points on a flat plane is a segment of a straight line drawn between those points; the geodesic between two points on a sphere is a shorter [[arc (geometry)|arc]] of the {{gli|great circle}} which connects both points. Geodesics may also be plotted on the surface of an ellipsoid, such as an idealized {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|reference ellipsoid}} used to model the {{gli|figure of the Earth|shape of the Earth}}.<ref name="ASCE/ACSM/ASPRS"/>}}

{{term|[[geodesy]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''geodetics'''.}}
{{defn|The science of accurately measuring and understanding the Earth's {{gli|figure of the Earth|geometric shape}}, orientation in space, and [[gravitational field]] and how these properties change over time.}}

{{term|[[geodetic control network]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''geodetic network''', '''reference network''', or '''control point network'''.}}
{{defn|}}

{{term|[[geodetic datum]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''geodetic system''', '''geodetic reference datum''', or '''geodetic reference system'''.}}
{{defn|A {{gli|geographic coordinate system|coordinate system}} and set of reference points used for locating places on the Earth, which defines {{gli|horizontal datum|horizontal}} and {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|vertical datum|vertical}} coordinates upon a particular {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|reference ellipsoid}} that approximates the {{gli|figure of the Earth}}. Geodetic datums are used in {{gli|geodesy}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|navigation}}, and {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|surveying}} applications to translate positions indicated on paper or digital {{gli|maps}} to their actual positions on the Earth; because the Earth is an imperfect ellipsoid, localized datums such as the [[ED50]] covering only specific countries or regions are often more accurate representations of their area of coverage than global standards such as the [[WGS 84]] of the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|World Geodetic System}}.}}

{{term|geodetic north}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|true north}}''.}}

{{term|geodetics}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|geodesy}}''.}}

{{term|[[geodynamics]]}}
{{defn|A subfield of [[geophysics]] and {{gli|Earth science}} that studies the [[dynamics (physics)|physical dynamics]] of the Earth by applying physics, chemistry, and mathematics to the understanding of how [[mantle convection]] and other internal processes lead to {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|plate tectonics}} and geological phenomena such as {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|orogeny|mountain formation}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|volcanism}}, [[earthquake]]s, and {{gli|fault|faulting}}, among others.}}

{{term|[[geofence]]}}
{{defn|A virtual boundary or perimeter drawn around a real-world geographic area in a {{gli|geographic information system|GIS}} software application, allowing distinctions between the properties of adjacent places which cannot be physically made on the ground to be made and stored digitally in an electronic database.}}

{{term|[[geographic coordinate system]]}}
{{defn|A [[coordinate system]] used in geography that enables every location on Earth to be specified by a set of numbers, letters, or symbols. Geographic coordinates are often chosen such that one of the numbers represents a vertical position such as {{gli|elevation}} and two or three other numbers represent a horizontal position such as {{gli|latitude}} and {{gli|longitude}}.}}

{{term|geographic factor}}
{{defn|Any physical or human condition that impacts the environment of a geographic place.}}

<span id="geographic information science"></span>{{term|[[geographic information science]] (GIS)}}
{{ghat|Also '''GIScience'''.}}
{{defn|The scientific study of data structures and computational techniques for capturing, representing, processing, and analyzing {{gli|geodata|geographic information}}.}}

<span id="geographic information system"></span>{{term|[[geographic information system]] (GIS)}}
{{defn|Any system of computer software tools designed to allow users to record, store, manipulate, analyze, manage, and present large sets of spatial or {{gli|geodata|geographic data}}.}}

<span id="GNIS"></span>{{term|[[Geographic Names Information System]] (GNIS)}}
{{defn|A digital public-domain database developed by the [[U.S. Geological Survey]] and the [[U.S. Board on Geographic Names]] which contains name and locative information about more than two million physical and cultural features located throughout the [[United States]] and its territories. Each feature recorded in the database receives a unique feature {{gli|geocode|record identifier}} called a ''GNIS identifier''.}}

{{term|geographic pattern}}
{{defn|Any observable model, style, or trend in some element of {{gli|geography}}, generally observed on {{gli|maps}}.}}

{{term|geographic process}}
{{defn|Any process or activity, natural or man-made, that brings changes to some aspect of physical or human geography.}}

{{term|geographical inertia}}
{{ghat|Also '''geographical momentum'''.}}
{{defn|The tendency of a place with established installations and services to maintain its size and its importance as a focus of economic or industrial activity after the conditions originally influencing its development have appreciably altered, ceased to be relevant, or disappeared.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[geographical mile]]}}
{{defn|A unit of length defined as the distance equal to one [[minute of arc]] along the Earth's {{gli|Equator}}: approximately {{convert|1,855.3|m|mi km}}. The precise length varies with the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|reference ellipsoid}} used to approximate the {{gli|figure of the Earth|shape of the Earth}}. Regardless of the particular ellipsoid, the length of one {{gli|degree}} of {{gli|longitude}} at the Equator is equal to exactly 60 geographical miles.}}

{{term|[[geography]]}}
{{defn|The scientific study of the lands, features, inhabitants, and phenomena of [[Earth]].}}

{{term|[[geoid]]}}{{anchor|geoids}}
{{defn|The shape that the surface of the Earth's {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|oceans}} would take under the influence of [[gravity of Earth|Earth's gravity]] and [[Earth's rotation|rotational acceleration]] alone, in the absence of other influences such as winds and {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|tides}}. It is often characterized as the precise mathematical {{gli|figure of the Earth}}: a smooth but irregular gravitational [[equipotential surface]] at every point of which, by definition, the direction of the force of gravity is always perpendicular and {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|spirit levels}} are always parallel. Its shape results from anomalies in the Earth's gravitational field caused by the uneven distribution of mass within and on the Earth's surface. A {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|reference ellipsoid}} is an idealized approximation of the more complex and accurate geoid.}}

{{term|[[geoinformatics]]}}
{{defn|The science and technology which develops and uses [[information science]] infrastructures to address problems and analyze data within {{gli|geography}}, {{gli|cartography}}, {{gli|Earth science|geoscience}}, and related branches of science and engineering.}}

{{term|geoinformation}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|geodata}}''.}}

{{term|[[geolocation]]}}
{{defn|The identification or estimation of the real-world geographic {{gli|location}} of an object, involving the generation of a set of {{gli|geographic coordinate system|geographic coordinates}} in order to determine a more meaningful description of location, such as a street address.}}

{{term|geolocking}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|geoblocking}}''.}}

{{term|[[geomatics]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''geospatial science'''.}}
{{defn|The scientific discipline that involves gathering, storing, processing, and delivering geographic or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|spatial reference system|spatially referenced}} information.}}

{{term|geometer}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|surveyor}}''.}}

{{term|[[geomorphology]]}}{{anchor|geomorphologic}}
{{defn|The study of the arrangement and form of the Earth's {{gli|crust}} and of the relationship between these physical features and the geologic structures beneath.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[geopotential]]}}
{{defn|no=1|defn=The potential of the Earth's [[gravitational field]], expressed as the sum, {{math|U}}, of the [[gravitational potential]] {{math|V<sub>g</sub>}} of the Earth at point {{math|P}} and the rotational potential {{math|V<sub>c</sub>}} at the same point, i.e. {{math|U {{=}} V<sub>g</sub> + V<sub>c</sub>}}.<ref name="ASCE/ACSM/ASPRS"/>}}
{{defn|no=2|defn=The negative of the sum of the gravitational potential {{math|V<sub>g</sub>}} and the rotational potential {{math|V<sub>c</sub>}}, i.e. {{math|U {{=}} −(V<sub>g</sub> + V<sub>c</sub>)}}. This alternative definition is often used by physicists.<ref name="ASCE/ACSM/ASPRS"/>}}
{{defn|no=3|The [[potential energy]] of a unit mass relative to the {{gli|geoid}}, numerically equivalent to the [[work (physics)|work]] which would be done in lifting the mass from the geoid against the force of gravity to the elevation at which the mass is actually located.<ref name="ASCE/ACSM/ASPRS"/>}}

{{defn|The study of geographical knowledge from any and all points of view, past or present, true or false;<ref>John K. Wright&nbsp;(1947).&nbsp;"Terrae Incognitae: The Place of the Imagination in Geography",&nbsp;''Annals of the Association of American Geographers'',&nbsp;37:1,&nbsp;1–15,&nbsp;doi:10.1080/00045604709351940</ref> the study of the nature and expression of geographical ideas.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[geosphere]]}}
{{defn|The collective non-living parts of the Earth: the {{gli|lithosphere}}, the {{gli|atmosphere}}, the {{gli|cryosphere}}, and the {{gli|hydrosphere}}.<ref name="USGS 2010"/>}}

{{defn|}}

{{term|[[ghetto]]}}
{{defn|A section of a city occupied by members of a minority group who live there because of social restrictions on their residential choices. Originally, the term referred specifically to a section of a European city to which [[Judaism|Jews]] were confined.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[ghost town]]}}
{{defn|A deserted or abandoned village, town, or city, especially one in which remaining buildings and infrastructure such as roads are still visible. The term is also sometimes used to refer to settlements that are still populated, but significantly less so than in previous years.}}

{{term|[[wikt:glacial|glacial]]}}
{{defn|Of or pertaining to a {{gli|glacier}} or to the consequences of {{gli|glaciation}}; formed, deposited, caused, or affected by {{gli|glaciological}} processes.<ref name="Troeh & Donahue">{{cite book |last1=Troeh |first1=Frederick R. |last2=Donahue |first2=Roy Luther |title=Dictionary of Agricultural and Environmental Science |date=2003 |publisher=Iowa State Press |location=Ames, Iowa |isbn=9780813802831 |ol=8026680M |edition=1st }}</ref>}}

{{defn|See ''{{gli|erratic}}''.}}
