{{term|[[glacial lake]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|lake}} or other enclosed {{gli|body of water}} created by historical or ongoing {{gli|glacial}} activity; e.g. the [[Great Lakes]] of North America.}}

{{term|[[glacial till]]}}
{{defn|The mass of rocks and finely ground material carried by a {{gli|glacier}} and deposited when the ice melts. This creates an unstratified material of varying composition.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[glacial trough]]}}
{{defn|}}

{{term|[[glaciation]]}}{{anchor|glaciated}}
{{defn|no=1|The process or state of being covered with a {{gli|glacier}}.}}
{{defn|no=2|Another name for a [[glacial period]], an interval of time that is marked by colder temperatures and advancing glaciers.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[glacier]]}}{{anchor|glaciers|glacial}}
{{defn|A persistent mass of dense [[ice]] that moves slowly but constantly under its own weight, and which is composed largely of compacted [[snow]] that forms over very long periods of time wherever the annual accumulation of snow exceeds its rate of melting and sublimation. Glaciers slowly deform and abrade the land beneath them, causing many unique geomorphological processes and creating a huge variety of landforms including {{gli|cirques}}, {{gli|moraines}}, and {{gli|fjords}}. They form exclusively on land and are distinct from the much thinner ice that forms on bodies of water.<ref name="USGS 2010"/>}}

{{term|[[glaciology]]}}{{anchor|glaciological}}
{{defn|The scientific study of {{gli|glaciers}}, including their formation, composition, behavior, causes, effects, and distribution;<ref name="Troeh & Donahue"/> or more generally of ice or any natural phenomena involving ice.}}

{{term|[[glacis]]}}
{{defn|A smooth, gently sloping surface at the foot of a {{gli|hill}}, {{gli|mountain}}, or any other high {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|promontory}}, whether natural or artificial. In the latter case, the term is used in particular to describe a stone or earthen {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|slope}} constructed at the base of some historical military fortifications.<ref name="Troeh & Donahue"/>}}

{{term|[[glade (geography)|glade]]}}{{anchor|glades}}
{{ghat|Also '''clearing'''.}}
{{defn|Any large, open, mostly treeless area within a {{gli|forest}}.}}

{{term|[[glen]]}}
{{defn|A long {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|valley}} bounded by gently sloping, concave sides, and typically narrower and deeper than a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|strath}}. The term is used primarily in [[Scotland]].}}

{{term|glint}}
{{defn|A steep {{gli|cliff}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|terrace}}, or edge of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|plateau}}.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[wikt:global|global]]}}{{anchor|globally}}
{{defn|no=1|Of or concerning all parts of the world (i.e. worldwide); affecting or distributed across the whole of the Earth.}}
{{defn|no=2|Of or relating to a {{gli|globe}} or sphere; spherical or approximately so.}}
{{defn|no=3|Comprehensive; total; encompassing all or nearly all considerations, categories, items, etc.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[global city]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''world city''', '''power city''', or '''alpha city'''.}}
{{defn|A {{gli|city}} which functions as an important or primary node in the [[global economy]]. Though criteria are not strictly defined, a global city typically is very large; dominates trade and economic interactions within a large surrounding area; supports a large and demographically diverse population; serves as a center of ideas and innovation in business, science, culture, and politics; and/or is a headquarters for major financial institutions, multinational corporations, or worldwide media and communications networks.}}

{{term|[[global navigation satellite system]] (GNSS)}}{{anchor|global navigation satellite system|GNSS}}
{{defn|}}

{{term|[[Global Positioning System]] (GPS)}}{{anchor|Global Positioning System|GPS}}
{{defn|A {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|satellite navigation|satellite}}-based {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|radionavigation}} {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|positioning system}} owned and operated by the [[United States Department of Defense]] and made available for use by both the military and the general public. It is one of several {{gli|GNSS}} standards that provides {{gli|geolocation}} and time information, transmitted via [[microwave]] signals, to enabled {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|satellite navigation device|satellite navigation devices}}, known as ''GPS receivers'', anywhere on or near the Earth where there is an unobstructed line of sight to at least four GPS satellites. Modern state-of-the-art GPS receivers can accurately pinpoint locations to within {{convert|30|cm|ft}}.}}

{{term|[[globalization]]}}
{{defn|The process of interaction and integration among people, companies, governments, and cultures across the world. A complex and multifaceted phenomenon, globalization is considered largely the result of economically motivated advances in transportation and communication technologies in the past several centuries which have dramatically increased interactions between otherwise isolated groups of people.}}

{{term|[[globe]]}}{{anchor|globes}}
{{defn|A true-to-scale {{gli|map}} of the Earth that duplicates its round shape and correctly represents relative areas, sizes, and shapes of physical features, distances, and directions.<ref name="OERI 1996"/>}}

{{term|gnamma}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|panhole}}''.}}

{{term|[[gore (surveying)|gore]]}}
{{defn|no=1|An irregularly shaped {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|parcel}} of land of any size, often approximately triangular, that is left between two adjoining {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|surveyed}} parcels as the result of incomplete or inaccurate {{gli|boundary}} surveys.<ref name="USDMATC"/>}}
{{defn|no=2|A lune-shaped {{gli|map}} which may be fitted to the surface of a {{gli|globe}} with a negligible amount of distortion.<ref name="USDMATC"/>}}

{{term|gorge}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|canyon}}''.}}

{{term|goulet}}
{{defn|A narrow passageway, particularly a narrow {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|strait}} or {{gli|inlet}} connecting a {{gli|gulf}}, {{gli|harbor}}, {{gli|lagoon}}, or {{gli|barachois}} to the sea, or a narrow {{gli|bar}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|neck}} of land between two bodies of water. See also ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|narrows}}'' and ''{{gli|gully}}''.}}

{{term|[[graben]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|depression}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|valley}} bounded on either side by distinct, parallel {{gli|escarpment|escarpments}} or {{gli|fault|faults}} and formed by the downward displacement of a block of the Earth's {{gli|crust}}. Grabens often occur side-by-side with {{gli|horst|horsts}}, their uplifted or non-displaced counterparts, in a repeated series of vertical displacements.}}

{{term|[[grade (slope)|grade]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|slope}}''', '''incline''', '''gradient''', '''pitch''', '''rise''', or '''mainfall'''.}}
{{defn|A physical surface that is inclined with respect to the horizontal, or the angle between that surface and the horizontal, typically expressed in degrees, or calculated as a ratio of "rise" (vertical distance) to "run" (horizontal distance) and expressed as a fraction or percentage; a larger number indicates a steeper incline. The term "grade" is often used to describe the incline of man-made surfaces such as roads and the roofs of buildings, whereas the term "slope" is more commonly used to describe natural surfaces such as the sides of {{gli|hills}} or {{gli|mountains}} or the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|streambed|beds}} and {{gli|banks}} of {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|watercourses}}.}}

{{term|[[grassland]]}}{{anchor|grasslands}}
{{defn|Any land area where the vegetation is dominated by grasses (i.e. plants of the botanical family [[Poaceae]]), sometimes also inclusive of [[graminoid|grass-like]] plants of other families. A large and important {{gli|biome}} occurring worldwide, grasslands may be natural or created for agricultural purposes.}}

{{term|graticule}}
{{defn|A network of lines on a {{gli|map}} or {{gli|chart}} (or imagined on the surface of the Earth) representing geodetic {{gli|circle of latitude|parallels}} of {{gli|latitude}} and {{gli|meridian|meridians}} of {{gli|longitude}}.<ref name="ASCE/ACSM/ASPRS"/>}}

{{term|[[gravimetry]]}}
{{defn|The measurement of the strength of a [[gravitational field]], especially the Earth's gravitational field, typically by calculating the acceleration due to gravity at a particular point on the Earth's surface. Because it can vary widely across the surface, knowing the local magnitude of the gravitational force is often necessary in order to produce accurate geographical data.}}

{{term|[[great circle]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''orthodrome'''.}}
{{defn|Any circle on the surface of a sphere created by the intersection of the sphere and a [[plane (geometry)|plane]] that passes through its center. A great circle divides the sphere into two equal hemispheres, and all of a sphere's great circles have the same center and circumference, which by definition is the largest possible circumference of the sphere. The mathematical properties of great circles make them useful in {{gli|geodesy}}, where they are often visualized upon the surface of the Earth (despite the fact that the Earth is {{gli|figure of the Earth|not a perfect sphere}}): for example, the {{gli|Equator}} of the idealized Earth is a great circle, and any {{gli|longitude|meridian}} with its {{gli|antimeridian}} forms a great circle. Because the shortest path between any two points on the surface of a sphere follows the arc of a great circle, {{gli|great-circle distance|great-circle distances}} are often used as approximations of {{gli|geodesics}} for the purposes of air and sea navigation. See also ''{{gli|small circle}}''.}}
[[File:Great circle passing through two points.svg|thumb|350px|A '''{{gli|great circle}}''' exactly bisects a sphere; the arc between points A and B is a '''{{gli|great-circle distance}}'''.]]

{{term|great-circle bearing}}
{{defn|The horizontal direction or {{gli|bearing}} followed by the arc of a {{gli|great circle}} through a given pair of terrestrial points, expressed as the angular distance from a reference direction.<ref name="USDMATC"/>}}

{{term|[[great-circle distance]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''orthodromic distance'''.}}
{{defn|The length of a line between two points which follows the arc of a {{gli|great circle}} as defined by the intersection of the Earth's surface with an imaginary plane passing through the Earth's center. It is the shortest route between those two points on the Earth's surface.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[green belt]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''greenway'''.}}
{{defn|A special land-use {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|zone}} designated in some cities to prevent development of wild, undeveloped, or agricultural land surrounding or adjacent to {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|urban}} areas, in order to conserve natural ecosystems, to allow the return and establishment of wildlife, and/or to create {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|urban green space}} for aesthetic or recreational purposes. The term may also refer more specifically to the boundary between developed and undeveloped areas rather than to the undeveloped area itself.}}

{{term|[[greenfield land|greenfield]]}}
{{defn|A previously undeveloped plot of land for which development is proposed or on which it is in progress,<ref name="Clark"/> or which is intentionally not being developed so as to permit it to evolve naturally. Compare ''{{gli|brownfield}}''.}}

{{term|[[grid reference|grid]]}}
{{defn|A pattern of lines on a {{gli|chart}} or {{gli|map}}, such as those representing {{gli|latitude}} and {{gli|longitude}}, which helps determine {{gli|absolute location}}.<ref name="OERI 1996"/>}}

{{term|grid magnetic angle}}
{{ghat|Also '''grid variation''' or '''grivation'''.}}
{{defn|The angular difference in direction between {{gli|grid north}} and {{gli|magnetic north}}, typically expressed in degrees east or west of grid north.<ref name="USDMATC"/>}}

{{term|[[grid north]]}}
{{defn|The direction northwards as indicated by the {{gli|grid|grid lines}} of a {{gli|map projection}}, which may or may not be aligned with {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|true north|geodetic north}} and {{gli|magnetic north}}.}}

{{term|grivation}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|grid magnetic angle}}''.}}

{{term|[[groundwater]]}}
{{defn|The water present beneath the Earth's surface in soil pore spaces and in fractures and voids within geological {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|stratum|strata}}. Contrast ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|surface water}}''.}}

{{term|[[grove (nature)|grove]]}}{{anchor|groves}}
{{defn|A small group of trees growing close together and generally surrounded by little or no undergrowth.}}

{{term|[[growing season]]}}
{{defn|The part of the year during which local weather conditions (i.e. temperature and precipitation) permit the normal growth of [[plant]]s in a given location. What defines a "growing season" is often informal and colloquial, and may vary widely by location and from year to year; in many places, the local growing season is defined as the period of time between the average date of the last [[frost]] (in temperate parts of the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|Northern Hemisphere}}, this typically occurs in the spring) to the average date of the first frost (in the autumn).<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[groyne]]}}
{{defn|A rigid, man-made hydraulic structure extending from an ocean {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|shore}} or river {{gli|bank}}, constructed to interrupt water flow and limit the movement of sediment by {{gli|longshore drift}}.}}

{{term|[[gulch]]}}
{{defn|A deep, V-shaped {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|valley}} formed by erosion, often containing a small stream or a dry {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|streambed}}, especially one in arid regions.}}

{{term|[[gulf (geography)|gulf]]}}{{anchor|gulfs}}
{{defn|A large arm or {{gli|inlet}} of an {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ocean}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|sea}} that lies within a curved coastline, similar to a {{gli|bay}} but usually larger and often with a narrower opening.}}

{{term|[[gully]]}}
{{defn|A landform resembling a large ditch or a small {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ravine}} created by the action of swift running water eroding deeply and sharply into soil, typically on a hillside.}}

{{term|[[gumbo (soil)|gumbo]]}}
{{defn|Any very fine, clayey soil which rapidly turns to sticky mud when wet. The term is used primarily in the United States and Canada.<ref name="Goudie"/>}}

{{term|[[guyot]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''tablemount'''.}}
{{defn|An isolated underwater {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|seamount}} with a flat top that is at least {{convert|200|m|ft}} below the water's surface.}}

{{term|gypsey}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|winterbourne}}''.}}

{{term|[[gyre]]}}{{anchor|gyres}}
{{defn|Any large system of circulating {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ocean currents}}, particularly those related to large-scale wind movements. Gyres are caused by the {{gli|Coriolis effect}} and play a fundamental role in the global {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|thermohaline circulation}}.}}
[[File:Currents.svg|thumb|right|400px|The Earth's oceans circulate within five major '''{{gli|gyres}}''' – the [[North Pacific Gyre|North Pacific]], [[North Atlantic Gyre|North Atlantic]], [[South Pacific Gyre|South Pacific]], [[South Atlantic Gyre|South Atlantic]], and [[Indian Ocean Gyre|Indian Ocean Gyres]] – as well as many smaller accessory {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ocean current|currents}}, depicted here on a map projection with a south polar aspect.]]

{{term|[[gyroscope]]}}
{{defn|A device consisting of a spinning disc or rotor mounted in such a way as to preserve the orientation and [[angular velocity]] of its axis of rotation with respect to an inertial reference frame, irrespective of perturbations to the mounting itself, which makes it possible to measure and maintain an unbiased equilibrium in the {{gli|attitude}} and/or {{gli|course}} of a moving object such as an airborne or waterborne vehicle or camera. Modern digital gyroscopes and their associated readouts are widely used in {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|navigation}} and {{gli|geodesy}} as the basic sensor in {{gli|direction}}-seeking, direction-keeping, and attitude stabilization systems.<ref name="USDMATC"/>}}

{{glossary end}}

==H==
{{glossary}}
{{term|[[habitus (sociology)|habitus]]}}
{{defn|An individual's sense of "home", or of their place in the world, comprising socially ingrained habits, beliefs, skills, and dispositions based on their geographical environment, cultural origin, inheritance, experiences, and the social networks they develop throughout their life, all of which may be subject to refashioning with passing time or increasing distance.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[hachure]]}}
{{defn|Any of a series of non-numerical lines used on a {{gli|map}} to indicate the general orientation and steepness of {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|topographical}} {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|terrain}}. Such lines vary in length, thickness, and spacing, with steeper slopes indicated by shorter, heavier, and more closely spaced lines.<ref name="Thompson 1988"/>}}

{{term|haff}}
{{defn|A coastal {{gli|lagoon}} of {{gli|fresh water|fresh}} or {{gli|brackish water}} on the south coast of the Baltic Sea, fed by a stream which is blocked by a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|nehrung}}, through which it is linked to the sea by a {{gli|channel}}.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|halo effect}}
{{defn|In the context of geography, the detrimental effect of a {{gli|border}} or other boundary on locations close to it, making those locations unattractive to people intending to visit or settle there; e.g. a political boundary in disputed territory, where {{gli|immigration}} across the boundary occurs frequently. There may also be beneficial effects on such locations.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|ham}}
{{defn|In southern England, a plot of meadow land, especially a tract of rich pasture near a river; or a small settlement, ranging in size from a single {{gli|homestead}} to a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|town}}.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[hamada]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''hammada'''.}}
{{defn|A {{gli|desert}} landscape consisting of high, largely barren, rocky {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|plateaus}} where most of the sand has been removed by {{gli|deflation}}, and thus lacking most surficial materials other than boulders and exposed {{gli|bedrock}}.<ref name="Goudie"/>}}

{{term|[[hamlet (place)|hamlet]]}}
{{defn|A small human settlement, variably defined as one the size of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|town}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|village}}, or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|parish}} or as a smaller subdivision of or satellite entity to a larger settlement.}}

{{term|[[hanging valley]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|tributary}} {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|valley}} that is higher in elevation than the main valley into which it drains, such that it appears to be "hanging" above the lower valley. Hanging valleys are commonly the result of differential {{gli|glacial}} erosion, when adjacent areas beneath a glacier are subjected to different rates of erosion.}}

{{term|[[harmonic tremor]]}}
{{defn|One of a series of continuous rhythmic {{gli|earthquake|earthquakes}} in the Earth's upper {{gli|lithosphere}} that can be detected by {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|seismographs}}. Harmonic tremors often precede or accompany {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|volcano|volcanic eruptions}}.<ref name="USGS 2010"/>}}

{{term|[[head of navigation]]}}
{{defn|The farthest point above the {{gli|mouth}} of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|river}} that can be navigated by watercraft, whether because of natural or man-made obstacles.}}

{{term|[[heading (navigation)|heading]]}}
{{defn|The {{gli|compass}} {{gli|cardinal directions|direction}} in which the bow or nose of a moving vessel or aircraft is pointed. This is not necessarily the same direction in which the vessel is actually traveling, known as its {{gli|course}}; any difference between heading and course is due to the motion of the air or water through which the vessel is moving, or other aerodynamic effects such as [[skid (aerodynamics)|skidding]] or [[slip (aerodynamics)|slipping]]. See also ''{{gli|bearing}}''.}}

{{term|[[headland]]}}{{anchor|headlands}}
{{defn|A high {{gli|coastal}} {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|promontory}} that extends out into a body of water, often surrounded by steep {{gli|cliffs}}. A very large headland is often called a {{gli|cape}}.}}

{{term|[[headwall]]}}
{{defn|A steep slope or sheer cliff face at the upper end of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|valley}} (e.g. at the back of a {{gli|cirque}}), or at the active face of a mine, pit, or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|quarry}}.<ref name="NRCS 2018"/>}}

{{term|[[headwaters]]}}
{{defn|no=1|Another name for the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|source}} of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|river}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|stream}}, or other {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|watercourse}}, i.e. the point or points furthest from the {{gli|mouth}} of a particular {{gli|channel}} at which precipitation, {{gli|meltwater}}, or {{gli|groundwater}} first accumulates into a persistent, identifiable, and/or named {{gli|body of water}} whose contents ultimately empty into that particular channel; or all of the uppermost {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|tributaries}} of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|watershed}} considered collectively (of which there may be thousands), typically including all streams identified as first-order through third-order in conventional {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|stream order}} systems.}}
{{defn|no=2|The entire {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|region}}, inclusive of land, surrounding these sources, often abutting the boundary of a {{gli|drainage divide}} that separates distinct watersheds.}}

{{term|[[hearth]]}}
{{defn|The source area of any innovation; the place from which an idea, crop, artifact, or good is diffused to other areas.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[wikt:heartland|heartland]]}}
{{defn|no=1|The central or interior part of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|region}}.}}
{{defn|no=2|A part of a region considered essential to the viability and survival of the whole.}}

{{term|[[heath]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''heathland'''.}}
{{defn|A shrubland habitat found mainly on free-draining, infertile, acidic soils and characterized by open, low-growing, woody vegetation.}}

{{term|[[hectare]] (ha)}}{{anchor|hectare|hectares}}
{{defn|A metric unit of area defined by a square with sides of 100 metres, equal to 10,000 m<sup>2</sup> or 2.471 {{gli|acres}}. There are 100 hectares in 1 square kilometre (km<sup>2</sup>).<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[hedgerow]]}}{{anchor|hedgerows|hedge|hedges}}
{{ghat|Also simply '''hedge'''.}}
{{defn|A line of closely spaced shrubs or trees, planted and trained so as to form a barrier or to mark a boundary between two neighboring areas, or to serve as a [[windbreak]] for crops in adjacent fields.}}

{{term|[[heliotrope (instrument)|heliotrope]]}}
{{defn|A device used in {{gli|geodetic}} {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|surveying}} to reflect sunlight onto a distant point so as to aid long-distance observations.<ref name="USDMATC">{{cite book |title=Glossary of mapping, charting, and geodetic terms |date=1973 |edition=3rd |publisher=United States Defense Mapping Agency Topographic Center |location=Washington, DC |url=https://archive.org/details/glossaryofmappin0000unit}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[Hemispheres of the Earth|hemisphere]]}}{{anchor|hemispheres}}
{{defn|One half of the Earth, usually conceived as resulting from the division of the globe into two equal parts of either {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|Northern Hemisphere|north}} and {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|Southern Hemisphere|south}} or {{gli|Eastern Hemisphere|east}} and {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|Western Hemisphere|west}}.<ref name="OERI 1996"/>}}

{{term|heteroclinal fold}}
{{defn|A geological {{gli|fold}} of which one side is sloped at an angle steeper than that of the other side.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|high plain}}
{{defn|A {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|plain}} lying at a high {{gli|elevation}}, generally above {{convert|600|m|ft}}.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[high water mark]]}}
{{defn|A natural or man-made demarcation that indicates the maximum rise of a {{gli|body of water}} over an area of land. Though not necessarily an actual physical mark, river or sea waters rising to a high point often leave a lasting physical impression such as a noticeable discoloration or deposited debris; such a mark is often the result of a [[flood]] or [[storm surge]]. High water marks may reflect an all-time high, an annual high, or the high point for some other period of time (e.g. a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|tidal}} cycle). A natural delineation created by debris deposited by a high tide is called a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|strandline}}. See also ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|wash margin}}'' and ''{{gli|mean high water}}''.}}

{{term|[[highland]]}}{{anchor|highlands}}
{{ghat|Sometimes used interchangeably with '''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|upland}}'''.}}
{{defn|no=1|Any elevated region of land, often one that is {{gli|mountain|mountainous}} or situated atop a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|plateau}}. The term is sometimes reserved for relatively low-elevation {{gli|mountain ranges}} or {{gli|foothills}}.}}
{{defn|no=2|Any area of land (mountainous or otherwise) that is higher in {{gli|elevation}} relative to another area. In this sense, the term is often used as a conditional descriptor to distinguish related [[habitat]]s or [[ecosystem]]s, especially freshwater {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|riparian area|riparian areas}}, on the basis of elevation above sea level.}}

{{term|[[highway]]}}{{anchor|highways}}
{{defn|Any major public or private road or other thoroughfare on land, especially one that is paved and capable of supporting high-capacity, rapid transit between {{gli|populated places}}.}}

{{term|[[hill]]}}{{anchor|hills|hilly|hillslope}}
{{defn|Any landform that extends above the surrounding {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|terrain}}. A hill is generally considered less steep than a {{gli|mountain}}.}}

{{term|[[hillock]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''knoll'''.}}
{{defn|A small {{gli|hill}}.}}

{{term|[[hinterland]]}}
{{defn|no=1|An area that is tributary to a place and linked to that place through lines of exchange or interaction.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}
{{defn|no=2|The area, not necessarily settled itself, that is nonetheless influenced by a particular {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|settlement}} or establishment; i.e. its {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|sphere of influence}}.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[historical geography]]}}
{{defn|A branch of {{gli|human geography}} that studies the ways in which geographic phenomena have changed over time, especially (though not necessarily limited to) geographic change as it relates to human activity; the geography of the past, whether real, perceived, or theoretical.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|hoe}}
{{defn|A projecting {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ridge}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|outcropping}} of land, its height ending abruptly or steeply. The term is used primarily in {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|placenames}} in Great Britain.}}

{{term|[[hogback (geology)|hogback]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''hog's back''' or '''hogsback'''.}}
{{defn|A long, narrow {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ridge}} or series of {{gli|hills}} with a narrow crest and steep, symmetrical slopes of nearly equal inclination on both flanks, especially one created by the differential erosion of an {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|outcropping}} which exposes [[homoclinal]] sedimentary rock strata. Compare ''{{gli|esker}}'', ''{{gli|drumlin}}'', and ''{{gli|cuesta}}''.}}
[[File:Hogback NM.jpg|thumb|right|350px|Aerial view of a '''{{gli|hogback}}''' in the southwestern United States]]

{{term|holding}}
{{defn|Land owned or occupied by legal right for the purpose of agriculture.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|homestead}}
{{defn|no=1|([[homestead (buildings)|dwelling]]) A house or home, especially an isolated farmhouse with its associated outbuildings on a large agricultural holding such as a [[ranch]]; or a small {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|rural}} settlement of dispersed farms.<ref name="Clark"/>}}
{{defn|no=2|([[homestead principle|legal concept]]) In the United States, a plot of land given legal meaning by a series of federal laws granting applicants ownership of land in the public domain upon the condition that they live on it and {{gli|improved land|improve}} it. Homesteaders were initially granted plots of {{convert|160|acre|sqkm}}, which was considered adequate to support a single family, but later as much as {{convert|640|acre|sqkm}}.}}

{{term|[[horizon]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''skyline'''.}}
{{defn|The apparent line that separates the ground from the sky, dividing all visible directions into two categories: those that intersect the Earth's surface and those that do not. When not obscured by buildings, trees, or mountains, the true horizon can be useful in navigation and determining positional orientation. In perfect visibility, to an observer on Earth standing at an elevation of {{convert|3|m|ft|sigfig=1}} from the horizontal, the horizon in any direction is approximately {{convert|6.5|km|mi|sigfig=1}} distant; at {{convert|30|m|ft|sigfig=1}}, it is {{convert|21|km|mi}} away.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|horizontal equivalent}}
{{defn|The distance between two points on a land surface when projected on to a perfectly horizontal (i.e. flat) plane, e.g. on a {{gli|map}}, as opposed to measuring the actual physical length along the real-world surface, which can be greatly increased by {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|slopes}} and other topographic variation. The distance between the start and end points of any route, even if at the same elevation, will often appear to be much shorter on a map than the shortest route that could actually be walked between them, because of the influence of real-world changes in vertical displacement along the path followed by the route.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|horn}}{{anchor|horns}}
{{defn|A {{gli|mountain}} formed by the back-to-back abutment of three or four adjacent {{gli|cirques}}, leaving a distinctly pyramidal peak.<ref name="Mayhew"/>}}

{{term|[[horst (geology)|horst]]}}
{{defn|A raised block of the Earth's {{gli|crust}}, bounded by parallel {{gli|escarpment|escarpments}} or {{gli|fault|faults}}, that has been displaced upward or has remained stationary while adjacent blocks on either side, known as {{gli|graben|grabens}}, have been displaced downward. Horsts and grabens often occur side-by-side in a repeated series of vertical displacements.}}

{{term|[[hotspot (geology)|hotspot]]}}{{anchor|hotspots}}
{{defn|An area in the middle of a {{gli|lithospheric plate}} where {{gli|magma}} rises from the {{gli|mantle}} and erupts at the Earth's surface, despite being far from the plate's {{gli|tectonic}} boundaries. {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|volcano|Volcanoes}} often occur above a hotspot.<ref name="USGS 2010"/>}}

{{term|hum}}
{{defn|A residual hill in limestone country, resembling a haystack, left standing when the surrounding land surface is eroded.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[human geography]]}}
{{defn|The branch of geography that studies humans and their communities, cultures, economies, and interactions with the environment by examining their relations with and across space and place. Along with {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|physical geography}}, it is one of the two major sub-fields of geography.}}

{{term|human–environment interaction}}
{{defn|The interdependent relationship between humans and the environment.}}

{{term|humanistic geography}}
{{ghat|Also '''humanist geography'''.}}
{{defn|An approach in {{gli|human geography}} which emphasizes the subjective as distinct from the objective in that it stresses the importance of perception, creativity, thinking, and beliefs as well as human experience and values in the formation of the attitudes of people toward their environment and in affecting their relationships with it.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[hummock]]}}
{{defn|A small {{gli|knoll}} or {{gli|mound}}, typically less than {{convert|15|m|ft}} in height and situated above an otherwise level ground surface.}}

{{term|[[humus]]}}
{{defn|Partially decomposed organic soil material.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[hundred (county division)|hundred]]}}
{{defn|In England, Scandinavia, and many other parts of the world, an administrative subdivision of a larger region, often a {{gli|county}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|shire}}, with its own judicial authority.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[hydrograph]]}}
{{defn|A graph showing the rate of flow (i.e. the {{gli|discharge}}) of water past a specific point of measurement in a river or other channel over time, typically expressed in cubic metres or cubic feet per second (m<sup>3</sup> or ft<sup>3</sup>/s).}}

{{term|[[hydrography]]}}{{anchor|hydrographic}}
{{defn|The study of the surface waters of the Earth.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[hydrosphere]]}}
{{defn|The totality of the water found on, under, and above the Earth's surface in liquid, solid, and gaseous forms, including all {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|oceans}}, {{gli|lakes}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|rivers}}, and {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|streams}}, as well as all ice and {{gli|glaciers}} and subsurface {{gli|groundwater}}. Some definitions restrict the hydrosphere to liquid water only, instead placing solid forms in the {{gli|cryosphere}} and gaseous forms in the {{gli|atmosphere}}.<ref name="USGS 2010"/>}}

{{term|[[hypsography]]}}
{{defn|The geographic representation on a {{gli|map}} of features related to {{gli|elevation}}, {{gli|altitude}}, and other measures of [[height]] above a reference surface (and sometimes inclusive of depths below the reference surface as well).}}

{{term|[[hypsometer]]}}
{{defn|Any instrument used to measure the height or {{gli|elevation}} of an object above a reference surface, either by trigonometry or by measuring changes in atmospheric pressure or boiling point. Trigonometric principles are applied when viewing the measured object from a distance, e.g. when determining the heights of trees or buildings, or when {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|surveying}} the elevations of distant landforms; whereas the principle that atmospheric pressure decreases predictably with elevation above {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|sea level}} is applied in instruments that measure their own height (i.e. the elevation of the instrument's location).<ref name="Troeh & Donahue"/>}}

{{term|[[hypsometry]]}}
{{defn|The study or measurement of the {{gli|elevation}} or depth of features of the Earth's surface relative to mean {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|sea level}}. In a narrower sense, hypsometry may refer to land elevations only, and therefore is sometimes viewed as the terrestrial equivalent of {{gli|bathymetry}}.}}

{{glossary end}}

==I==
{{glossary}}
{{term|[[ice age]]}}
{{defn|Any very long period of Earth's history during which surface and atmospheric temperatures are greatly reduced, resulting in the development or expansion of continental and {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|polar ice cap|polar ice sheets}} and widespread {{gli|glaciation}}. The most recent such period was the [[Pleistocene Epoch]], which ended approximately 12,000 years ago.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[ice cap]]}}{{anchor|ice caps}}
{{defn|A flattened, often dome-shaped mass of ice that covers less than {{convert|50000|sqkm|sqmi}} of land area and is not constrained by topographical features such as mountains; larger masses of ice are termed {{gli|ice sheet|ice sheets}}. Contrast ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|polar ice cap}}''.}}

{{term|[[ice floe]]}}{{anchor|ice floes}}
{{defn|A large piece of floating {{gli|drift ice}}, typically with a flat surface and at least {{convert|20|m|ft}} across at its widest point.}}
[[File:Walruses on ice floes.jpg|thumb|350px|Walruses on '''{{gli|ice floes}}''' in the Arctic Ocean]]

{{term|[[ice sheet]]}}{{anchor|ice sheets}}
{{ghat|Also '''continental glacier'''.}}
{{defn|A mass of {{gli|glacial}} ice that covers more than {{convert|50000|sqkm|sqmi}} of land area; smaller masses of ice may be termed {{gli|ice caps}} or {{gli|ice shelves}}. The two {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|polar ice cap|polar ice sheets}} are the only ice sheets that currently exist on Earth.}}

{{term|[[ice shelf]]}}{{anchor|ice shelves}}
{{defn|A large floating platform of ice formed when a {{gli|glacier}} or {{gli|ice sheet}} in a {{gli|coastal}} area flows onto the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ocean}} surface. By contrast, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|sea ice}} is formed directly over the water and is typically much thinner.}}

{{term|[[ice stream]]}}
{{defn|A region of relatively fast-moving ice within an {{gli|ice sheet}} that flows like a stream under its own weight (making it essentially equivalent to a {{gli|glacier}}) and empties into the ocean. Ice streams are responsible for the majority of the mass lost from both the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets.}}

{{term|[[iceberg]]}}{{anchor|icebergs}}
{{defn|A large chunk of {{gli|fresh water}} ice which has broken away from a larger body of ice (such as a {{gli|glacier}} or {{gli|ice shelf}}) and is floating freely in open water.}}

{{term|[[icefall]]}}
{{defn|A portion of a {{gli|glacier}} where a steepening or narrowing of the underlying bed causes the ice to move more rapidly than elsewhere, resulting in a chaotic, highly fractured surface characterized by numerous {{gli|crevasses}} and {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|seracs}}.}}

{{term|[[igneous rock]]}}
{{defn|Rock formed when molten (melted) materials harden.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[immigration]]}}
{{defn|To move to another country. People that move to another country are called immigrants.}}

{{term|[[impact crater]]}}
{{defn|A type of {{gli|crater}} formed by the hypervelocity collision of a solid astronomical body, such as a [[meteor]], with the Earth's surface. Unlike {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|volcanic crater|volcanic craters}}, impact craters typically have raised rims higher in elevation and depressed floors lower in elevation than the surrounding terrain.}}

{{term|impoundment}}
{{defn|no=1|Another name for a {{gli|dam}} that impounds a {{gli|body of water}}.}}
{{defn|no=2|The {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|reservoir}} created by such a dam.}}

{{term|[[land management|improved land]]}}
{{defn|Any land area which has been intentionally altered from its natural condition by human activity, such as ploughing, clearing, cultivation, or some other form of management, and thereby made more valuable or productive for human purposes (not necessarily to the benefit of any other organism or the environment in general). Legal definitions vary with location, but in most countries the term refers primarily to certain types of agricultural land or to property which has been developed for residential or commercial use.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[inclinometer]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''clinometer''', '''declinometer''', '''tilt meter''', '''gradient meter''', '''slope gauge''', and '''level gauge'''.}}
{{defn|An instrument used to measure angles of {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|slope}}, {{gli|elevation}}, or {{gli|depression}} with respect to the direction of the gravitational force, i.e. in the vertical plane, including both inclines and declines. The measure may be expressed in degrees, percentage points, or topos.<ref name="Goudie"/>}}

{{term|index contour}}
{{defn|A {{gli|contour line}} drawn with a heavier line weight to distinguish it from intermediate contours. Depending on the {{gli|contour interval}}, index contours are usually indicated every fourth or fifth contour, along with their assigned numerical values, in order to facilitate ease of interpretation.<ref name="USDMATC"/>}}

{{term|index map}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|map index}}''.}}

{{term|indigenous}}
{{defn|Originating in or native to a particular place or region, usually used of a living organism.}}

{{term|inertia costs of location}}
{{defn|Costs borne by an activity because it remains located at its original site, even though the distributions of [[supply and demand]] have changed.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[wikt:influent|influent]]}}
{{defn|(of a stream, river, or any natural water flow) Flowing into a larger watercourse or body of water.<ref name="Troeh & Donahue"/>}}

{{term|[[infrastructure]]}}
{{defn|The broad set of facilities and interrelated systems that serve a {{gli|city}}, {{gli|country}}, or any other inhabited area, encompassing the structures and services necessary for its industries, economies, and residential spaces to function. Infrastructure may include public and private physical structures such as roads, railways, bridges, tunnels, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|reservoir|water reservoirs}}, {{gli|canals}}, sewers, and electrical and telecommunications networks, among other things. A well-developed infrastructure is essential to enable, sustain, and improve living and working conditions in any society or organization.}}

{{term|[[ingression coast]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''ingressed coast''' and '''depressed coast'''.}}
{{defn|A generally flat {{gli|coastline}} whose shape has been largely defined by the penetration of the sea into relatively low-lying areas of the land surface, often as a result of {{gli|crustal}} movements or a rise in {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|sea level}}, such that the boundary between land and water closely matches the topographic contours of the land prior to its being covered by seawater.}}

{{term|[[wikt:inland|inland]]}}
{{defn|Of, relating to, within, or towards the interior of a {{gli|landmass}}, i.e. distant from the {{gli|coast}}.}}

{{term|[[inland sea]]}}
{{defn|A very large, isolated expanse of open water in the interior of a {{gli|landmass}}, either completely surrounded by dry land or connected to the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ocean}} by a river, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|strait}}, or other narrow {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|waterway}}.}}

{{term|inland waters}}
{{defn|Any surface {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|watercourse}} or {{gli|body of water}} surrounded entirely by land, including {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ponds}}, {{gli|lakes}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|reservoirs}}, and {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|rivers}}, or all such waters within a polity considered collectively.<ref name="Troeh & Donahue"/> See also ''{{gli|internal waters}}''.}}

{{term|[[inlet]]}}{{anchor|inlets}}
{{defn|An indentation of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|shore|shoreline}}, usually long and narrow, which leads to an enclosed body of {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|salt water}}, such as a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|sound}}, {{gli|bay}}, {{gli|lagoon}}, or {{gli|marsh}}.}}

{{term|[[inselberg]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''monadnock'''.}}
{{defn|An isolated rocky {{gli|hill}}, knob, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ridge}}, or small {{gli|mountain}} that rises abruptly from a virtually level surrounding {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|plain}}. Compare ''{{gli|mogote}}''.}}

{{term|inset}}
{{defn|A subsection of a {{gli|map}} that is reserved for depicting another map of the same place at a different {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|scale}}, often a smaller scale to show relative {{gli|location}} within a larger geographic area (e.g. a country's location on the {{gli|globe}}) or a larger scale to show increased detail (e.g. of public transit routes in a {{gli|downtown|downtown area}}), or with different features or overlays in order to provide additional information that would be difficult to interpret if presented in the main map area. Insets are usually outlined with an obvious boundary to prevent confusion, and may include their own set of cartographic elements such as a scale, {{gli|graticule}}, and {{gli|legend}}.<ref name="Clarke 1999">{{cite book|title= Getting started with geographic information systems |author-first= Keith C. |author-last= Clarke |date= 1999 |publisher= Prentice Hall |location= Upper Saddle River, N.J. |isbn= 9780139238895}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[wikt:inshore|inshore]]}}
{{defn|(relative to a position on a body of water) Near to or moving towards the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|shore}}; shorewards of a position as opposed to seawards of it. See also ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|onshore}}'' and ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|offshore}}''.}}

{{term|[[island|insular]]}}
{{defn|Of or relating to an {{gli|island}}, or suggestive of the isolated condition of an island.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|integrated drainage}}
{{defn|A drainage pattern in which {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|stream}} systems have developed to the point that all parts of the landscape drain into some part of a stream and to a common base level, the initial or original surfaces having essentially eroded away entirely, such that few or no {{gli|endorheic basin|closed}} {{gli|drainage basin|drainage systems}} are present.<ref name="NRCS 2018"/>}}

{{term|[[integrated geography]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''integrative geography''', '''environmental geography''', or '''human–environment geography'''.}}
{{defn|The branch of geography that describes and explains the spatial aspects of interactions between human individuals or societies and their natural environment.}}

{{term|intercardinal directions}}
{{ghat|Also '''intermediate directions''' or '''ordinal directions'''.}}
{{defn|The set of four intermediate directions used in {{gli|cartography}} and {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|navigation}}, each of which is located halfway between a pair of {{gli|cardinal directions}}: northeast (NE), southeast (SE), southwest (SW), and northwest (NW). They are often included in the {{gli|compass rose}} and are used to define further subdivisions such as the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|secondary-intercardinal directions}}.}}

{{term|[[interfluve]]}}
{{defn|A narrow, elongated, and {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|plateau}}-like or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ridge}}-like landform between two {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|valleys}}, or an area of higher ground between two rivers in the same {{gli|drainage basin}}.}}

{{term|intermediate directions}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|intercardinal directions}}''.}}

{{term|[[intermittent stream]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|stream}} or other {{gli|watercourse}} in which water does not flow continuously but dries up occasionally, often predictably with the seasons, as opposed to a {{gli|perennial stream}} which flows year-round. See also ''{{gli|bourne}}''.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[intermontane]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''intermountain'''.}}
{{defn|Situated between {{gli|mountains}} or {{gli|mountain ranges}}, e.g. the high {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|plateaus}} lying between the eastern and western ranges of the Andes.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[International Date Line]]}}
{{defn|A line of {{gli|longitude}} generally 180 degrees east and west of the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|Prime Meridian}}. The date is one day earlier to the east of the line.<ref name="OERI 1996"/>}}

{{term|[[international waters]]}}
{{defn|}}

{{term|[[interpolation]]}}{{anchor|interpolate|interpolates|interpolated|interpolating}}
{{defn|In {{gli|geographic information science}}, the estimation of the values of {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|spatially dependent variables}} at unsampled points based on known values of surrounding points, under the assumption that any unknown quantity can be calculated based on its distance to each surrounding quantity. Interpolation techniques such as spline and {{gli|kriging}} are commonly {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|raster}} operations, but can also be applied in {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|vector}} environments using a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|triangulated irregular network}} to model a surface.<ref name="Wade and Sommer 2006"/>}}

{{term|[[interruption (map projection)|interruption]]}}
{{defn|Any place where the contiguous geographic area represented in a {{gli|map projection}} has been split, separating to distant parts of the projection certain features and locations which are in reality much closer to each other, in order to permit the representation of a three-dimensional space on a two-dimensional map. All {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|world maps}}, for example, have at least one interruption, conventionally along the length of a single {{gli|meridian}}, thus forming an east–west boundary despite that the approximately spherical {{gli|figure of the Earth|shape of the Earth}} is continuous, with no such boundaries; features on either side of the interruption, though very close to each other on the actual Earth, are depicted on opposite edges of the map, appearing to be separated by thousands of miles. Some world map projections attempt to reduce distortion of scale by having more than one interruption, which divide the projected area into multiple {{gli|gores}}, each with its own central meridian.<ref name="Wade and Sommer 2006"/>}}

{{term|intervening opportunity}}
{{defn|The existence of a closer, less expensive opportunity for obtaining a good or service, or for a migration destination. Such opportunities lessen the attractiveness of more distant places.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[Intracoastal Waterway]] (ICW)}}{{anchor|Intracoastal Waterway}}
{{defn|A system of navigable inland {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|waterway}} channels, maintained through [[dredging]] and sheltered for the most part by a series of linear offshore islands, that follows the Atlantic and Gulf Coasts of the United States more than {{convert|4800|km|mi}} from [[Boston, Massachusetts]], around the southern tip of [[Florida]], to [[Brownsville, Texas]].<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|inversac}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|estavelle}}''.}}

{{term|[[inverted river delta]]}}
{{defn|}}

{{term|[[island]]}}{{anchor|islands}}
{{ghat|Also '''isle'''.}}
{{defn|Any piece of sub-continental land that is entirely surrounded by water; or more generally, any isolated habitat that is surrounded by a different habitat, including different types of land.}}

{{term|[[island nation]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|country}} or polity whose territory consists primarily or entirely of one or more {{gli|islands}} or parts of islands.}}

{{term|isle}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|island}}''.}}

{{term|[[islet]]}}{{anchor|islets}}
{{defn|A very small {{gli|island}}.}}

{{term|isometric}}
{{defn|Having equal measure.}}

{{term|[[isopleth]]}}
{{defn|Any line on a {{gli|map}} connecting places of equal value of some specified variable. The variable may be a physical or natural quantity, such as elevation above sea level (as with {{gli|contour lines}}) or temperature (as with [[isotherm (contour line)|isotherm]]s), or a quantity related to social or economic statistics, such as population, wealth, or transport costs.}}

{{term|[[isostasy]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''isostatic equilibrium'''.}}
{{defn|The state of gravitational equilibrium between the Earth's {{gli|crust}} and its {{gli|mantle}}, such that the crust "floats" at an {{gli|elevation}} that depends on its thickness and density. This concept is invoked to explain how different {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|topographic}} heights can exist at Earth's surface. Isostatic theory maintains that where equilibrium exists at the surface, equal mass must underlie equal surface area, and that the thickness of crustal features and the depth of the world's {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|oceans}} tend to change over time in order to compensate for the uneven distribution of mass in the {{gli|lithosphere}}. For example, the instability of {{gli|continental margin|continental margins}} where high mountains are found adjacent to deep oceanic trenches is explained by the subterranean movement of magma to effect a return to regional equilibrium, a process known as isostatic adjustment.<ref name="Clark"/>}}
[[File:Isostasy.jpg|thumb|300px|The theory of '''{{gli|isostasy}}''' explains the phenomena of {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|plate tectonics}} in terms of the tendency of Earth's {{gli|crust}} and {{gli|mantle}} to gravitationally balance each other, such that e.g. a change in the mass of the crust results in local displacement of the mantle underlying it.]]

{{term|[[isthmus]]}}
{{defn|A narrow piece of land {{gli|land bridge|connecting}} two larger land areas across an expanse of water by which they are otherwise separated.}}

{{glossary end}}

==J==
{{glossary}}
{{term|[[jetty]]}}
{{defn|Any man-made structure that projects from land out into a body of water, serving as a {{gli|breakwater}}, a walkway, or a landing stage for watercraft, or, in pairs, as a means of constricting a {{gli|channel}}.}}

{{term|[[jhum cultivation]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''jhoom cultivation''' or '''slash-and-burn agriculture'''.}}
{{defn|Clear-cutting and/or setting fire to an area of land so it can be used for farm cultivation.}}

{{term|[[wikt:junction|junction]]}}
{{defn|A meeting or intersection of two or more {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|routes}} of travel, as of roads, rivers, or lines on a map, or a place at which a single route diverges into two or more different routes.}}

{{term|[[jungle]]}}
{{defn|An area covered with dense vegetation dominated by large trees, often tropical.}}

{{term|[[jurisdiction]]}}
{{defn|no=1|The right and power to apply the law in a particular place or within a defined field of responsibility.}}
{{defn|no=2|The geographical area to which such authority applies.}}

{{term|[[juvenile water]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''magmatic water'''.}}
{{defn|Water present within or derived from the {{gli|magma}} of the Earth's {{gli|mantle}} and which when brought to the surface by {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|volcanism|volcanic eruptions}} is entering the [[water cycle]] for the first time (or at least for the first time in millions of years, having previously circulated in the oceans or the atmosphere but becoming [[subduction|subducted]] beneath the surface and returned to the mantle).<ref>{{cite web |title=EarthWord – Juvenile Water |url=https://www.usgs.gov/news/earthword-juvenile-water |website=www.usgs.gov |publisher=U.S. Geological Survey |language=en |date=November 2, 2015}}</ref>}}

{{glossary end}}

==K==
{{glossary}}
{{term|[[kame]]}}{{anchor|kames}}
{{defn|An irregularly shaped {{gli|hill}} or {{gli|mound}} composed of sand, gravel, and {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|till|glacial till}} which accumulates in a depression on a retreating {{gli|glacier}} and is subsequently deposited on the land surface with further melting of the glacier. Kames are often associated with {{gli|kettle|kettles}}.}}
[[File:Receding glacier-en.svg|thumb|500px|right|'''{{gli|kame|Kames}}''' and '''{{gli|kettles}}''' are just two of the many characteristic landforms created in the wake of a melting {{gli|glacier}}.]]

{{term|[[wikt:karre|karre]]}}
{{defn|A furrow or {{gli|channel}} varying in depth from a few millimetres to more than a metre, and separated from others by {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ridges}}, caused by solution on limestone surfaces.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[karst]]}}{{anchor|karstic}}
{{defn|An area possessing surface {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|topography}} resulting from the underground solution of subsurface [[limestone]] or [[Dolomite (rock)|dolomite]].<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[kettle (landform)|kettle]]}}{{anchor|kettles}}
{{ghat|Also '''kettle hole''' or '''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|pothole}}'''.}}
{{defn|A shallow, sediment-filled body of water formed by blocks of [[ice calving]] from a retreating {{gli|glacier}}, or by draining floodwaters.}}

{{term|key}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|cay}}''.}}

{{term|key col}}
{{defn|}}

{{term|[[kill (body of water)|kill]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''kil'''.}}
{{defn|A river, stream, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|strait}}, or tidal {{gli|inlet}}. The term is used primarily in areas of Dutch influence in the northeastern United States.}}

{{term|[[knickpoint]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''nickpoint'''.}}
{{defn|no=1|A point of abrupt inflection in the longitudinal profile of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|river}} or its {{gli|channel}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|valley}}, such as occurs at a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|waterfall}}.}}
{{defn|no=2|Any interruption or break in the character of a {{gli|grade|slope}}.<ref name="NRCS 2018"/>}}

{{term|knob}}
{{defn|A peak or projection from the top of a {{gli|hill}} or {{gli|mountain}}, or any rounded protrusion of land, especially a small but {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|topographic prominence|prominent}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|topographic isolation|isolated}} hill with steep sides; a boulder or an area of {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|outcrop|resistant rock}} protruding from the side of a hill or mountain. The term is used primarily in the southern United States.<ref name="NRCS 2018"/>}}

{{term|knoll}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|hillock}}''.}}

{{term|[[kolk (bog)|kolk]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''colc''' and '''colk'''.}}
{{defn|no=1|A violently rotating underwater vortex capable of {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|plucking}} and scouring {{gli|depressions}} in {{gli|bedrock}}, which may leave behind distinct pits or lakes known as {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|rock-cut basin|rock-cut basins}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|potholes}}.}}
{{defn|no=2|Another name for a {{gli|bog pond}}.}}

{{term|kopje}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|tor}}''.}}

{{term|[[krai]]}}
{{defn|In Russia and other Slavic countries, a generic term for a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|region}}, historically and politically reserved for {{gli|border}} regions in particular, and variously translated as {{gli|march}}, {{gli|frontier}}, or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|territory}}. The term is cognate with the [[name of Ukraine]].}}

{{term|[[kriging]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''Gaussian process regression''' and '''Wiener–Kolmogorov prediction'''.}}
{{defn|In {{gli|geostatistics}}, an {{gli|interpolation}} technique in which, for a given {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|spatially dependent variable}}, a predicted value for an unmeasured location is derived by weighting the surrounding measured values based on the distance between them and to the unmeasured location, as well as the overall spatial arrangement of the measured points. Widely used in {{gli|GIS}} applications, kriging is based on [[regionalized variable theory]], which assumes that the spatial variation in the data being modeled is homogeneous across the surface.<ref name="Wade and Sommer 2006"/>}}

{{term|[[wikt:kum|kum]]}}
{{defn|A sandy {{gli|desert}} of Central Asia, roughly equivalent to the Saharan {{gli|erg}}.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{term|[[wikt:kyle|kyle]]}}
{{defn|In Scotland, a narrow {{gli|channel}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|strait}} between two {{gli|islands}}, or between an island and the {{gli|mainland}}.<ref name="Clark"/>}}

{{glossary end}}

==L==
{{glossary}}
{{term|[[wikt:lacustrine|lacustrine]]}}
{{defn|Of or pertaining to a {{gli|lake}}; formed by or deposited in a lake.<ref name="Troeh & Donahue"/>}}

{{term|[[lacustrine plain]]}}
{{defn|A nearly level land area formed by the infilling of a {{gli|lake}} with sediment and the complete drainage or evaporation of water from the lake, leaving the deposited sediments behind.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[lagoon]]}}{{anchor|lagoons}}
{{defn|A small area of water connected to the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ocean}} but otherwise blockaded by one or more {{gli|islands}}.}}

{{term|[[lahar]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''mudflow''' or '''debris flow'''.}}
{{defn|A flowing mixture of water and debris (intermediate between a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|volcanic avalanche}} and a water [[flood]]) that forms on the slopes of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|volcano}}.<ref name="USGS 2010"/>}}

{{term|[[lake]]}}{{anchor|lakes}}
{{defn|A {{gli|body of water}} localized in a {{gli|depression|basin}} and surrounded entirely by land. Lakes are often defined as separate from any {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|river}} or stream that serves to feed or drain them.}}

{{term|[[land bridge]]}}
{{defn|Any piece of land connecting larger land areas that are otherwise separated by water, especially one over which living organisms, such as terrestrial animals and plants, are able to cross and thereby colonize previously inaccessible lands. Land bridges may be created by [[marine regression|falling sea levels]], {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|plate tectonics|tectonic activity}}, or [[post-glacial rebound]]. Compare ''{{gli|isthmus}}''.}}
[[File:Beringia-Map Bathymetry web72 final.png|thumb|400px|A map of the hypothetical [[Beringia]] '''{{gli|land bridge}}''' thought to have connected Asia and North America about 21,000 years ago, during the [[Last Glacial Maximum]]]]

{{term|[[land cover]]}}
{{defn|The physical material present on the surface of the Earth, including categories such as vegetation (grasslands, shrubs, forests, etc.), bare ground, water, asphalt and artificial surfaces, and many others.}}

{{term|land-fast ice}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|fast ice}}''.}}

{{term|[[landform]]}}{{anchor|landforms}}
{{defn|A natural feature of the solid surface of the Earth. A combined set of landforms makes up the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|terrain}} of a given area, and their arrangement in a landscape is known as {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|topography}}.}}

{{term|[[landlocked]]}}
{{defn|no=1|(of a country or other polity, or a geographical region) Completely surrounded by land and thus lacking a marine {{gli|coastline}}; having no territory directly connected to or bordering the {{gli|ocean}}.}}
{{defn|no=2|(of a property or parcel of land) Completely surrounded by privately owned property and having no access to a public road.}}

{{term|[[landmark]]}}{{anchor|landmarks}}
{{defn|Any natural or artificial feature that is recognizable enough to be used for {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|navigation}}; a feature that stands out enough from its environment to be visible across long distances.}}

{{term|[[landmass]]}}{{anchor|landmasses}}
{{defn|Any large contiguous area of {{gli|land}} typically surrounded by an {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ocean}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|sea}}. Compare ''{{gli|continent}}''.}}

{{term|[[landscape]]}}{{anchor|landscapes}}
{{defn|no=1|A broad or distinct area of land consisting of a collection of {{gli|landforms}} which define a general {{gli|geomorphologic}} form or setting, e.g. a {{gli|mountain range}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|valley}}, {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|plain}}, {{gli|coast}}, etc. Landforms within a landscape are spatially associated but may vary in formation processes and age.<ref name="NRCS 2018"/>}}
{{defn|no=2|The visible features of an area of land, its landforms, and how they integrate with natural or man-made features. In the broadest sense, landscapes may include geophysical landforms such as hills and mountains; {{gli|bodies of water}} such as rivers, lakes, and the sea; living elements of {{gli|land cover}} such as vegetation; human elements such as buildings, structures, and various forms of {{gli|land use}}; and transitory elements such as lighting and weather conditions. They reflect both physical origins and the {{gli|cultural landscape|cultural overlay}} of human presence in a living synthesis of people and place.}}

{{term|landscape studies}}
{{defn|A branch of geography which examines the structure and organization of {{gli|landscapes}}, focusing on landscapes as the settings for cultural and ecological patterns, processes, and histories, as well as on the social and cultural evolution of landscapes, including the ways in which they shape and are shaped by human societies and the interrelationships between {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|place-making}} and personal and social memory.<ref name="Mayhew 2023"/>}}

{{term|[[landslide]]}}{{anchor|landslides}}
{{ghat|Also '''landslip'''.}}
{{defn|A sudden {{gli|mass movement}} of earth from a hill, mountain, or cliff, in which displaced material slides, flows, falls, or collapses under the force of gravity yet often retains form as it moves; or the visible evidence of this movement after the displaced material has come to rest. Landslides may have many causes, though they are commonly associated with heavy precipitation, underground {{gli|aquifers}}, wave action, and earthquakes.<ref name="Mayhew 2023"/>}}

{{term|land-tied island}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|tied island}}''.}}

{{term|[[lateral blast]]}}
{{defn|A sideways-directed explosion from the side or summit of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|volcano}}.<ref name="USGS 2010"/>}}

{{term|[[lateral moraine]]}}{{anchor|lateral moraines}}
{{defn|}}

{{term|[[latitude]]}}{{anchor|latitudes|latitudinal|latitudinally}}
{{defn|A measure of distance north or south of the {{gli|Equator}}. One degree of latitude equals approximately {{convert|111|km|mi|sp=us}}.<ref name="IIP 2008"/> Lines of latitude, also called {{gli|circle of latitude|circles of latitude}} or ''parallels'', are the imaginary lines that cross the surface of the Earth in an east-west direction (parallel to the Equator) and measure how far north or south of the Equator a place is located.<ref name="OERI 1996"/>}}

{{term|[[lava]]}}
{{defn|The term used for {{gli|magma}} once it has erupted onto the Earth's surface.<ref name="USGS 2010"/>}}

{{term|layer of no motion}}
{{defn|In {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|oceanography}}, a hypothetical layer at some depth in the ocean within which the water is assumed to be at rest, implying that the isobaric surfaces within that layer are level and hence that such surfaces can be used as points of reference when calculating absolute-gradient {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ocean current|currents}}.<ref name="ASCE/ACSM/ASPRS"/>}}

{{term|lea}}
{{defn|A pasture, {{gli|meadow}}, or grassy {{gli|field}}.<ref name="Troeh & Donahue"/>}}

{{term|[[soil leaching|leaching]]}}
{{defn|A process of soil nutrient removal through the erosive movement and chemical action of water.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[windward and leeward|lee]]}}
{{defn|The side or {{gli|grade|slope}} of a physical feature (such as a {{gli|hill}} or {{gli|mountain}}) which faces downwind, i.e. away from the direction in which the wind is blowing, or which faces away from an advancing {{gli|glacier}} or {{gli|ice sheet}}. The lee side is often sheltered by the topography from exposure to the wind and any moisture it brings.<ref name="NRCS 2018"/>}}

{{term|[[leeward]]}}
{{defn|Toward the {{gli|lee}} side; sheltered from the wind; the direction downwind from a point of reference. Contrast ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|windward}}''.<ref name="USGS 2010"/>}}

{{term|[[legend (map)#Map symbology|legend]]}}
{{defn|A key for understanding the meanings of the symbols or pictures on a {{gli|map}}.<ref name="OERI 1996"/>}}

{{term|[[levee]]}}{{anchor|levees}}
{{ghat|Also '''dike''', '''embankment''', '''floodbank''', and '''stopbank'''.}}
{{defn|An elongated naturally occurring {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|ridge}} or an artificially constructed wall or barrier which regulates water levels in areas prone to flooding. It is usually earthen and often parallel to the course of a {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|river}} or a {{gli|coast|coastline}}.}}

{{term|[[lithosphere]]}}
{{defn|The Earth's hard, outermost shell. It comprises the crust and the upper part of the mantle. It is divided into a mosaic of 16 major slabs or plates, which are known as {{gli|lithospheric plates}} or {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|tectonic plates}}.<ref name="USGS 2010"/>}}

{{term|lithospheric plates}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|tectonic plates}}''.}}

{{term|[[loam]]}}
{{defn|A type of easily worked, highly fertile [[soil]] composed of clay, silt, and sand in an approximate ratio of 20:40:40. Loams generally heat rapidly, are well-aerated, and drain neither too quickly nor too slowly.<ref name="Mayhew"/>}}

{{term|[[Localism (politics)|localism]]}}
{{defn|A movement or philosophy that prioritizes local or small-scale politics, issues, and values over {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|regional}} or broader concerns, rejecting things like [[centralized government]] and economic [[outsourcing]] in favor of local production and consumption of goods, local control of government, and the promotion of local history, local culture, and local identity.<ref name="Mayhew 2023"/>}}

{{term|localization}}
{{defn|The set of processes by which social, cultural, economic, or other activities become embedded in specific places or {{gli|locations}}, rather than in alternative places or across many places, either in contrast to or as a related aspect of {{gli|globalization}}. In the former sense localization may be deliberately practiced as a form of resistance to globalization through the promotion of increased local control, self-government, and economic self-sufficiency.<ref name="Oxford">{{cite book |last1=Castree |first1=Noel |last2=Kitchin |first2=Rob |last3=Rogers |first3=Alisdair |title=A Dictionary of Human Geography |date=2013 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford, England |isbn=9780199599868 |edition=1st}}</ref> See also ''{{gli|deglobalization}}''.}}

{{term|[[wikt:location|location]]}}{{anchor|locations}}
{{defn|A particular point or place in physical space. Compare ''{{gli|absolute location}}''.}}

{{term|[[location theory]]}}
{{defn|A group of theories which seek to explain the siting of economic activities in particular {{gli|locations}}.}}

{{term|[[loess]]}}
{{defn|A soil made up of small particles that were transported by the wind to their present location.<ref name="IIP 2008"/>}}

{{term|[[longitude]]}}{{anchor|longitudes|longitudinal|longitudinally}}
{{defn|A measure of distance east or west of the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|Prime Meridian}}, a line drawn between the {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|North Geographic Pole|North}} and {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|South Geographic Pole|South Poles}} and passing through the [[Royal Observatory, Greenwich|Royal Observatory]] at [[Greenwich, England]].<ref name="IIP 2008"/> Lines of longitude, also called {{gli|meridians}}, are the imaginary lines that cross the surface of the Earth in a north-south direction (parallel to the Prime Meridian) and measure how far east or west of the Prime Meridian a place is located.<ref name="OERI 1996"/>}}

{{term|[[longshore drift]]}}
{{ghat|Also '''longshore current''' and '''littoral drift'''.}}
{{defn|A geological process by which sediment is transported along a {{gli|coast}} parallel to the {{gli|shoreline}} due to incoming wind-driven waves meeting the shore at an oblique angle; this generates a water current which moves unidirectionally along the shore within the {{gli|surf zone}}. A well-known example occurs on sandy {{gli|beaches}} when {{gli|breaking waves}} send swash up the beach at an angle but gravity drains the {{gli|backwash}} straight downslope, perpendicular to the shoreline, causing the same sand particles to gradually move down the beach over multiple cycles. The same process occurs at many different scales and affects all sediment sizes, and can vary with the wind direction even at the same location.}}
[[File:Longshore drift.svg|thumb|400px|A diagram of '''{{gli|longshore drift}}''']]

{{term|[[lowland]]}}{{anchor|lowlands}}
{{defn|Any area of land that is lower in {{gli|elevation}} relative to another area. The term is often used as a conditional descriptor to distinguish related [[habitat]]s or [[ecosystem]]s, especially freshwater {{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|riparian area|riparian areas}}, on the basis of elevation above sea level. Lowland areas are usually relatively flat and characterized by slow-flowing waterways and {{gli|alluvial plains}}. Contrast ''{{gli|highland}}'' and ''{{gli|glossary=Glossary of geography terms (N–Z)|upland}}''.}}

{{glossary end}}
