{{Politics of China |expanded = Related }}

'''''Hukou''''' ({{lang-zh|s=户口|l=household individual}}; {{IPA|zh|xû.kʰòʊ̯|IPA}}) is a system of [[household registration]] used in [[mainland China]].<!--hukou system is not applied in HK and Macau--> The system itself is more properly called ''huji'' ({{lang-zh|c=户籍|l=household origin}}; {{IPA|zh|xû.t͡ɕǐ|IPA}}), and has origins in [[History of China|ancient China]]; ''hukou'' is the registration of an individual in the system.{{efn|'' Kou'' literally means "mouth", which originates from the practice of regarding family members as "mouths to feed", similar to the phrase "[[per capita|per head]]" in English.}} A household registration record officially identifies a person as a permanent resident of an area and includes identifying information such as name, parents, spouse and date of birth. A ''hukou'' can also refer to a [[family register]] in many contexts since the household register ({{lang-zh|s=户口簿|t=戶口簿|p=hùkǒu bù}}) is issued per family, and usually includes the births, deaths, marriages, divorces, and moves of all members in the family.

The system descends in part from ancient Chinese household registration systems. The hukou system also influenced similar systems within the public administration structures of neighbouring East Asian countries, such as Japan ([[koseki]]) and Korea ([[hoju]]), as well as the Southeast Asian country Vietnam ([[hộ khẩu]]).<ref>{{Cite book |title=Teacher Educator International Professional Development as Ren |last=Liu  |first=Laura Blythe  |publisher=Springer |year=2016 |isbn= 978-3-662-51648-5 |pages=37}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=China's Urban Billion: The Story behind the Biggest Migration in Human History |last=Miller |first=Tom  |year=2012 |publisher=Bloomsbury Academic |isbn=978-1-78032-141-7}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=China's Economy: What Everyone Needs to Know? |last= Kroeber |first=Arthur R. |publisher= Oxford University Press |year=2016 |isbn=978-0-19-023903-9 |pages=73–75}}</ref> In South Korea, the [[hoju]] system was abolished in January 2008.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Gender issues and Confucian scriptures: Is Confucianism incompatible with gender equality in South Korea?|first=Eunkang|last=Koh|journal=Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London|volume=71|number=2|pages=345–362|jstor=40378774|doi=10.1017/s0041977x08000578|year=2008}}</ref> While unrelated in origin, [[propiska in the Soviet Union]] and [[resident registration in Russia]] had a similar purpose and served as a model for modern China's hukou system.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Li  |last2=Kuang |first2=Lei  |year=2012 |editor-last=Denson |editor-first=Tom  |title=Discrimination against Rural-to-Urban Migrants: The Role of the Hukou System in China |journal=PLOS ONE|volume=7 |issue=11 |article-number=e46932 |publisher=PLOS |publication-date=5 November 2012|pmc=3489849 |pmid=23144794 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0046932 |bibcode=2012PLoSO...746932K |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=Theorizing Chinese Citizenship |last1=Guo |first1=Zhonghua |last2=Guo |first2=Sujian |publisher=Lexington Books |year=2015 |isbn=978-1-4985-1669-3 |publication-date=15 October 2015 |pages=104}}</ref>

In the modern era, the hukou system functions as an administrative tool to address challenges of rapid urbanisation, primarily through population management and controlled migration to [[Megacity|megacities]] and large urban centres. A central rationale of such policies, particularly in first-tier cities, has been to prevent severe overcrowding, infrastructure overload, and the emergence of large-scale [[slum]]s during [[Reform and opening up|China's rapid industrialisation and urbanisation]] phases. Shahid Yusuf, a Senior Adviser in the World Bank’s Development Research Group, noted that the hukou system served as a "cornerstone of China's urbanisation strategy" by controlling migration and channelling migrants toward small or medium-sized cities rather than allowing unchecked inflows to the largest urban areas. He described China's ability to achieve rapid urbanisation while largely avoiding widespread slum formation as one of its "greatest successes" in managing its urbanisation pathway, stating: "One of China’s greatest successes in its rapid urbanisation has been that it has managed to contain the process to the extent that there are crowded living conditions but very few slums. This is an important achievement for a developing country."<ref name=":14">{{Cite web|title=China's Rapid Urbanization: Benefits, Challenges & Strategies|url=https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/feature/2008/06/19/chinas-rapid-urbanization-benefits-challenges-strategies|website=World Bank|access-date=2026-02-02|language=en}}</ref>

However, there is ongoing debate regarding the future role of the system, and in recent years China has created reforms whose aim is to relax hukou restrictions gradually.<ref name=":14" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Hukou System In China|url=https://orcasia.org/hukou-system-in-china|website=orcasia|access-date=2026-02-02|language=en|last= |date=8 August 2023 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=China is Relaxing Hukou Restrictions in Small and Medium-Sized Cities|url=https://www.china-briefing.com/news/china-relaxing-hukou-restrictions-small-medium-sized-cities/|website=China Briefing News|date=2019-04-17|access-date=2026-02-02|language=en-US|first=China|last=Briefing}}</ref> In their 1990 study of Chinese peasants, anthropologists Sulamith Heins Potter and Jack M. Potter described the rural–urban status distinction as "[[caste|caste-like]]", emphasizing inherited status and social stratification.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Potter|first1=Sulamith Heins|last2=Potter|first2=Jack M.|year=1990|title=China's Peasants: The Anthropology of a Revolution|chapter=A caste-like system of social stratification: the position of peasants in modern China's social order|publisher=Cambridge University Press|pages=296–312|doi=10.1017/CBO9780511607783.018|isbn=978-0-521-35521-6}}</ref> The hukou system has been the source of much inequality over the decades since the [[establishment of the People's Republic of China]] in 1949, as urban residents received benefits that ranged from retirement pension to education to health care, while rural citizens were often left to fend for themselves.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":11">{{Cite news |date=2024-12-27 |title=How a Mao-era system creates second-class citizens in modern China |url=https://www.ft.com/content/a2fa8e3f-da7b-4525-93f5-790fa5423ebc |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241227031914/https://www.ft.com/content/a2fa8e3f-da7b-4525-93f5-790fa5423ebc |archive-date=2024-12-27 |language=en-GB}}</ref> Since 1978, the [[State Council of the People's Republic of China|central government]] has undertaken reforms of the system in response to protests and a changing economic system.<ref name=":11" /><ref>{{cite news |last1=Lu |first1=Rachel |title=China Is Ending Its 'Apartheid.' Here's Why No One Is Happy About It |url=https://foreignpolicy.com/2014/07/31/china-is-ending-its-apartheid-heres-why-no-one-is-happy-about-it/ |access-date=14 August 2018 |work=Foreign Policy |date=31 July 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Sheehan |first1=Spencer |title=China's Hukou Reforms and the Urbanization Challenge |url=https://thediplomat.com/2017/02/chinas-hukou-reforms-and-the-urbanization-challenge/ |access-date=14 August 2018 |work=The Diplomat |date=22 February 2017}}</ref>

In 2014, the State Council called for a unified household registration system, replacing the agricultural and non-agricultural categories with resident registration.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Jiao |last2=Wei |first2=Kezhen |last3=Shuai |first3=Qinghong |date=2025-05-16 |title=Impact of the new round of Hukou system reforms on rural household development resilience in China |journal=Scientific Reports |language=en |volume=15 |issue=1 |article-number=17098 |doi=10.1038/s41598-025-01783-9 |issn=2045-2322 |pmc=12084379 |pmid=40379778 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2025NatSR..1517098L }}</ref>

==Nomenclature: ''huji'' vs. ''hukou''==
The formal name for the system is ''huji''. Within the ''huji'' system, a ''hukou'' is the registered residency status of a particular individual in this system. However, the term ''hukou'' is used colloquially to refer to the entire system, and it has been adopted by English-language audiences to refer to both the ''huji'' system and an individual's ''hukou''.<ref name=":0" />

==Household registration in mainland China==
[[File:Hukou zh.jpg|right|thumb|An individual household's register or ''hukou'' booklet. The local police station held a copy of these records in its central register.]]
[[File:The_inside_pages_of_hukou_booklet.png|right|thumb|The inside pages of hukou booklet in China]]
The hukou system has origins in China that date back to ancient times, but the system in its current form came into being with the 1958 ''People's Republic of China Hukou Registration Regulation''.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=China's hukou system: markets, migrants and institutional change|author=Young, Jason|isbn=978-1-137-27730-5|location=Basingstoke|chapter=2|oclc=847140377|date=3 June 2013}}</ref>

Historically, each citizen was classified in an agricultural or non-agricultural hukou (commonly referred to as rural or urban) and further categorised by location of origin.<ref name=":0" /> This two-fold organisational structure was linked to social policy, and those residents who held non-agricultural (i.e., urban) hukou status received benefits not available to their rural counterparts, and vice versa.<ref name=":1">Chan, K. W. (2015). Five Decades of the Chinese Hukou System. In ''Handbook of Chinese Migration: Identity and Wellbeing'' (pp. 23-47). Northampton, MA: Edward Elgar Publishing, Inc.</ref>

Internal migration was also tightly controlled by the central government, and only in the past few decades have these restrictions been loosened. While this system has played a major role in China's fast economic growth, hukou has also promoted and aggravated social stratification and contributed significantly to the deprivation of many of China's rural workers.<ref name=":0" />

Steps have been taken to alleviate the inequalities promulgated by the hukou system, with major reforms announced in March and July 2014, which included a provision that eliminated the division between agricultural and non-agricultural hukou status.<ref name=":1" />

===Rationale and function===
In the middle of the 20th century, China's weak industrial sector and food security needs meant that mass migration was a threat to stability in both urban and rural areas.<ref name=":12">{{Cite book |last=Lin |first=Zhongjie |title=Constructing Utopias: China's New Town Movement in the 21st Century |date=2025 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=978-0-19-779330-5 |location=New York, NY}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=15}} By restricting peasants' ability to move, the system aimed to ensure sufficient agricultural production and to maintain social stability in urban areas with limited work opportunities.<ref name=":12" />{{Reference page|page=15}} In its original legislation, the hukou system was justified as created to<blockquote>"...maintain social order, protect the rights and interests of citizens and to be of service to the establishment of socialism".<ref name=":0" /> </blockquote>The central government asserted that because rural areas had greater capacity to absorb and use excess labor, the majority of the population should be concentrated in these regions.<ref name=":0" /> Furthermore, free movement of people was considered dangerous, as it would lead to overpopulation of cities and could threaten agricultural production.<ref name=":0" /> Under the hukou system, the rural population was structured to serve as support for urban industrialisation, both in agricultural production<ref name=":0" /> and workers for [[State-owned enterprises # China | state-owned businesses]].<ref name="rethinks">Luard, Tim. [https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/asia-pacific/4424944.stm "China rethinks peasant 'apartheid'"], ''[[BBC News]]'', 10 November 2005.</ref>

The hukou system served other purposes as well. After establishing the People's Republic of China in 1949, the [[Communist Party of China|Chinese Communist Party]] enacted policies based on the notions of stability and rapid modernisation, and the hukou system was no exception.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|title=Cities and stability: urbanisation, redistribution, & regime survival in China|last=L.|first=Wallace, Jeremy|isbn=978-0-19-937898-2|location=New York|oclc=871534491|year = 2014}}</ref>{{page needed|date=November 2024}} Urban areas have historically been where authoritarian regimes are most vulnerable: to combat this, the central government gave preferential treatment to city residents, hoping to prevent uprisings against the state, particularly in the early years when it was especially susceptible to rebellion.<ref name=":2" />{{page needed|date=November 2024}} The structure of the hukou system also bolstered the power of the central government over its urban citizens: by making city residents dependent upon the government for all aspects of daily life, the central government could force obedience from problematic individuals.<ref name=":0" />{{page needed|date=November 2024}}

The central government's efforts to contain migration have been a major factor in the rapid development of the [[Economy of China|Chinese economy]]. Their tight check on migration into urban areas has helped prevent the emergence of several problems faced by many other developing countries.<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Xin-Rui|last2=Hui|first2=Eddie Chi-Man|last3=Choguill|first3=Charles|last4=Jia|first4=Sheng-Hua|date=2015|title=The new urbanisation policy in China: Which way forward?|journal=Habitat International | volume=47 | pages=279–284|doi=10.1016/j.habitatint.2015.02.001|hdl=10397/27398|hdl-access=free}}</ref> For example, the appearance of slums outside of urban areas due to a massive influx of individuals searching for work has not been an issue, nor have poor health conditions due to high population density.<ref name=":10" /> And regardless of its other imperfections, the hukou system's ability to maintain stability has contributed to China's economic rise.<ref name=":2" />{{page needed|date=November 2024}}

== History ==
The legacy of the Chinese hukou system may be traced back to the pre-dynastic era, as early as the 21st century BC.<ref name=":0" /> In its early forms, the household registration system was used primarily for taxation and conscription, as well as regulating migration.<ref name=":0" /> The xiangsui and [[baojia system]]s were early models of the hukou system. The xiangsui system, established under the [[Western Zhou]] dynasty ({{Circa}} 11th–8th centuries BC), was used as a method of organising and categorising urban and rural land.<ref name=":0" /> The function of the baojia system, propagated by Lord Shang Yang of the 4th century BC, was to create a system of accountability within groups of citizens: if one person within the group violated the strict rules in place, everyone in the group suffered.<ref name=":0" /> This structure was later utilized and expanded upon during the [[Qin dynasty]] (221–207 BC)<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia|url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Qin-dynasty|title=Qin dynasty {{!}} China [221-207 BC]|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia Britannica|access-date=2017-11-16|language=en}}</ref> for taxation, population control, and conscription.<ref name=":0" />

According to the ''Examination of Hukou'' in [[Wenxian Tongkao]] published in 1317, there was a minister for population management during the [[Zhou dynasty]] named Simin ({{lang-zh|c=司民|links=no}}), who was responsible for recording births, deaths, emigrations and immigrations. The [[Rites of Zhou]] notes that three copies of documents were kept in different places. The administrative divisions in the Zhou dynasty were a function of the distance to the state capital. The top division nearest the capital was named Dubi ({{lang-zh|c=都鄙|links=no}}); top divisions in more distant areas were named Xiang ({{lang-zh|c=鄉|links=no}}) and Sui ({{lang-zh|c=遂|links=no}}). Families were organized under the Baojia system.<ref>{{cite book|author=Jason Young|title=China's Hukou System: Markets, Migrants and Institutional Change|publisher=Palgrave Macmillan|page=30}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Fan Zhang|title=China's Urbanization and the World Economy|publisher=Edward Elgar Publishing|page=29}}</ref>

[[Guan Zhong]], Prime Minister of the [[Qi (state)|Qi state]] in the  7th century BC, imposed different taxation and conscription policies on different areas.<ref>[[Guanzi (text)|Guanzi]]:国门内外，都鄙井田，山泽川隰</ref> In addition, Guan Zhong also banned immigration, emigration, and separation of families without permission.<ref>[[Guanzi (text)|Guanzi]]:禁迁徙、止流民、圉分异</ref> In [[the Book of Lord Shang]], [[Shang Yang]] also described his policy restricting immigrations and emigrations.<ref>Guanzi: 禁迁徙、止流民、圉分异 chapter 2:使民无得擅徙</ref>

[[Xiao He]], the first Chancellor of the [[Han dynasty]], added the chapter of ''Hu'' ({{lang-zh|c=户律|links=no}}, "Households Code") as one of the [[Nine Chapter Law|nine basic law codes of Han]] ({{lang-zh|c=九章律|links=no}}), and established the ''hukou'' system as the basis of tax revenue and conscription.[[File:Qing China 1820.png|thumb|264x264px|Precursors to the hukou system were used during the Qing dynasty to monitor individuals and raise funds for war.]]
The first formal codification of the hukou system arose at the end of the [[Qing dynasty]] (1644–1912)<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia|url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Qing-dynasty|title=Qing dynasty {{!}} Chinese history|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia Britannica|access-date=2017-11-16|language=en}}</ref> with the 1911 Huji Law.<ref name=":0" /> Although movement was nominally free under this statute, registration of individuals with the government was required, and it was used by the government to pursue communist forces and as a basis for taxation for the funding of wars.<ref name=":0" /> The law also expanded upon the baojia system, and was intended to establish a sense of stability.<ref name=":0" />

In the period following the fall of the Qing dynasty, China was ruled by various actors, each of which employed some system of household or personal identification.<ref name=":2" /> During the Japanese occupation, the Japanese employed a system used to identify those under their rule and to fund their war effort.<ref name=":2" /> Similarly, the [[Kuomintang]] utilized the system to monitor the activities of their opponents, the Chinese Communist Party, and the Chinese Communist Party in turn used a system called lianbao, which bundled families into groups of five to aid tracking and impede counterrevolutionaries.<ref name=":2" />

=== 1949–1978: Maoist era ===
At the time of its founding in 1949, the People's Republic of China was a highly agricultural nation. About 89% of its citizens lived in rural areas – about 484 million resided in the countryside, versus about 58 million in the city.<ref name=":3">Duan, C., Gao, S., & Zhu, Y. (n.d.). The Phenomenon of Internal Migration in China. In Chinese Migration and Families-at-Risk (pp. 14-36). Cambridge Scholars Publishing.</ref> However, with efforts to increase industrialisation and Soviet help (156 projects), more and more rural residents flocked to the cities in search of better economic opportunities: between 1957 and 1960, there was a 90.9% increase in the urban labour force.<ref name=":3" />

A major objective of the hukou system implemented by the central government was thus to control the stream of resources moving away from the agricultural sector.<ref name=":0" /> According to academic Kam Wing Chan, the hukou system effectively forbade the peasantry to exit agriculture."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Kine |first=Phelim |date=December 21, 2023 |title=Enter the dragon: Here comes 2024 |work=[[Politico]] |url=https://www.politico.eu/newsletter/china-watcher/enter-the-dragon-here-comes-2024/ |access-date=December 21, 2023}}</ref> The instability and high rates of movement that characterised the years following the establishment of the nation impeded the central government's plan for society and the economy.<ref name=":0" /> Although the hukou system in its current form was not officially brought into being until 1958, the years preceding its establishment were characterised by growing efforts by the Chinese Communist Party to assert control over its populace.<ref name=":0" /> In 1950, the Minister of Public Security, [[Luo Ruiqing]], published a statement detailing his vision for the implementation of the hukou system in the new era.<ref name=":0" /> By 1954, rural and urban citizens had been registered with the state, and rigorous regulations on the conversion of hukou status had already been implemented.<ref name=":0" /> These required that applicants have paperwork that documented employment, acceptance to a university, or immediate family relations in the city to be eligible.<ref name=":0" /> In March of the same year, the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Labour issued the Joint Directive to Control Blind Influx of Peasants into Cities, which proclaimed that henceforth, all employment of rural workers in city firms would be controlled entirely by local labour bureaus.<ref name=":2" />

On 9 January 1958, the People's Republic of China Hukou Registration Regulation was signed into law.<ref name=":0" /> This divided the populace into nongmin (rural citizen), with an agricultural hukou, and shimin (urban citizen), with a non-agricultural hukou, and grouped all citizens by locality.<ref name=":0" /> The key difference, however, lay in the distinction between agricultural and non-agricultural hukou status.<ref name=":0" /> Because the central government prioritized industrialization, state welfare programs, which were tied to hukou status, heavily favored urban residents; holders of agricultural hukous were unable to access these benefits and were saddled with inferior welfare policies.<ref name=":0" /> Furthermore, transfer of hukou status was highly restricted, with official quotas at 0.15-0.2% per year and actual conversion rates at about 1.5%.<ref name=":1" /> In the following years, government oversight over the movement of people was expanded. In 1964, greater limits were imposed on migration to big cities, particularly major ones like Beijing and Shanghai, and in 1977 these regulations were furthered.<ref name=":0" /> Throughout this era, the hukou system was used as an instrument of the command economy, helping the central government implement its plan for industrialising the nation.<ref name=":0" />

=== 1978–present: Post-Mao ===
From the establishment of the People's Republic of China until [[Mao Zedong|Chairman Mao]] died in 1976, the central government tightened its control over migration, and by 1978, intranational movement was controlled entirely by the government.<ref name=":0" /> Because living "outside the system" was virtually impossible, nearly all movement of people was state-sponsored.<ref name=":0" />

However, with [[Deng Xiaoping]]'s rise to power in 1978 came the initiation of reforms that steadily began to alleviate some of the disparity between agricultural and non-agricultural hukou holders.<ref name=":2" /> Restrictions have been loosened on movement from rural areas to smaller cities, although migration to large cities such as [[Beijing]] and [[Tianjin]] is still heavily regulated.<ref name=":1" /> Greater autonomy has also been ceded to local governments in deciding quotas and eligibility criteria for converting hukou status.<ref name=":1" /> Legislation has been enacted that allow migrant workers to obtain temporary residency permits, although these permits do not allow them access to the same benefits as possessed by urban residents.<ref name=":0" /> However, with living outside the system now much more practical than it used to be, some migrant workers do not acquire the temporary residency permits – primarily because they do not have the resources or concrete employment offers to do so – and, as such, live in danger of being forced to return to the countryside.<ref name=":0" />

In 2014, the central government announced reform that among other things eliminated the division between agricultural and non-agricultural hukou status.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2025MesaLago">{{Cite book |last=Mesa-Lago |first=Carmelo |title=Comparing Socialist Approaches: Economics and Social Security in Cuba, China, and Vietnam |publisher=[[University of Pittsburgh Press]] |year=2025 |isbn=978-0-8229-4847-6 |series=Pitt Latin American Series |location=Pittsburgh, PA}}</ref>{{Rp|page=75}} Although some large cities have enacted unification, the process has been slow and according to various local policies.<ref name=":2025MesaLago" />{{Rp|page=75}}

The 2014-2020 [[National New-Type Urbanization Plan]] sought to attribute an urban hukou to 100 million people by 2020.<ref name=":22">{{Cite book |last=Froissart |first=Chloé |title=The Chinese Communist Party: a 100-Year Trajectory |date=2024 |publisher=[[ANU Press]] |isbn=978-1-76046-624-4 |editor-last=Doyon |editor-first=Jérôme |location=Canberra |chapter=Adapting the Hukou to Modernise the Country While Maintaining Social Polarisation and Stratification |editor-last2=Froissart |editor-first2=Chloé}}</ref>{{Rp|page=280}} It relaxed restrictions on small cities (fewer than 500,000 people) and medium cities (more than 1 million people).<ref name=":22" />{{Rp|page=280}} It maintained strong ''hukou'' restrictions on cities of more than 5 million inhabitants.<ref name=":22" />{{Rp|page=280}}

China established a digital social security card, which had been issued to 715 million citizens by the end of 2022.<ref name=":1232222">{{Cite book |last1=Lee|first1=John|title=The Communist Party of China: Understanding the Durability of the World's Most Powerful Political Organization|last2=Drinhausen|first2=Katja|date=2025|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|isbn=978-1-009-66843-9|editor-last=Hillman|editor-first=Ben|edition=|location=New York|chapter=Digital Power: Technological Leadership, Smart Governance, and Ideological Control|doi=10.1017/9781009668385|editor-last2=Ji|editor-first2=Fengyuan}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=227}} For migrant workers, the digital social security card facilitates their access to benefits and avoids the need to return to their place of household registration to access their benefits.<ref name=":1232222" />{{Reference page|page=227}}

== Effect on rural population ==
{{See also|Migration in China}}
[[File:Elevated Sports Field of Beijing No. 8 High School.jpg|thumb|Sports field of a high school in Beijing.]]
Under the hukou system implemented by the central government in 1958, while holders of the non-agricultural hukou status were given ration cards for everyday necessities, including food and textiles, rural residents were forced to produce everything themselves.<ref name=":0" /> Whereas the state provided housing in the city, rural individuals had to construct their own homes.<ref name=":0" />{{page needed|date=November 2024}} The state invested in [[Education in China|education]], arranged employment, and provided retirement benefits for city residents, and provided none of these services for their rural citizens.<ref name=":0" />{{page needed|date=November 2024}} These disparities have left the rural populace highly disadvantaged, and events such as the famine of the [[Great Leap Forward]] primarily affected rural Chinese citizens.<ref name=":2" />

=== Surviving the famine ===
During the [[Great Chinese Famine]] from 1958 to 1962, having an urban versus a rural hukou could mean the difference between life and death.<ref>Becker, Jasper. ''Hungry Ghosts: Mao's Secret Famine''. New York: Holt, 1998. 220-232.</ref> During this period, nearly all of the approximately 600 million rural hukou residents were collectivised into village communal farms, where their agricultural output—after state taxes—would be their only source of food. With institutionalised exaggeration of output figures by local Communist leaders and massive declines in production, state taxes during those years confiscated nearly all food in many rural communes, leading to mass starvation and the deaths of approximately 30 million Chinese people.<ref>Becker, Jasper. ''Hungry Ghosts: Mao's Secret Famine''. New York: Holt, 1998. 270.</ref>

The 100 million urban hukou residents, however, were fed by fixed food rations established by the central government, which declined to an average of 1500 calories per day at times but still allowed survival for almost all during the famine. An estimated 95% or higher of all deaths occurred among rural hukou holders. With the suppression of news internally, many city residents were not aware that mass deaths were occurring in the countryside at all. This was essential to preventing organised opposition to Mao's policies.<ref>Becker, Jasper. ''Hungry Ghosts: Mao's Secret Famine''. New York: Holt, 1998. 220.</ref>

=== Post–1978 ===
During China's transition from state socialism to market socialism (1978–2001), migrants, most of whom were women, worked in newly created export-processing zones in city suburbs under sub-standard working conditions.<ref name="TheStar">"Chinese apartheid: Migrant labourers, numbering in hundreds of millions, who have been ejected from state concerns and co-operatives since the 1980s as China instituted market capitalism, have to have six passes before they are allowed to work in provinces other than their own. In many cities, private schools for migrant labourers are routinely closed down to discourage migration." "From politics to health policies: why they're in trouble", ''[[The Star (South Africa)|The Star]]'', 6 February 2007.</ref><ref name="Whitehouse">Whitehouse, David. [https://ccs.ukzn.ac.za/files/Whitehouse%20China.pdf "Chinese workers and peasants in three phases of accumulation"], Paper delivered at the Colloquium on Economy, Society and Nature, sponsored by the Centre for Civil Society at the University of KwaZulu-Natal, 2 March 2006. Retrieved 1 August 2007.</ref> There were restrictions upon the mobility of migrant workers that forced them to live precarious lives in company dormitories or [[shanty towns]] where they were exposed to abusive treatment.<ref name="Chan">Chan, Anita. ''China's Workers Under Assault: The Exploitation of Labour in a Globalising Economy'', M.E. Sharpe, 2001, p. 9.</ref>

The impact of the ''hukou'' system upon migrant labourers became onerous in the 1980s after hundreds of millions were ejected from state corporations and cooperatives.<ref name="TheStar" /> Since the 1980s, an estimated 200 million Chinese live outside their officially registered areas and under far less eligibility for [[education]] and government services, living therefore in a condition similar in many ways to that of [[illegal aliens|illegal immigrant]]s.<ref name="rethinks" /> The millions of [[Peasant#Chinese farmers|peasants]] who have left their land remain trapped at the margins of the urban society. They are often blamed for rising crime and unemployment, and, under pressure from their citizens, the city governments have imposed discriminatory rules.<ref name="Macleod">Macleod, Calum. [https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/asia/china-reviews-apartheid-for-900m-peasants-9178285.html "China reviews `apartheid'  for 900m peasants"], ''[[The Independent]]'', 10 June 2001.</ref> For example, the children of farm workers ({{lang-zh|s=农民工|p=nóngmín gōng|links=no}}) can face restrictions on enrollment in city schools, and some live with their grandparents or other relatives to attend school in their hometowns.<ref>{{cite report |title=中国案例研究：2019冠状病毒病（COVID-19）疫情对亚洲的影响及应对分析 |publisher=UNICEF and UNESCO |date=October 2021 |page=22 |language=zh |url=https://www.unicef.cn/media/21476/file/%E4%B8%AD%E5%9B%BD%E6%A1%88%E4%BE%8B%E7%A0%94%E7%A9%B6.pdf}}</ref> They are commonly referred to as the [[Left-behind children in China|"stay-at-home" or "left-behind" children]]. There are around 130 million such left-behind children, living without their parents, as reported by Chinese researchers.<ref>"从1000万到1.3亿:农村留守儿童到底有多少", http://www.cnki.com.cn/Article/CJFD2005-QLTS200502000.htm {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210824160656/http://www.cnki.com.cn/Article/CJFD2005-QLTS200502000.htm |date=24 August 2021 }}</ref>

As rural workers provide their workforce in the urban areas, which also profit from the respective taxes, while their families use public services in the rural areas (e.g. schools for their children, health care for the elderly), the system leads to a wealth transfer to the wealthier urban regions from the poorer regions on the public sector level. Intra-family payments from the working-age members to their relatives in the rural areas counteract that to some extent.

=== Migrant workers in cities ===
[[File:Xinhui 新會 中心南路 Zhongxin Nanlu 甘蔗 三輪車 Tricycle morning.JPG|thumb|Many rural migrants find work as laborers in cities.]]
{{Main|Mingong}}

With the loosening of restrictions on migration in the 1980s came a large influx of rural residents seeking better opportunities in the cities.<ref name=":4">Maurer-Fazio, M., Connelly, R., & Tran, N. T. (2015). Negative native-place stereotypes and discriminatory wage penalties in China's migrant labour markets. In ''Handbook of Chinese Migration: Identity and Wellbeing'' (pp. 71-104). No, MA: Edward Elgar Publishing, Inc.</ref> However, these migrant workers have had to confront several challenges in their pursuit of financial security. Urban residents received priority over migrants when it came to employment opportunities, and when migrant workers did find jobs, they tended to be positions with little potential for growth.<ref>Li, C. (2013). Institutional and non-institutional paths: Migrants and non-migrants' different processes of socioeconomic status attainment in China. In China's Internal and International Migration (pp. 29-39). New York, New York: Routledge.</ref> While urban workers were supported by employment benefits and laws that favoured them over their employers in case of disputes, rural hukou holders were not privy to such substantial protections.<ref name=":4" /> And because city officials' performance was evaluated based on the prosperity of residents and the local economy, they had little incentive to improve the migrant workers' quality of life.<ref name=":4" />

In 2008, the central government passed the [[Labour Contract Law of the People's Republic of China|Labour Contract Law]], which guaranteed equal access to jobs, established a minimum wage, and required employers to provide contracts to full-time employees that included employment benefits.<ref name=":4" /> However, a 2010 study revealed that rural workers earned 40% less than urban workers, and only 16% received employment benefits.<ref name=":4" /> Migrant workers' labour rights are also frequently violated – they work excessively long hours in poor conditions, and face physical and psychological harassment.<ref name=":5">Cheng, Z., Nielsen, I., & Smyth, R. (n.d.). Determinants of Wage Arrears and Implications for the Socioeconomic Wellbeing of China's Migrant Workers: Evidence from Guangdong Province. In Handbook of Chinese Migration: Identity and Wellbeing (pp. 105-125). Edward Elgar Publishing Limited.</ref>

Migrant workers are also disproportionately affected by wage [[arrears]], which occur when employers either fail to pay employees on time or in full.<ref name=":5" /> Although such incidences are technically illegal and punishable by seven years' jail time, wage arrears still occur, and labour contracts and pensions may be disregarded.<ref name=":5" /> In a study conducted at the end of the 1990s, 46% of migrant workers were missing three or more months of pay, and some workers had not been paid in a decade.<ref name=":5" /> Fortunately, over the past couple of decades, the prevalence of wage arrears has decreased, and in a study conducted from 2006 to 2009, it was found that 8% of migrant workers had experienced wage arrears.<ref name=":5" />

=== Children of migrant workers ===
Following Mao's death in 1976 came economic reforms that caused a surge in demand in the labour market.<ref name=":6">Chen, M., & Sun, X. (n.d.). Parenting and Grandparenting of Left-Behind Children in Rural China. In Chinese Migration and Families-at-Risk (pp. 37-51). Cambridge Scholars Publishing.</ref> Rural residents rushed to fill this void, but without the support of hukou status-based government social programs, many of them were forced to leave their families behind.<ref name=":6" /> Economic growth throughout the years has maintained a high demand for labour in the cities that continues to be filled by migrant workers, and, in 2000, the Fifth National Population Census revealed that 22.9 million children between the ages of 0-14 were living without either one or both of their parents.<ref name=":6" /> In 2010, that number had gone up to 61 million, equal to 37.7% of rural children and 21.88% of all Chinese children.<ref name=":7">Gao, S., & Xue, J. (n.d.). Future Orientation and School Bonding among Left-Behind Children in Mainland China. In Chinese Migration and Families-at-Risk (pp. 78-104). Cambridge Scholars Publishing.</ref> These children are usually cared for by their remaining parent and/or their grandparents, and although there is a 96% school enrolment rate among left-behind children, they are susceptible to several developmental challenges.<ref name=":6" /> [[Left-behind children in China|Left-behind children]] are more likely to resist authority and experience problems interacting with their peers;<ref name=":6" /> they are more likely to start smoking, and have an increased likelihood of developing mental health issues, including loneliness and depression.<ref name=":7" /> And although left-behind children may have greater academic opportunities due to their parents' expanded financial capacity, they are also often under greater pressure to perform academically and thus are more vulnerable to school-related stress.<ref name=":6" />
[[File:Chinese children in Beijing.JPG|thumb|284x284px|Children who migrate with their parents face difficulties not experienced by their local counterparts.]]
Children of rural workers who do migrate with their parents also face challenges. Without a local, non-agricultural hukou, migrant children have limited access to public social infrastructure. For example, urban students' educational opportunities are far superior to those of their migrant student counterparts.<ref name=":8">Sun, X., & Chen, M. (n.d.). Inequality in Educational Opportunities of Migrant Children in China. In Chinese Migration and Families-at-Risk (pp. 52-77). Cambridge Scholars Publishing.</ref> The central government reformed the education system in 1986 and then again in 1993, yielding greater autonomy to local governments in the regulation of their education system.<ref name=":8" /> Limited space and the desire to protect local interests in turn induced local governments to avoid enrolling migrant children in their public schools.<ref name=":8" /> Furthermore, because the central government subsidised public schools based on enrolment rates of children with local hukous, migrant children were required to pay higher fees if they wanted to attend.<ref name=":8" /> Consequently, many migrant families elect instead to send their children to private schools that specifically cater to migrants.<ref name=":8" /> However, to lower enrolment and attendance fees, these institutions must cut spending in other areas, resulting in a lower quality of education.<ref name=":8" /> School facilities are often in poor condition, and many teachers are unqualified.<ref name=":8" />

In subsequent years, the central government has enacted several reforms, with limited impact. In 2001, it asserted that public schools should be the primary form of education for the nation's children, but did not specify how it would financially support schools in enrolling more migrant children, resulting in little change.<ref name=":8" />{{page needed|date=November 2024}}  Similarly, in 2003, the government called for lower fees for migrant children, but again failed to detail how it would help schools pay for this.<ref name=":8" />{{page needed|date=November 2024}} And in 2006, the government created the New Compulsory Education Act, which asserted equal rights to education and ceded responsibility for enrolling migrant children to provincial governments.<ref name=":8" />{{page needed|date=November 2024}}  However, this too failed to improve the lot of migrant children. Students with non-local hukou had to pay inflated admission fees of 3,000 – 5,000 yuan – out of an average annual household income of 10,000 yuan – and were required to take [[The National College Entrance Examination]] (''Gaokao'') at their hukou locality, where it is often harder to get into college.<ref name=":8" />{{page needed|date=November 2024}}  Since 2012, some regions began to relax the requirements and allow some children of migrants to take the College Entrance Exam in the regions. By 2016, Guangdong's policies were the most relaxed. A child of migrants can take the Entrance Exam in Guangdong if he or she has attended 3 years of high school in the province, and if the parent(s) have legal jobs and have paid for 3 years of social insurance in the province.<ref>
{{cite news |last1=Hornby |first1=Lucy |last2=Mao |first2=Sabrina |date=2012-12-30 |title=Chinese cities to relax school entry for rural migrants |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-china-migrants-education/chinese-cities-to-relax-school-entry-for-rural-migrants-idUSBRE8BT03D20121230 |location=Beijing, China}}
{{cite news |last=Jin |first=Dan |date=2016-06-07 |title=Nearly 10,000 migrant students sit for gaokao in Guangdong |url=http://www.chinadaily.com.cn/china/2016-06/07/content_25637706.htm }}
</ref>

The difficulties faced by migrant children cause many to drop out, and this is particularly common in the middle school years: in 2010, only 30% of migrant children were enrolled in secondary education.<ref name=":8" /> Migrant children also disproportionately deal with mental health issues – 36% versus 22% among their local hukou counterparts – and 70% experience academic anxiety.<ref name=":8" /> They frequently face stigmatisation and discrimination based on differences in how they dress and speak, and have difficulty interacting with other students.<ref name=":8" />

=== Impact on rural elderly ===
Not only has the mass exodus of rural residents from the countryside in search of work impacted the children of migrant workers, but it has also affected the elderly left behind. With the institution of the [[one-child policy]] in the 1970s,<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia|url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/one-child-policy|title=one-child policy {{!}} Definition & Facts|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia Britannica|access-date=2017-10-24|language=en}}</ref> the average age in China has undergone an upward shift: 82% of migrant workers were between the ages of 15–44 in 2000.<ref name=":9">Zhuo, Y., & Liang, Z. (n.d.). Migration and Wellbeing of the Elderly in Rural China. In Handbook of Chinese Migration: Identity and Wellbeing (pp. 126-147). Edward Elgar Publishing Limited.</ref> This has called into question the traditional custom of filial piety, and while retired urban workers are supported by government retirement programs, rural workers must rely on themselves and their families.<ref name=":9" /> It appears that the effects of migration on left-behind elderly are ambiguous: while parents of migrant children are often better off financially and are happy with their economic situation, they also tend to report lower life satisfaction than do elderly without migrant children.<ref name=":9" /> Like the children of migrant workers, parents are known to experience psychological issues such as depression and loneliness,<ref name=":9" /> and those who take care of their grandchildren may feel burdened by this responsibility.<ref name=":6" />

=== Reform ===
Since the commencement of the [[reform and opening up]] period in 1978, the [[People's Republic of China]] has taken steps toward reforming the hukou system by implementing a variety of reform policies. 1979-1991 can be identified as the first reform period.<ref name=":64">{{cite journal |last1=Cui |first1=Rong |last2=Cohen |first2=Jeffrey H. |title=Reform and the HuKou System in China |journal=Migration Letters |date=1 September 2015 |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=327–335 |doi=10.33182/ml.v12i3.283 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Specifically, in October 1984, the state issued "A Document on the Issue of Peasants Settling Down in Cities", which required local governments to integrate rural migrants as part of their urban population and to enable rural migrants to register in their migrant cities.<ref name=":64" /> In 1985, the state also implemented a policy called "Interim Provisions on the Management of Transient Population in Cities", which allowed rural migrants to stay in their migrant cities even if they had neither changed their hukou status nor returned to their original rural residency.<ref name=":64" /> In the same year, the state also published a document called "The Regulations on Resident Identity Card", which enabled rural migrants to work in cities even if they did not carry an identity card of urban status.<ref name=":64" /> However, what followed these policies was not only a 30 million rural-to-urban migration, but also a phenomenon in which many false urban identity cards were sold to rural migrants for gaining urban benefits.<ref name=":64" /> It hence stimulated the state to implement another policy, "A Notice on Strictly Controlling Excessive Growth of 'Urbanization,'" in 1989 for regulating rural-to-urban migration.<ref name=":64" /> Under this policy, rural migrants were monitored again.

1992–2013 can be identified as the second hukou reform period.<ref name=":64" /> There were various kinds of reform implemented by the state. Beginning in the late 1980s, one was to offer a "lan yin", or "blue stamp", hukou to those who possessed professional skills and/or ability to make some sort of investments (at least 100 million [[Renminbi|Renminbi yuan]]) in specific cities (usually the big cities such as [[Shanghai]]), allowing them to live in cities and enjoy urban welfare entitlements.<ref name=":64" /><ref name=":73">{{Cite book |last=Fan |first=C. Cindy |title=China Urbanizes: Consequences, Strategies, and Policies |publisher=The World Bank |year=2008 |editor-last=Yusuf |editor-first=Shahid |location=Washington |chapter=Migration, Hukou and the City |editor-last2=Saich |editor-first2=Tony|pages=65–89|url=https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/370371468023116682/pdf/424850PUB0ISBN101OFFICIAL0USE0ONLY1.pdf}}</ref> This "blue stamp hukou" was then conducted by many other big cities (including [[Nanjing]], [[Tianjin]], [[Guangzhou]], and [[Shenzhen]]) in 1999.<ref name=":64" /> The second kind was not applied to big cities but to certain selected towns and small cities. In 1997, the state implemented a policy that granted urban hukou to the rural migrants who had a stable job in their newly resided towns and small cities.<ref name=":73" /> Meanwhile, according to two 1997 government documents, the "Pilot Scheme for Reform of the Hukou System in Small Towns" and "Instructions on Improving the Management of Rural Hukou System", rural migrant workers could register as permanent residents with equal access to urban privileges in certain small towns.<ref name=":64" /> These policies were then made official in 2012 with the state document "Notice on Actively Yet Prudently Pushing Forward the Reform of Hukou System Management."<ref name=":64" /> Moreover, in 1999, the state also allowed more groups of people to gain urban hukou, including children whose parent(s) had urban hukou, and the elderly whose child(ren) had been granted urban hukou.<ref name=":73" /> The third kind was applied to the [[Special economic zones of China|special economic zones and districts]] that were established particularly for economic growth (such as Shenzhen). Specifically, in 1992, the state allowed all people living in the [[Special economic zones of China|special economic zones and districts]] to carry two hukous: Their original hukou and another hukou related to their job in the special zones and districts.<ref name=":64" /> This policy hence made it easier for rural migrants to gain access to different urban opportunities in the special zones and districts.<ref name=":64" /> However, in 2003, the state published the "Administrative Permit Laws", which sent rural migrants back to their original residency in rural areas.<ref name=":64" />{{failed verification|date=November 2024}}<!--No relevant occurrence of the words 'administrative permit laws' or '2003'.--> Under this policy, rural migrants' life chances were once again determined by their hukou status.

The third reform period began in 2014, when the state published and implemented the [[National New-Type Urbanization Plan]] (2014–2020) in March to tackle various problems derived from China's fast urbanization process.<ref name=":10" /> For instance, the plan aims to shorten the 17.3% gap between urban residents who live in cities but do not carry urban hukou and urban residents with urban hukou in 2012 by 2% by 2020.<ref name=":10" /> Meanwhile, the plan also intends to offer welfare entitlements to people who have rural hukou (from rural migrants to urban residents who carry rural hukou), including education, welfare housing, and health care to at least 90% (about 100 million) of migrants by 2020.<ref name=":10" /><ref name=":93">{{Cite web |last=Sheehan |first=Spencer |date=22 February 2017 |title=China's Hukou Reforms and the Urbanization Challenge |url=https://thediplomat.com/2017/02/chinas-hukou-reforms-and-the-urbanization-challenge/ |access-date=22 April 2018 |website=The Diplomat}}</ref><ref name=":122">{{Cite journal |last=Chan |first=Kam Wing |date=2014 |title=Achieving Comprehensive Hukou Reform in China |journal=Paulson Policy Memorandum}}</ref> In fact, with this plan, the state has been putting effort into achieving their goals. For instance, the state has granted many left-behind children the right to attend urban schools so that they can reunite with their rural migrant parents; it has also offered many rural migrants job training.<ref name=":64" /> Moreover, in July of the same year, the government also published "Opinions on Further Promoting the Reform of the Hukou System" to abolish the hukou restrictions in towns and small cities, to gradually remove the restrictions in middle-sized cities, to relax the restrictions in big cities—but to maintain the restrictions in the very large cities.<ref name=":122" /> As a result, according to an announcement of the Ministry of Public Security, by 2016, the state had already issued urban hukou to about 28.9 million rural migrants.<ref name=":93" /> Furthermore, in 2016, the local government of [[Beijing]] announced that they would abolish the official distinction between urban hukou and non-urban hukou within Beijing, meaning that all residents living in Beijing would be identified as Beijing residents regardless of their original hukou status.<ref>{{Cite web |last=白 |first=墨 |date=20 September 2016 |title=观察: 户籍改革里程碑 北京取消农业户口 |url=http://www.bbc.com/zhongwen/simp/china/2016/09/160920_ana_beijing_hukou_reform |access-date=26 April 2018 |website=BBC}}</ref> Having said that, in November 2017, the government of Beijing implemented a 40-day "clean-up" campaign which was claimed as a way of getting rid of the unsafe structures and shantytowns in the city (where at least 8.2 million rural migrants lived). However, some saw the campaign as intended to send millions of rural migrants back to their original rural areas.<ref name=":102">{{Cite web |last=Pabon |first=John |date=4 December 2017 |title=Beijing's Heavy-Handed Solution to Urbanization |url=https://thediplomat.com/2017/12/beijings-heavy-handed-solution-to-urbanization/ |access-date=22 April 2018 |website=The Diplomat}}</ref>

It has been brought into question whether the reforms mentioned above apply to the majority of rural-to-urban migrants. Specifically, many reform policies, especially those during the first and second periods, appear to require rural migrants to possess some sort of capital, either [[human capital]] (such as professional skills and titles) or property-related capital (such as the ability to become an urban homeowner) or both. Some scholars hence also call some reform policies as ways of "selling" hukou.<ref name=":73" /> Meanwhile, many migrants have claimed that their lack of [[social network]]s (part of what is called "[[Guanxi|guan xi]]")—which in some sense is also accumulated with [[wealth]]—also has made it harder for them to find a stable job, let alone a lucrative job.<ref name=":93" /> Hence, if wealth is a precondition to change from rural hukou to urban hukou, many rural migrants indeed are unable to gain that access, as many are "unskilled" (because many skills, such as farming, are not categorised as professional skills) and poor. However, in some large cities, even if a rural migrant does carry certain professional skills, it is not a guarantee that one will be granted urban hukou. This situation is particularly revealed from many highly educated migrants. Despite their educational background, many would not be granted urban hukou unless they become homeowners.<ref name=":112">{{Cite journal |last=Suda |first=Kimoko |date=2016 |title=A Room of One's Own: Highly Educated Migrants' Strategies for Creating a Home in Guangzhou |journal=Population, Space and Place |volume=22 |issue=2 |pages=146–157 |doi=10.1002/psp.1898}}</ref>{{page needed|date=November 2024}} However, given the high price of real estate in many large cities (such as Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou), many are unable to do so even if some cities do offer housing [[Subsidy|subsidies]] to migrants.<ref name=":93" />{{failed verification|date=November 2024}}<!--The source says it about many migrants in general, but not specifically about 'highly educated migrants', which is who the wiki text makes the claim about.--> Given their lack of urban hukou, many not only face the difficulty of purchasing an apartment—let alone purchasing a house—but also the disadvantage of being a renter. Because of the lack of rent control in many large cities, even if one rents a room—or rarely, an apartment—one can face the possibility of being asked to leave.<ref name=":112" /> Many of those educated migrant youths hence are also called "yi zu", literally "a group of ants", as many do not have their own room and have to live in a tiny room with many others.<ref>{{Cite web |title=蚁族: 在现实中找出路 |url=http://finance.ifeng.com/money/special/yizufd/ |access-date=26 April 2018 |website=凤凰财经}}</ref>

Many large cities are still strict about granting rural migrants with urban hukou and about using the hukou system to determine whether or not one should be granted welfare entitlements. Even if the "National New-type Urbanisation Plan (2014-2020)" and the "Opinions on Further Promoting the Reform of the Hukou System" implemented in the third reform period intend to create a more people-centred system, they claim that larger cities should have different hukou registration systems from the smaller cities and towns; and that the hukou regulation will continue to be stricter in larger cities.<ref name=":10" /> However, the very large cities (such as Beijing) are usually the ones that attract rural migrants the most, given their extensive job opportunities. In this case, although the state has actively implemented many reform policies, the hukou rural/urban division still functions and represents a division system of life chances. In 2008, Kam Wing Chan and Will Buckingham argued that the hukou reforms up to that point had not fundamentally changed the hukou system but had only decentralized the powers of hukou to local governments, and that it remained active and continued to contribute to China's rural and urban disparity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chan |first1=Kam Wing |last2=Buckingham |first2=Will |date=2008 |title=Is China Abolishing the Hukou System? |journal=The China Quarterly|volume=195 |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/china-quarterly/article/abs/is-china-abolishing-the-hukou-system/A5059789A06B696C455D76E2C42525B7|pages=582–606 |doi=10.1017/S0305741008000787 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Meanwhile, others have also argued that by concentrating on cities, the hukou reforms have failed to target the poorer regions, where social welfare such as education and medical care are often not offered to the residents.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Li |first=Bingqin |date=19 May 2017 |title=China Going Nowhere on Hukou Reform |url=https://asiatimes.com/article/china-going-nowhere-hukou-reform/ |access-date=25 April 2018 |website=Asia Times}}</ref> Still, others seem excited, remarking that some cities have been offering a condition that encourages more migrant parents to bring their children along.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fish |first=Eric |title=How Hukou Reform is Changing the Makeup of Chinese Factory Towns |url=https://asiasociety.org/blog/asia/how-hukou-reform-changing-makeup-chinese-factory-towns |access-date=25 April 2018 |website=[[Asia Society]]|date=19 September 2017 }}</ref> In short, the majority of rural migrants thus are still largely overlooked due to their lack to urban hukou, which is often seen as starting point for gaining access to life well-being.<ref name=":19">{{Cite book |last=Chan |first=Kam Wing |title=The Encyclopedia of Global Human Migration |publisher=Wiley-Blackwell |year=2013 |editor-last=Ness |editor-first=Immanuel |location=Hoboken |chapter=China: Internal Migration|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/book/10.1002/9781444351071|doi=10.1002/9781444351071.wbeghm124 |isbn=978-1-4443-3489-0 }}</ref>{{page needed|date=November 2024}}

In July 2024, the State Council's five-year urbanization action plan called for implementing the removal of settlement restrictions in cities with urban resident populations below 3 million, relaxing requirements in cities of 3–5 million,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Huang |first1=Tianlei |last2=Tan |first2=Yeling |date=5 September 2024 |title=Will China’s latest urbanization push work? |url=https://www.piie.com/blogs/realtime-economics/2024/will-chinas-latest-urbanization-push-work |website=Peterson Institute for International Economics |access-date=29 October 2026}}</ref> and improving points-based settlement in larger cities.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lee |first=Lizzi C. |date=August 2, 2024 |title=China Unveils Ambitious 5-Year Plan to Overhaul the Hukou System |url=https://thediplomat.com/2024/08/china-unveils-ambitious-5-year-plan-to-overhaul-the-hukou-system/ |access-date=2026-10-24 |website=[[The Diplomat (magazine)|The Diplomat]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

In May 2026, further reforms were announced by the [[State Council of China|State Council]], which stated that hukou holders can enroll in social insurance programmes in the cities where they are employed regardless of where their hukou is registered.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Chen |first=Meredith |date=2026-05-22 |title=China removes hukou hurdle for migrant workers in social insurance shake-up |url=https://www.scmp.com/news/article/3354575/china-removes-hukou-hurdle-migrant-workers-social-insurance-shake |access-date=2026-05-23 |website=[[South China Morning Post]] |language=en}}</ref> The State Council guidelines also call on the local governments to help more migrant children to attend public schools while letting those eligible to take entrance exams in the places they reside.<ref name="ReutersPublicServices2026">{{Cite news |date=22 May 2026 |title=China to expand public service access for migrant workers |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/china/china-expand-public-service-access-migrant-workers-2026-05-22/ |access-date=23 May 2026 |work=[[Reuters]]}}</ref> They additionally call for expanded access to rental housing ⁠programmes, coverage of those without local hukou with stable employment, participation of employees in social insurance programs in their workplaces, as well as easing of hukou restrictions in child care, elderly care and disability support. Additionally, the guidelines call on province-level local governments to boost fiscal support for public services in areas with population inflows.<ref name="ReutersPublicServices2026" />

=== Hukou conversion today ===
The Floating Population Dynamic Monitoring Surveys, which have been conducted every year since 2010 by the National Health and Family Planning Commission, have reported that a significant number of migrant workers are in fact not interested in converting their hukou status.<ref name=":13">{{Cite journal |last1=Chan |first1=Chuanbo |last2=Fan |first2=C. Cindy |date=October 2016 |title=China's Hukou Puzzle: Why Don't Rural Migrants Want Urban Hukou? |journal=China Review |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=9–39|jstor=43974667}}</ref> While hukou policy reform has been gradual over the years, barriers to conversion have been lowered.<ref name=":13" /> However, many rural residents are hesitant to give up their agricultural hukou status.<ref name=":13" /> As rural hukou holders, they have property rights not afforded to their urban counterparts, which allow them to use land both for agricultural production and for personal use.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tyner |first1=Adam |last2=Ren |first2=Yuan |date=2016 |title=The Hukou System, Rural Institutions, and Migrant Integration in China |journal=Journal of East Asian Studies |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=331–348 |doi=10.1017/jea.2016.18 |doi-access=free}}</ref> And with the steady expansion of cities, property values of land near cities have significantly increased.<ref name=":13" /> Owners of these tracts of land may elect to give up agriculture in favour of renting out their homes to migrant workers.<ref name=":13" /> Furthermore, with the continued process of urbanization, land owners near cities can expect the central government to buy their land for a handsome sum sometime in the future.<ref name=":13" /> These benefits combined with the overall improvement in rural social welfare relative to that in cities have caused many rural residents to hesitate in converting their hukou status.<ref name=":13" />

==Special administrative regions of China==
{{see also|Special administrative regions of China}}
Hukou is not employed in the [[special administrative regions of China]] ([[Hong Kong]] and [[Macau]]) though identification cards are mandatory for residents there.<ref>"China Law Deskbook: A Legal Guide for Foreign-invested Enterprises, Volume 1", by James M. Zimmerman, p. 406, publisher = American Bar Association, year = 2010</ref> Instead, both SARs grant [[right of abode]] to certain persons who are allowed to reside permanently in the regions.

When a person with household registration in mainland China is settling in [[Hong Kong]] or [[Macau]] by means of a [[People's Republic of China Permit for Proceeding to Hong Kong and Macao|One-way Permit]], they must relinquish their household registration, therefore losing citizen rights in mainland China. However, they need to settle in the SARs for seven years to be eligible for permanent resident status (which is associated with citizen rights) in the SARs. Therefore, in the period before they get permanent resident status, though still a [[Chinese nationality law|Chinese citizen]], they cannot exercise citizen rights anywhere (like voting in elections, getting a passport) and are considered [[second-class citizen]]s.

==Cross-strait relations==
{{see also|Cross-Strait relations|Household registration in Taiwan}}
The [[Government of China|People's Republic of China (Mainland China)]] and the [[Government of the Republic of China|Republic of China (Taiwan)]] each claim the territories under the other's control as part of their respective state. Thus, legally, each treats the people on the other side's territory as their citizens. However, citizenship rights are only available to the people under their own control respectively; this is defined by law as holding household registration in [[Taiwan Area]] (in the [[Taiwan|Republic of China]]) or in [[Mainland China|Mainland Area]] (in the People's Republic of [[China]]).

The [[Government of the Republic of China]] (ROC) considers ethnic [[overseas Chinese]] and [[Taiwanese diaspora|Taiwanese]] born to at least one ROC parent as its [[Taiwanese nationality law|nationals]], and issues [[Taiwan passport]]s to them. However, this does not grant them the [[right of abode]] or any other citizen rights in Taiwan; those rights require household registration in Taiwan. Persons [[national without household registration|without household registration]] are subject to immigration control in Taiwan, but after they settle in Taiwan they can establish a household registration there to become a full citizen.
